threads.answer:
Hello Mr
Thank you for your email to Director
We reviewed the information presented to the International Mobility Worker Unit in Montreal. From our view, it appears that the foreign nationals do not meet the requirements of the business visitors category under R187(2) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR).
When a Canadian employer has directly contracted services from a foreign company, the employee of the foreign company performing the services for the Canadian company is entering the labour market and requires a work permit and Labour Market Impact Assessment.
It appears that the foreign nationals in this scenario are coming to Canada to collect information from the Canadian company. The data collection activity meets the definition of work as per the IRPR since it is part of the consulting services they are providing. Without collecting information, the foreign nationals will not be able to fulfil their contractual obligations.
In addition, since the foreign employer is receiving payment for the service that is being provided from a Canadian company, it is deemed that the foreign worker's principal source of remuneration is from a Canadian source. Therefore, the recommendation would be for the foreign nationals to seek a Labour Market Impact Assessment from ESDC.
Trusting this information is of assistance.
Best regards,

threads.answer:
Dear Ms
Our sincere apologies for not responding sooner.
Question:
Would the C16 exemption still apply in the event that a French-speaking foreign national decides to apply for a new work permit prior to the expiry of his current IEC Work Permit (working holiday WP, allowed to work for any employer, anywhere in Canada) based on the offer of employment from his current Canadian employer in BC. If the FN is already working for the company that is located outside of the Province of Quebec (BC, in this case) in the job of NOC skill level A and the company would like to continue to utilize his services, would C16 exemption still apply in this case, or would the employer need to file for the LMIA since the FN hadn't been recruited via the Francophone immigration promotional event? Response:
We are working on clarifying the requirement under the Mobilité Francophone exemption to have been recruited through a Francophone immigration promotional event coordinated between the federal government and Francophone minority communities.
There are a myriad of ways that an applicant could demonstrate that they meet this criterion. For example, if the applicant has been in communication with the Canadian embassy regarding immigration issues; has requested information from the embassy; has had discussions by email with the embassy regarding his or her situation and plans; participated in a recruitment or promotional event; or has attended an information session online or in person, it could be deemed that he/she qualifies for the C16 exemption.
Please note that foreign nationals cannot make an initial work permit application under this exemption from inside Canada. Initial work permit applications must be submitted online or via a visa application centre overseas.
I hope this answers your question.

threads.subject: how to prevent PR card renewal erroneously sent residence questionnaire-REP-2017-0066-
threads.question:
How can I have a decision about sending a residence questionnaire reviewed? and how can I prevent it in the future in similar such cases? My client meets the physical presence requirement SOLELY because he has employed abroad by Canadian employer during every day of his absence from Canada. We included with the application full proof of that showing that on his travel days abroad, ALL were in course of employment of Canadian employer. It included a letter from the employer confirming the employment abroad for the Canadian employer, T4s from the employer for each of the 5 years, and Canadian tax returns for those years, all showing the employment income from the Canadian employer. In OB 536, it says
and Cizenship Canadaot Citoyenneté Canada
L'nmndmion When a local CIC office receives a referral from PRCC Sydney, the application is assessed to determine whether additional information is required. When there is insufficient information, applicants are required to complete the Questionnaire: Determination of Permanent Residency Status [IMMB 5511], a supplementary absences form, as well as submit any additional supporting documents. Since the ONLY reason my client qualifies for the PR card renewal is due to this employment, and documentation of that employment was clearly included in the original application, there is NO reason why a residence questionnaire should have been sent to him. There is no additional information which could be provided in response to the questionnaire which would shed any light on whether it is approvable. There is not one question on the questionnaire that was not already answered in the original application package. This puts the application into an indefinite black hole. Moreover, it will be a complete waste of time for the official reviewing it to review the questionnaire response as it contains the exact same information as the original application and again CLEARLY says and shows that the only reason for the qualification is due to this employment. Moreover the employer (and the applicant) are well known in the Province ofNova Scotia, and the application was sent to Halifax. The employment abroad could have been easily confirmed with one phone call to the Canadian employer. How can I get the decision to send the questionnaire reviewed by a supervisor? I am about to send another application based on the applicant's time outside of Canada with his Canadian citizen spouse. How can I be sure that it, too won't be sent into a black hole with a residence questionnaire when we provide full documentation up front?
threads.answer:
Good afternoon,
In response to your inquiry,
Please be aware that the OB 536 is currently being revised. An OB provides general guidance on procedures, and it is not equivalent/does not supersede the law.
A questionnaire can be sent in order to clarify information previously provided as per R56 (in particular if not all days were accounted for in past 5 years when application was filled out, etc.), and this is also to ensure a certain due diligence in that even though the applicant states having respected residency for having worked overseas for a Canadian business, the officer can still look at the physical residency. That way, the officer is looking at “all the possible ways" the applicant could show he/she respected his/her residency obligation –this is to his/her advantage. The request for the questionnaire should not be interpreted as the officer wrongfully looking or focusing solely on physical residency (whereby the applicant stated that he has respected the residency obligation on the basis of having worked overseas for a Canadian business), it is meant to be able to thoroughly “examine all the possible ways" he could show that he/she meets A28. A16(1) states that: "A person who makes an application must answer truthfully all questions put to them for the purpose of the examination and must produce [..] all relevant evidence and documents that the officer reasonably requires". We would therefore recommend the applicant to provide what is requested, but failure to do so would not necessarily mean that the card would be refused, but rather that the officer will base his/her decision on the information available.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Changes to Job Offer/Employer Compliance Portal-REP-2017-0059-
threads.question:
Please advise on the circumstances that give rise to a requirement to amend a filed Job Offer through the Employer Compliance Portal. For instance, if a US national is in Canada on an Intra-company transferee and their physical location of employment changes does this require that we file a new Job Offer and pay and additional $230?
What if it were that same individual who changes job duties sufficient that it would put them into a new NOC Code. Is a new Job Offer and $230 fees required then? If so, please advise how one would go about doing this?
Page 1025
is withheld pursuant to section est retenue en vertu de l'article
of the Access to Information Act de la Loi sur l'acces a l'information
threads.answer:
Tc
Good day,
Q1: If a US national is in Canada on an Intra-company transferee and their physical location of employment changes does this require that we file a new Job Offer and pay and additional $230?
Response:
In the case of an employer-specific LMIA-exempt work permit, there are two different sets of conditions involved – those imposed on the employer based on the Offer of Employment, and those imposed on the worker as per the work permit.
Employer conditions: location'is normally considered as part of the condition that the employer must provide the 'same working conditions.' The change in work location can't be less favourable to the employee. In addition, the location can't be changed if the location was part of the LMlA-exemption requirement/justification (e.g. provincial nominees). IRCC does not require proactive notification of changes, but it is required that the employer maintain any documentation regarding the changes and provide it as justification at time of inspection. Employers who believe that they are not meeting conditions can use the Voluntary Disclosure process.
Worker conditions: the foreign national may have specific conditions imposed on them with the work permit. These conditions may include 'not authorized to work at any other location'. If this condition is imposed and a specific location is specified then the worker would need a new work permit (including a new offer of employment in case of an LMIA-exempt work permit) in order to change locations.
Therefore, if the foreign worker's work permit conditions change, they will be required to apply for a new Change of conditions work permit, and the Canadian employer will need to submit a new Offer of Employment on-line through the employer portal and pay a new employer compliance fee of $230.00 CAD. If the foreign worker's work permit was not issued under any conditions of location, then they may not need to apply for a new work permit.
Q2: What if it were that same individual who changes job duties sufficient that it would put them into a new NOC Code. Is a new Job Offer and $230 fees required then? If so, please advise how one would go about doing this?
Response:
Yes, if the job duties change to the extent that they are now doing a different job than was stated on the work permit, then a new Offer of Employment will need to be submitted to IRCC and the foreign worker will need to apply for a new work permit.
Employers must comply with the elements stated in the Offer of Employment information provided to IRCC. If an employer becomes the subject of an employer compliance inspection (random or otherwise), they will be assessed on the basis of the Offer of Employment under which the work permit was issued, and any substantial change from the Offer of Employment must be justified as per subsection 203(1.1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection
Cioyenneté Canada
Regulations (IRPR). As per the IRPR regulations, the employer is required to retain all documents related to the foreign worker for up to six years after the date of issuance of the work permit, including details about the job change, to ensure information can be provided to an IRCC officer in the event of an inspection. Employers who believe that they are not meeting conditions can use the Voluntary Disclosure process.
A work permit is issued for a specific occupation and the foreign national, as stated in Q1, is required to meet the conditions of the work permit. The foreign worker must receive a new Offer of Employment and work permit prior to the implementation of the change, otherwise they are working in violation of the work authorization issued, and they must stop working until the new work permit based on the new NOC is issued. If a new work permit for the job change has not been previously approved and the temporary foreign worker is found to be working in an occupation other than what was stated on the Offer of Employment, this may constitute non-compliance by the employer.
Furthermore, in regard to intra-company transferees (ICT), this category allows the transfer of certain employees to Canada from qualifying foreign entities for temporary periods. To be eligible in this category, the foreign employee must be employed by a foreign entity and be transferred to a position with the Canadian entity in an executive, senior managerial or specialized knowledge capacity. This requires a qualifying corporate relationship between the foreign and Canadian entity. The worker's employment conditions, i.e. wage, tasks, location, change, then the ICT is obligated to obtain a new work permit in order to work legally in Canada.
Also, if the qualifying relationship ceased to exist, OR if the elements of the original Offer of Employment changed in terms of location, wages, occupation/Noc, job duties, then a new work permit would be required, and possibly an LMIA (if the job position no longer fit the eligibility criteria of an LMIA exempt position, i.e. intra-company transferee). Otherwise, if the new position continued to be LMIA-exempt, the employer could submit the new Offer of Employment through the Employer Portal under the International Mobility Program, and with the LMlA-exemption number (A######) generated from that submission, the foreign worker would need to apply for a new work permit.
For more information, see the section "Occupation, Wages and Working Conditions" in the Employer Compliance Inspections page on the IRCC website.
IRCC provides instructions to assist employers in providing accurate information when submitting the Offer of
Employment in the Employer Portal User Guide.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Dependent child?-REP-2017-0101-
threads.question:
Dear Officer,
My client, a Canadian citizen wants to sponsor her mother (the Applicant). My client will not sponsor her father. The Applicant's husband (my client's father) recently had a child with another woman while still married to the Applicant. The couple are now separated, although still married. The Applicant has no relationship with this child. Is this child considered a family member of the Applicant?
Obviously this will impact the family size and LICO that my client would have to meet for a parental sponsorship.
Thank you,
and Cizenship Canedaot Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Good day, Since this request does not indicate whether the client's mother and father are already divorced or separated, this response includes scenarios in which they are still legally married and in which they are already separated or divorced. This is general guidance only; this is not case-specific, and this application will be assessed by one of our officers when received based upon the information provided.
1. The Application
If the client's mother and father are still legally married, then the principal applicant who is being sponsored as a member of the family class -who is the mother in this case -must include in the application her spouse and any dependent children of the principal applicant and those of the spouse or common-law partner, irrespective of whether they are accompanying her. All these family members, whether accompanying or not accompanying the principal applicant to Canada, must be examined in addition to being declared on the application. If family members are not examined, it is generally not possible to sponsor them at a later date. Failure to declare family members on the application and failure to having them examined goes against the duty to provide truthful and accurate information, and may cause them to be found inadmissible to Canada. However, note that if the mother and father are separated or divorced, or if they have commenced divorce proceedings, then the father does not need to be examined as he would not be considered to be a dependant of the mother, and the
dependent child referred to above should not be included in the application as a dependant.
2. LICO
If the intention is for the mother alone to immigrate to Canada and the father is not included on the application due to divorce or separation, neither the father nor the dependent child will need to be considered in terms of LiCO.

Any period of employment during which time the foreign national was engaged in full-time study will not be included in calculating work experience under the Canadian Experience Class (CEC), nor will it count for the purposes of points assigned under the Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS). Question:
I am seeking your guidance regarding the process that should be followed in a situation where the employer company ("Company A") of an individual who holds an lEC Young Professional based work permit will soon be acquired by another company (“Company B”). Upon completion of the acquisition, Company A will cease to operate, and Company B will assume all of Company A's interests, obligations, assets and liabilities.

Response:
Please see Guide to Corporate Mergers and Acquisitions [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/work/mergers.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/work/mergers.asp)
The new employer–Company B - (i.e., the surviving entity in the case of a merger or the new employer in the case of an acquisition) assumes all of the assets and liabilities of Company A’s entities. If Company B is the successor of interest and operates the same type of business as Company A, and if the conditions of the work permit have not changed, i.e. if the worker's employment conditions, including wage, tasks, location, etc, remain unchanged, then, the foreign worker is not obligated to obtain a new work permit and can continue to work legally in Canada for the duration of the period stated on the work permit. Neither does the new employer (Company B) need to submit a new offer of employment to IRCC – until Company B wishes to extend the foreign worker's work permit.
The new employer (Company B) assumes all liabilities associated with the conditions under subparagraph R209.2(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), for the Offer of Employment whereby the foreign worker was issued the work permit. Those conditions include:
- providing a workplace that is free from abuse
- complying with Canadian federal and provincial labour laws
- remaining active during the work permit period, and
- ensuring that working conditions and occupation comply with the original offer of employment (as submitted to IRCC).
Note that Company A is responsible for these conditions until the date the merger takes effect.
Generally, any substantial change from the Offer of Employment must be justified as per subsection 203(1.1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR).
Both employers should keep all documents related to the title change to ensure they can be provided if inspected.

threads.answer:
Dear Mr We apologize for the delay in our response. Question: Can a foreign national who is a member of the SCLPC class apply for a SCLPC work permit at a port of entry? Response: Although there is no legislative impediment to an applicant under the SCLPC class applying for an open work permit under the One Year pilot at a port-of-entry, this is not a service prescribed in the pilot. At a port-of-entry, every case will be examined on its own merits, including a thorough assessment of the reasons for the applicant's absence from Canada and whether they continue to meet SCLPC requirements.
To be eligible for an open work permit, the applicant must be a spouse or common-law partner living in Canada who is being sponsored under the SCLPC class. They must have valid temporary resident status (as a visitor, student or worker) and live at the same address as their sponsor.
If they have already submitted an application for permanent residence but have not yet received approval in principle under the SCLPC class or have not yet applied for an open work permit, they can complete the work permit application. Send their completed application, along with appropriate fee, to the Case Processing Centre in Vegreville at:
CPC-Vegreville WP -Unit 777 6212–55 Avenue Vegreville, AB T9C 1X6
If they have already received approval in principle on their permanent residence application—meaning they received a letter from stating they meet the permanent residence eligibility requirements but have not yet passed the medical, security and background checks—they may apply for an open work permit online.
If they were provided with a work permit under the initial pilot, they must apply for a work permit extension before it expires.

Hi,
Please could you assist with a question about when a Police Certificate is required under the new spousal sponsorship program. Under the Basic Guide 5525, it provides that a Police Certificate is required for the country where you currently live and the country where you have spent most of your adult life since the age of 18.
Since she turned 18, my client has spent 6 years in her country of citizenship (the USA), 5 years in China and 3 years in Taiwan. Can you please confirm that this means she only requires a Police Clearance from the USA?

threads.answer:
Good afternoon,
Thank you for consulting with us with your inquiry regarding the submission of police certificates under Immigration, Refugee 's spousal sponsorship program.
As with all applications for Permanent Residence, applicants under the Spousal Sponsorship program must satisfy an officer that they are not criminally inadmissible under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.
In this context, the normal and ordinary meaning applies to "the largest part of the applicant's adult life". We refer to the place where the individual has spent the greatest/largest part of their life, since the age of 18. From the information you provided us, the applicant has lived the longest in the USA and is currently living in the USA. As such, the applicant would initially need only submit a police certificate from the USA (the country they currently reside and the country in which they have spent most of their adult life). Based on the information provided, a police certificate from both China and Taiwan would not be expected at the initial stage of processing.
An IRCC officer however, at his or her own discretion, may request that the applicant provide a police certificate from China and or Taiwan in order to be satisfied that the applicant is not criminally inadmissible.
If the applicant, while preparing their application, has already obtained the police certificates from other countries in which they have spent a total of six months or more, they may wish to submit these certificates at the same time as the one from the USA. This could save time later in processing if the police certificates are requested by the IRCC officer.
We trust that this information will be useful to you.

Whether it is a foreign national employed by a foreign enterprise that was contracted to provide service to a Canadian enterprise, or a foreign national directly hired by a Canadian enterprise, for the purposes of the Immigration and Refugees Protection Act and Regulations, IRCC and under the requirements of the IMP, the Canadian company that has contracted the services of a foreign national or a foreign company is the primary employer (in Canada) and must complete and submit the offer of employment through the Employer Portal before the foreign national makes an application for a work permit.
Although the foreign national may often be -and remain -a direct-hire employee of the foreign company, and the foreign company may pay the wages of the foreign national, it is the Canadian company that is creating the need for the foreign national to enter Canada. threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for your inquiry.
Please note that visa-exempt foreign nationals to whom a Visitor Record (VR) has been issued are not automatically issued an eTA. This currently only applies to initial work and study permits issued on or after August 1, 2015.
IRCC's eTA check status tool allows clients to verify the status of their eTA by inputting their initial work permit or study permit number that was issued at the POE or at an overseas visa office, along with specific passport information. In the case where a visitor record number is inputted in the tool, it will provide the status of the visitor record rather than an
eTA indicator. We are currently working to amend this tool to eliminate this confusion.
A VR gives status to the holder, which allows them to stay in Canada under the condition set out on the VR, whereas an eTA allows visa-exempt foreign nationals to board their flight to Canada. Visa-exempt foreign nationals who have been issued a VR at a visa office will require to apply for an eTA separately. If a visa-exempt foreign national were issued a Visitor Record on arrival to Canada, presumably, they would have had an eTA to travel to Canada in the first place. If not, though, and if they wish to leave and re-enter Canada by air on or after September 30, 2016, they will need to apply for an eTA at www.Canada.ca/eTA.
Sincere regards,

threads.subject: ICCRC#:Inquiry regarding Express Entry-REP-2017-0052-
threads.question:
et Cioyenneté Canada
I have a client whose bridging work permit was based on an initial LMIA work permit. The original work permit had expired while the processing of his CEC file was still active and he obtained the open bridging work permit. The client has now switched employers and is no longer working for the employer on his LMIA work permit. My question: for Express Entry purposes, is he considered to still have an offer of Arranged Employment (since he is still working full time another employer in the same skilled capacity)? Or does the fact that he has switched employers exclude him for obtaining the points for having arranged employment? Thank you,
Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Hello Mrs
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Section 29(2) of the Express Entry Ministerial Instructions specifies that a qualifying offer of employment is one of the following:
- (a) an arranged employment as defined in subsection 82(1) of the Regulations, if o(i) the offer is supported by a valid assessment — provided by the Department of Employment and Social Development at the request of the employer or an officer and on the same basis as an assessment provided for the issuance of a work permit — that the requirements set out in subsection 203(1) of the Regulations with respect to the offer have been met, o(ii) the foreign national holds a valid work permit, the offer of employment is made by an employer for whom the foreign national currently works and who is specified on the work permit, the work permit was issued based on a positive determination made by an officer under subsection 203(1) of the Regulations with respect to the foreign national's employment with that employer in an occupation that is listed in Skill Type 0 Management Occupations or Skill Level A or B of the National Occupational Classification matrix and the assessment provided by the Department of Employment and Social Development on the basis of which the determination was made is not suspended or revoked, or o (iii) the foreign national holds a valid work permit issued under the circumstances described in paragraph 204(a) or (c) or section 205 of the Regulations, the offer is made by an employer who is specified on the work permit and the foreign national works for that employer and has accumulated at least one year of full-time work experience, or the equivalent in part-time work, over a continuous period of work for that employer
Per 29(2)(a)(ii), the foreign national must be currently working for the employer specified on the work permit that was issued based on the LMlA. Therefore, in the scenario described below, your client does not appear to have a qualifying offer
of arranged employment and would not get assigned the CRS points for arranged employment.
We trust this information will assist you.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Canadian educational credentials 30 (1) The points that are to be assigned for a Canadian educational credential are the following: •(a) O points, if the foreign national has a secondary school educational credential;
- (b) 15 points, if the foreign national has an eligible credential from a one-year or two-year post-secondary program; and

In order to be eligible under the federal skilled trades program, Express Entry candidates must meet the minimum requirements below.
Minimum requirements
To be eligible, you must:
- meet the required levels in English or French for each language ability (speaking, reading, writing and listening),
- have at least two years of full-time work experience (or an equal amount of part-time work experience) in a skilled trade within the five years before you apply,

- have an offer of full-time employment for a total period of at least one year or a certificate of qualification in that skilled trade issued by a Canadian provincial or territorial authority.

threads.answer:
Good day Mr.
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Note that the LMIA-exemptions specific to R204(a) or (c) and R205 covered in the Ministerial Instructions and senior executive points level are two separate factors.

Express Entry is a competitive system that actively and purposefully issues invitations only to the candidates who are best positioned for economic success in Canada. Because invitations are issued on a 'top down basis, elevating candidates with lower levels of human capital (by providing higher levels of points for arranged employment) necessarily results in fewer invitations to candidates with higher levels of human capital. Dear
Thank you for your question on implied status. Thank you for your patience while we consulted on the response. Please see below.
Question: Can the individual continue working under implied status until a decision is made on the open work permit application?
Response:
Regulation 201 allows foreign nationals to apply for a renewal of their work permit only if the application is made before their work permit expires. Regulation 186(u) allows foreign nationals to work without a work permit if they continue to comply with the conditions set out on the expired work permit, have not left Canada, and a decision on the renewal of their application has not yet been made. R183(6) requires that they continue to meet the conditions that were in place when the application for extension was submitted.
A temporary resident who holds a valid work permit and submits an application in Canada for another work permit is considered to be 'renewing.'A renewal of a work permit can be for a new employer, same employer or an open work permit.
For example, an International Experience Canada participant who nearly reached the validity period of their 24-months working holiday open work permit and received an offer of employment from a new employer to work in a different LMIA exemption. If the foreign national applied for a new work permit before their lEC open work permit expires, they may continue working without a permit but under the conditions of their previous valid work permit (e.g., open employer, open occupation) until the decision is made on the renewal application and the new work permit issued. Also, if a foreign national held an employer-specific work permit at the time of the renewal application, they may continue working with the same employer until a decision is made on their new application. They may not work for the new employer while on implied status as that would be a different condition.
I trust this information will be of assistance.
Regards,
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Good day,
An Offer of Employment (OOE) cannot be withdrawn once a work permit has been issued based on that same OOE. Typically, any substantial change from the Offer of Employment must be justified as per subsection 203(1.1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). An officer may find that a change in an employee contract that increases the salary is justified under R203(1.1) in that it is similar to a change in the provisions of a collective agreement. In addition, an increase in wages may result in a finding that the employer did not provide "substantially the same" wages if the increase would have affected the ability of the foreign national to qualify for the LMIA-exemption.
In cases where the employer has promoted or otherwise changed the foreign worker's duties, the foreign worker must receive a new Offer of Employment and work permit prior to implementing the change.
Amongst other conditions, foreign workers are also subject to other federal (such as ESDC who leads the Temporary Foreign
Workers Program) and provincial or territorial legislative and regulatory requirements. Employers should meet those
requirements for compliance purposes.
For ease of reference, we are including certain sections of IRCC publications and manuals on Employer compliance inspections: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/work/permit/compliance.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/work/permit/compliance.asp)
Wages
"Substantially the same – but not less favourable – wages" means that
wages paid cannot be less than those outlined in the Offer of Employment provided as per R209.11; any unusual deductions (such as recovery of the employer compliance fee, transportation costs) should be stated in the Offer of Employment.
The offer of employment requires input of hourly wages in Canadian dollars. Foreign workers can be paid in Canadian currency or in another legal currency, so long as the foreign worker is paid the Canadian equivalent wage stated in the Offer of Employment throughout the period of employment. The foreign currency must be noted in the Offer of Employment information.
Wages paid in a foreign currency must be verified at the time of the work permit application to ensure they observe the minimum provincial or territorial wage laws.
Amongst the scenarios provided in your request, the following ones would require a new Offer of Employment in order for the foreign worker to apply for a new work permit as it not substantially the same than the original offer. It would rather be considered as less than favourable than the original offer:
Original Offer of Employment indicates that they would be paid in foreign currency and subsequently the company localizes the employee and places them on Canadian payroll: typically, any substantial change from the Offer of Employment must be justified as per subsection 203(1.1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). An officer may find that a change in an employee contract that increases the salary is justified under R203(1.1) in that it is similar to a change in the provisions of a collective agreement. In addition, an increase in wages may result in a finding that the employer did not provide "substantially the same" wages if the increase would have affected the ability of the foreign national to qualify for the LMIA-exemption. Original Offer of Employment indicates 10 hours per day and subsequently the foreign worker is moved to an 8 hour work day-which impacts the original wage/salary: a reduction of hours are considered to be less than favourable than initially outlined in the OOE. Original Offer of Employment indicates the foreign worker will be paid in foreign currency and will receive annual Cost of Living Allowance. Subsequently, the Cost of Living Allowance fluctuates downward, resulting in what may appear to be a lesser salary: a reduction of the salary is also considered less favourable than initially outlined in the OOE.
For the remaining scenarios, it would not be required to notify IRCC of changes in the work conditions as it is substantially the same and not less favourable than the original offer:
Original Offer of Employment indicates that no overtime is payable and subsequently the business decides to compensate for overtime Original Offer of Employment does not stipulate benefits and subsequently the employer provides benefits
Employers who believe that they are not meeting conditions can use the Voluntary Disclosure process: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/work/employers/hire-after.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/work/employers/hire-after.asp)
We trust this information is helpful.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Bonjour
Nous sommes désolés du délai dans notre réponse.
Questions:
1. Doit-on faire une modification en envoyant une nouvelle offre d’emploi en indiquant que cette nouvelle offre d’emploi est associé à tel permis de travail?
2.Refaire une modification en envoyant une offre d’emploi lorsqu’il revient au salaire initial de l’offre d’emploi en indiquant que cette nouvelle offre d’emploi est associé à tel permis de travail?
3.Faire une nouvelle offre d’emploi à chaque fois qu’il y a un changement dans le salaire et un nouveau permis de travail?
4. Envoyer un courriel pour signifier ce changement en utilisant la boîte au lettre du portail de l’employeur?
5. Ne pas faire de démarches, puisque l’employeur fournit au ressortissant étranger un emploi qui est dans la même profession que celle précisée dans l’offre d’emploi et dont le salaire et les conditions de travail sont essentiellement les mêmes – mais non moins avantageux- que ceux précisés dans l’offre?
Réponse : En général, tout changement substantiel à l’offre d’emploi doit être justifié en vertu du paragraphe 203(1.1) des Règlements sur l’immigration et la protection des réfugiés (RIPR). Un agent peut trouver qu’un changement dans le contrat de l’employé augmentant son salaire est justifié sous R203(1.1) en ce sens que c’est similaire à un changement dans les dispositions d’une convention collective. De plus, une augmentation de salaire peut mener à la conclusion que l’employeur n’a pas fourni “ substantiellement le même" salaire si l’augmentation pourrait affecter l’habilité de l’étranger à se qualifier pour une dispense de l’étude d’impact sur le marché du travail (EIMT).
Dans les cas où l’employeur a promu ou modifié les tâches du travailleur étranger, le travailleur étranger doit recevoir une nouvelle offre d’emploi et un permis de travail avant que le changement de tâches ne soit effectif.
Veuillez prendre note que la divulgation proactive d’un changement de salaire n’est pas requise sous le Programme de mobilité internationale. Cependant, cette information peut être demandée avec une justification pour le changement de salaire lorsque le travailleur étranger dépose une demande de prolongation de son permis de travail ou lorsqu’un nouveau travailleur étranger dépose une demande de permis de travail pour le même employeur.
Regards,

Question:
Could you please clarify whether or not a spouse with an open work permit as described above can continue to work and use their open work permit, regardless of whether or not their spouse meets the original conditions of their stay in Canada (i.e. they are no longer a student or a temporary foreign worker)?
Answer:
Spouses or common-law partners of full-time students or temporary foreign workers (TFW) (Labour Market Impact
Assessment exemption code C41 and C42) can continue work even if the study permit holder is no longer studying or the TFW is no longer working as long as their open work permits remain valid. Once the open work permit has expired, the spouse or common law-partner of the full-time student/TFW will not be able to renew their open work permit under exemption code C41 or C42 since the conditions on which the work permit was issued to the spouse/common-law partner are no longer valid.
The spouse or common-law partner may be eligible to apply under a different program if they would like to continue working in Canada. Please note the spouse or common-law partner would have to apply for their new work permit before the open work permit expires.

threads.subject: eTA when a TRP is issued-REP-2017-0071
threads.question:
Hello,
What is the policy or procedures for an individual who holds a valid Work Permit and Temporary Resident Permit, but was denied an eTA due to criminality? Does the TRP negate the requirements for an eTA? If not, how does one obtain an eTA
when they have criminality, but also hold a TRP?
Page 1291
is withheld pursuant to section est retenue en vertu de l'article

and Cizenship Canedaot Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for your email.
Visa-exempt foreign nationals who have been issued a temporary resident permit (TRP) are not authorized to hold an eTA, as they have been found to be inadmissible to enter Canada.
Visa-exempt foreign nationals who have been issued a TRP by an overseas office to permit travel to Canada will be able to board a plane to Canada, so long as their TRP document remains valid and they have the appropriate travel document (e.g. a passport) in their possession. eTA's are not issued alongside a TRP.
A traveller issued a TRP at a port of entry does not require an eTA to enter Canada. An individual in possession of a TRP and who is in Canada can remain in Canada under the condition described in the TRP.

threads.subject: Durée des offres d'emploi dans le Portail des employeurs-REP-2017-0105-
threads.question:
Bonjour,
Puisqu’il n’y a plus de limite quant à la durée des permis de travail, cela signifie-t-il que les employeurs, eux aussi, ne sont plus limités quant à la durée des offres d’emploi dispensées d’EIMT et soumises dans le Portail des employeurs d’IRCC?
À titre d’exemple, nous nous apprêtons à soumettre une offre d’emploi pour un professeur titulaire d’une Chaire de recherche du Canada. La Chaire dure 7 ans. Il est dispensé d’EIMT car il s’agit d’une Chaire canadienne.
Pouvons-nous soumettre une offre pour 7 ans?
Merci,
Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Bonjour,
Question:
Pouvons-nous soumettre une offre pour 7 ans?
Réponse:
De façon générale, plus le séjour temporaire est long, plus la personne devra fournir la preuve du caractère temporaire de son séjour au moment de présenter sa demande de permis de travail ou de prorogation.
Quant à la durée de l’offre d’emploi, il faut prendre les facteurs ci-dessous en considération :
- La durée de validité du passeport en vertu du paragraphe R52(1) : l’agent ne délivrera pas un permis de travail ni n’accordera le statut de travailleur temporaire pour une durée de validité supérieure à celle du passeport. Des exceptions s’appliquent en vertu du paragraphe R52(2). Une exception supplémentaire s’applique aux permis de travail délivrés aux personnes qui n’ont pas le statut de résident temporaire [R202];
- L’étude d'impact sur le marché du travail (EIMT) (sujet à la validité du passeport, l’agent doit délivrer le permis de travail pour la durée complète de l’EIMT en tenant compte de la durée de validité du CAQ, selon le cas);
- La durée maximale accordée par un programme ou accord particulier auquel l’intéressé participe. Certains programmes et accords limitent la durée de validité initiale, la durée des prorogations ou la durée totale d’emploi au Canada.
Il faut noter que dans tous les cas, l’étranger doit démontrer, à la satisfaction de l’agent, qu’il quittera le Canada à la fin de la période de séjour.
Cordialement,
La boîte aux lettres des représentants en immigration

For the purpose of assessing an Express Entry application under section A11.2 both for the purposes for CRS points and for the purpose of points in the FSW points grid, a qualifying job offer must be valid at the time the invitation to apply (ITA) is issued and must continue to be valid to the point of visa issuance.

threads.answer:
Dear
It appears that you have two questions.
Question #1: If the employer was paying the applicant a substantially lower wage than specified in their LMlA during the time the applicant worked in Canada, does that qualify as Canadian work experience for the CEC?
Answer #1: According to IRPR section 87.1(3)(b) 'unauthorized work' shall not be included in calculating a period of work experience for Canadian Experience Class. The applicant's work was authorized by the terms of the LMIA. If the terms of the LMIA were violated, then the work may be considered unauthorized. However, we cannot provide a definite determination because this would depend on the individual circumstances of an application and we cannot respond to case specific questions in this forum.
Please also note that conditions are imposed on the employer of a foreign national working in Canada on a Labour Market Impact Assessment ("LMIA") or LMIA-exempt work permit: they must provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment, and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as -but not less favourable than -those set out in that offer. If it is determined that an employer is not compliant with these conditions a range of penalties may apply. For example, if the employer is not paying the foreign worker in their employ the right wages ("right" wages meaning as per the condition "wages that are substantially the same-but not less favorable"), they may be found non-compliant.
Question #2: If the employer is offering the applicant a job at a substantially lower wage than specified in the LMlA, is a new LMIA required in order to gain CRS points for arranged employment?
Answer #2: : Any and all deviations from the terms and conditions under which an LMIA is issued should be reported to Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC). If an LMIA is no longer deemed to be valid (i.e. suspended or revoked), either a positive decision on that existing LMIA or a new LMIA would need to be obtained. Employers with questions on LMIA should call ESDC at 1 (800) 367-5693.

Any period of employment when the applicant was engaged in full-time study (including a full time Master's program) will not be included in calculating the period of qualifying work experience for CEC (e.g., work experience gained through co-op work permits, off-campus work permits while a full-time student and on-campus work permits).

threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam,
On your website the following is indicated at [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/perm/express/intake-](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/perm/express/intake-) complete.asp:
Translation of documents
and Cizenship Canedaot Cioyenneté Canada
If a supporting document is in a language other than English or French, the applicant must provide IRCC with a copy of the original document as well as a version translated by a certified translator.
If a supporting document is in a language other than English or French, the applicant must provide IRCC with:
the English or French translation; and
•an affidavit from the person who completed the translations; and
- a certified photocopy of the original document.
Our understanding is that the requirement for and affidavit and a certified photocopy of the original document applies only if the translation is not provided by a member in good standing of a provincial or territorial organization of translators and interpreters in Canada.
In many cases our clients police certificates/birth and marriage certs etc. are issued by countries outside of Canada in languages other than English or French. In many cases, the translation takes place in the country of issuance or the issuing institution. Some police clearances, such as a Chinese Notary Certificate of No Criminal Convictions, are in the form of a booklet of three pages, issued directly by the Notary Public Office, the three pages consists of: 1. Title page, 2. Police Clearance written in Chinese, 3. Police Clearance written in English. In such a case, does the client additionally need to provide a certified copy of the three page document?
In Lebanon, police clearances are issued in Arabic, therefore, our understanding is that unless the translation of such police clearances are completed by a member in good standing of a provincial or territorial organization of translators and interpreters in Canada, a certified photocopy of the original Lebanese police clearance which issued in Arabic would need to be included with the translation and the affidavit of the translator. Could you please confirm? This requirement for a certified copy is causing issues for many of our clients. For example, in Lebanon, a Public Notary does not have the right to stamp, notarize, nor certify documents as “true copies" if they did not produce the original document. Is there any solution that you can recommend in these situations?
Thank you very much in advance for your clarification and guidance.
Kind regards,
Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Dear Mrs I
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Per our application guides, any document that is not in English or French must be accompanied by all three of the following:
the English or French translation; and an affidavit from the person who completed the translation; and a certified copy of the original document.
Translations may be done by a person who is fluent in both languages (English or French and the unofficial language). The translation must be accompanied by an affidavit swearing to the accuracy of the translation and the language proficiency of the translator.
An affidavit for a translation is a document stating that the translation is a true and accurate version of the original text. The translator swears in front of a commissioner authorized to administer oaths in the country where the translator lives, that the contents of their translation are a true translation and representation of the contents of the original document.
To answer your first question, yes, your client would need to provide a certified copy of the entire original document, regardless of how
many pages it contains.
To answer your second question, a certified copy of the original document is always a requirement to be included with the translation and the affidavit of the translator, as stated above. We encourage you to consult the local authorities of the country in which the translator lives, in order to determine where you are able get a copy certified in order to submit with an application for permanent residence.
We trust this information will assist you.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Good morning,
As a rule, lEC clients cannot benefit from implied status. The program is governed by a series of bilateral agreements/arrangements with its 33 partner countries which, depending on the agreement/arrangement in place, may require a citizen to return home before they can apply again, if eligible for a second participation (called a discontinuance requirement), may limit the maximum length of time they can stay in Canada (up to 24 months over two lEC participations, for example), or the type of work permit they may apply for (employer-specific (Young Professionals or International Co-op categories) or an open work permit (Working Holiday category)).
Given that for each lEC participation, candidates need to submit a profile into one or more of lEC's three categories, and if picked from a pool, may be invited to submit a work permit application. As such each participation in lEC is separate from the other. All IEC applications are considered to be an overseas work permit application – even though the application process is completely online and the system does not recognized where in the world the lEC client is applying from. Some IEC participants may be able to apply to change their status from "worker" to "visitor" after they have completed their lEC work experience.
When lEC participants can benefit from implied status is limited to very specific situations that are outlined on IRCC's website and is limited to when either an lEC work permit can be changed or extended.
We hope this information will be useful to you.

This includes the Canadian entity's responsibility to submit the client's offer of employment and pay the $230 employer compliance fee. threads.subject: Bridging open work permits for certain federal economic class applicants-e-APR R10 completeness check-REP-2017-0189-
threads.question:
Dear Madam, Dear Sir,
The present correspondence refers to bridging open work permit applications for foreign nationals who submitted an electronic permanent residence application under Express Entry (e-APR) and are still waiting for a final decision from (IRCC) on their e-APR.
It is our understanding that one of the eligibility parameters to apply for the bridging open work permit is to prove that « the electronic application for permanent residence (e-APR) submitted under the Express Entry has passed the R10 completeness check »(Please see attached document)
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada According to our knowledge and experience, (IRCC) does not issue any document proving the e-APR completeness check. We have also noted that even though at the end of the e-APR process, when confirmation of permanent residence documentation is ready to be issued, no mention of R10 completeness is mentioned in any correspondence from IRCC. Therefore could you please give us some clarification about this process and let us know how to obtain this information and what would be the delay to obtain said information.
In addition, we understand on page 3 of the attached document that « if a foreign national submits and APR using Express Entry, they may apply for a BOWP if they meet the eligibility requirements ». Does the mentioned « elibility requirements » refers to the bridging open work permit application or to the e-APR application ?. Does it mean that no decision will be made on the bridging open work permit application until the end of the e-APR process (issuance of confirmation of permanent residence documents)?
We thank you in advance for your clarification regarding this process and stay at your disposal for any additional information you may require.
Awaiting for your next communication, we remain,
Yours truly,
mmigration, Réfugiés
threads.answer:
Dear Mrs
Thank you for your email correspondence to (IRCC) Immigration Representatives mailbox.
An applicant is only eligible to apply for a bridging open work permit (BOWP) if they are currently working in Canada on work permit that is due to expire within 4 months and after they submit their electronic application for permanent residence (eAPR) in Express Entry. The Acknowledgment of receipt (AOR)- Application for permanent residence letter, which is automatically issued to applicants in their online account, must be submitted along with the BOWP application to support the above claim. It is true, as you indicated, that the R10 completeness is not mentioned in the AOR letter.
However, the applicant's eAPR must first pass the completeness check in accordance with section 10 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations before a BOWP can be issued. Officers will check our processing system internally to ensure that the eAPR is complete before issuing a BOWP. If an eAPR is found to be incomplete, the application will be rejected and the applicant is no longer eligible for a BOWP. In this case, the application for a BOWP will be refused.
Thus, to answer your question, the eligibility requirements your referred to in page 3 of the attachment that you provided refer to the BWOP eligibility and not the Express Entry eAPR.
We trust this information will assist you.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: implied status-REP-2017-0139-
threads.question:
Does an application to extend a work permit that is included in an H&C PR application create implied status for the applicant until the H&C matter is determined? We find no support for this process in the law or elsewhere but our client, who has an employee in this position and
who is uncertain whether the employee is in status, has had varying answers from CIC. Regards

threads.answer:
Good day,
Question:
Does an application to extend a work permit that is included in an H&C PR application create implied status for the applicant until the H&C matter is determined?
Response:
Based on the information you provided and assuming you are referring to an H&C application and not a Spouse or Common- law partner in Canada application under the public policy, here is our response.
R201 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations allows a foreign national to apply for a renewal of their work permit only if the application is made before their work permit expires. R186(u) allows that foreign national to continue working under the same conditions in the event that they submitted an application under R201, and a decision on the renewal application has not yet been made (implied status). Once the original work permit expires, and the foreign national is working without a permit, they cannot submit another application under R201, because they no longer have a valid work permit.
However, note that if the applicant is applying to renew their temporary resident status in Canada (student, visitor, worker, etc.) at the same time as their application for H&C, they must not include their temporary resident renewal application in the same envelope. They must pay the fees for the application to extend their stay in Canada separately and must mail it to the Case Processing Centre in Vegreville. Conversely, the Backlog Reduction Office in Vancouver (BRO-V) only processes H&C applications. See the instruction guide. Therefore, if the work permit application is received at the BRO-V it will be returned to the applicant without processing.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Dear Mr.
Thank you for your email correspondence to Citizenship and Immigration Canada's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Your Question: How can an FSWC PR application be filed under IRPR 76(3) since the Express Entry System does not allow for this option under Canadian Immigration law.
Answer: It is not possible to submit an application for permanent residence under any of the immigration programs now managed through Express Entry without being invited to do so as a candidate in the Express Entry pool.
Therefore, only those candidates who meet the eligibility criteria for entry into the Express Entry pool and who receive an Invitation to Apply from IRCC are able to apply through the electronic application for permanent residence (eAPR).
Substituted evaluation for FSW cannot be used to overcome a prospective candidate's failure to meet minimum entry criteria in the creation of an Express Entry profile. An Express Entry profile is not an application. There is no provision for substituted evaluation in the Ministerial Instructions governing the submission of an expression of interest (i.e. Express Entry profile) to immigrate to Canada.
This means that substitution of evaluation under IPRP 76(3) may only be considered in limited circumstances by an officer for applications made under Express Entry (i.e. a change in circumstance after an applicant has been deemed to meet the minimum requirements of the program to which they have been invited to apply and the requirements of section 11.2 of IRPA).

Research award recipients paid by foreign institutions

threads.answer:

1) As there is no mention of the level study, is it correct that regardless of the award recipients level of studies (undergraduate, masters or Ph.D), they may apply for a LMIA-exempt work permit under C44? Yes, award recipients are eligible to apply for an LMlA-exempt work permit under C44 regardless of level of study. To be eligible, the foreign national must meet the requirements as outlined in the program delivery instructions, International Mobility Program: Public policy, competitiveness and economy.
Applicant criteria

Is its primary function to engage in research activities and/or advance education or policy? Does it possess the capacity (e.g., resources, expertise, network) to conduct and/or support research activities? What is its source of funds (e.g., government, commercial enterprise)? threads.answer:
Dear Mrs.
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
Any period of employment during which time the foreign national was engaged in full-time study will not be included in calculating work experience under the Canadian Experience Class (CEC), nor will it count for the purposes of points assigned under the Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS). This includes any Canadian work experience that is gained while a student is on an academic break or a co-op term.
Work experience that is gained after a student has completed their studies, or in the case identified below has graduated, but before they are issued a post-graduate work permit, may qualify as valid Canadian work experience under the CEC or the CRS if the applicant can satisfy an officer that they were not engaged in full-time studies during that time (e.g. proof of completion of full-time study in combination with evidence of skilled work over the same period). To ensure that the CRS points are awarded properly, the applicant must indicate No' when asked if studying full-time when entering this work experience in their Express Entry profile and application.
The work experience mentioned in both scenarios of your enquiry may qualify for work experience in the Federal Skilled Worker class, provided it was paid (volunteer work, unpaid internships do not count). Please be advised that the minimum work experience requirements for the Federal Skilled Worker class are as follows: the work must have been full-time, paid (or the equivalent in part-time, paid hours), worked continuously for at least one year (1,560 total hours) in the same occupation at skill type 0, or skill levels A or B of the 2011 National Occupation Classification.

threads.subject: Inquiry : Co-Op work experience and Express Entry-REP-2017-0406
threads.question:
Dear Sir or Madam,
I am writing to you today in regard to an inquiry about Co-Op work experience as it falls under the gamut of Express Entry:
Under all scenarios listed below, assume the student completed 1 year of skilled work experience as part of a co-op program under an NOC O, A or B and was remunerated accordingly for the position. During the period of work, the student was not
attending classes and was only performing the work as required by the co-op program.
Canadian Experience Class: Under the CEC, it is clear that the work experience gained under a co-op cannot count as your 1 year of Canadian work experience to qualify for the program. That being said, assuming the candidate gained 1 year of Canadian skilled work experience after graduation (not part of the Co-op) and can now qualify under CEC, can the candidate earn additional CRS points under the ‘Canadian Work Experience' factor for their work completed under the Co-Op ? For example, if the candidate completed 1 year of work under the co-op and then 1 year of work after graduation, can the candidate indicate 2 years of Canadian work experience and earn CRS points accordingly ?
Federal Skilled worker: under this program it is unclear how Co-Op work experience is qualified. Assuming a candidate has gained 1 year Canadian work experience under a co-op program, can this be counted as work experience and earn points to qualify for FSW as per the 67 point grid ? In addition, can the candidate indicate the work experience earned under the co-op
as ‘Canadian work experience' in their EE profile and earn additional CRS points accordingly.
Thank you for your clarifications.
and Cizenship Canedaot Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Good day,
Canadian Experience Class: Under the CEC, it is clear that the work experience gained under a co-op cannot count as your 1 year of Canadian work experience to qualify for the program. That being said, assuming the candidate gained 1 year of Canadian skilled work experience after graduation (not part of the Co-op) and can now qualify under CEC, can the candidate earn additional CRS points under the 'Canadian Work Experience' factor for their work completed under the Co-Op? For example, if the candidate completed 1 year of work under the co-op and then 1 year of work after graduation, can the candidate indicate 2 years of Canadian work experience and earn CRS points accordingly?
Answer:
*Note that any period of employment when an applicant was engaged in full-time study (including a full time Master's program) will not be included in calculating the period of qualifying work experience for CEC (e.g., work experience gained through co-op work permits, off-campus work permits while a full-time student and on-campus work permits). As well, if an applicant is studying in Canada part time, they must be in Canada on a study permit. Full time work while in Canada on a study permit only would be 'unauthorized work' and would not count toward Canadian work experience. However, if the applicant holds a valid PGWP at the same time as they are studying part time in Canada on a valid study permit, then the applicant is authorized to work full time and that experience does count toward Canadian full time work experience for the purposes of CEC. IRCC follows the definition of 'full time study' provided by the academic institution in question.
As you clearly stated, no work experience gained under a co-op will qualify as Canadian work experience and as a result the prospective candidate in the aforementioned scenario above would not be credited with 2 years of Canadian work experience. In regards to the 1 year of work experience after graduation, work experience that is gained after a student has completed their studies may qualify as valid Canadian work experience under the CRS. To ensure that the CRS points are awarded properly, the applicant must indicate 'No' when asked if studying full-time when entering this work experience in their Express Entry profile and application.
Please note* that if an applicant receives an ITA under CEC, the onus is on the applicant to provide evidence (i.e. transcripts, letter from the educational institution etc.) to satisfy an officer that they were not engaged in full-time studies during the period of Canadian work experience claimed on their electronic application for permanent residence (eAPR).
Federal Skilled worker: under this program it is unclear how Co-Op work experience is qualified. Assuming a candidate has gained 1 year Canadian work experience under a co-op program, can this be counted as work experience and earn points to qualify for FSW as per the 67 point grid ? In addition, can the candidate indicate the work experience earned under the co-op
as ‘Canadian work experience’ in their EE profile and earn additional CRS points accordingly.
Answer:
Please note that under FSW, there are no restrictions for work experience acquired while studying. To meet the minimum work experience requirements for the Federal Skilled Worker class, applicants must have accumulated at least one year of continuous full-time (or the equivalent in part-time) paid work experience, within the 10 years before the date IRCC receives
Citoyenneté Canada
their application for Permanent Residence (APR).
For more information, please see the IRCC's website: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/perm/econ/fsw/minimum.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/perm/econ/fsw/minimum.asp) [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/immigrate/skilled/apply-who.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/immigrate/skilled/apply-who.asp)
Thank you.

threads.answer:

To be assigned CRS points for Canadian work experience as per subsection 15(3) of the Ministerial Instructions, Canadian work experience is work experience that:

Meaning, under Canadian experience class valid Canadian work experience is based on a candidate legally (l.e temporary status on work permit, work permit extension or post graduate work permit) accumulating paid work experience in Canada. threads.subject: [CPD-2017-0208] FW: Prohibition to Citizenship Application-Probation-REP-2017-0375-
threads.question:
Dear Madam, Sir,
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
Linformation divulguée en vertu de la loi sur l’accés à Finformation I would appreciate some clarification with regards to what constitutes a prohibition to apply for Canadian citizenship, more specifically with regards to probation orders.
Indeed, the citizenship application form asks if the applicant has been under a probation order during the 6 years prior to their application or since becoming a permanent resident. However, art. 22(1)(a)(i) of the Citizenship Act states "..a person shall not
be granted citizenship ... while the person is, pursuant to any enactment in force in Canada, under a probation order,...", making
no reference to the 6 years before the application.
Therefore, if a person was under a probation order in the last 6 years, but is no longer under a probation order at the time of the submission of their citizenship application, would they be eligible to apply for citizenship or must they wait until their probation period no longer falls within the 6 years calculated in their application?
Sincerely,
Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for your enquiry.
You are correct that, as per subparagraph 22(1)(a)(i) of the Citizenship Act, a person is prohibited from being granted citizenship or from taking the oath of citizenship while the person is (pursuant to any enactment in force in Canada) under a probation order.
In relation to the six year reference in the question on the application form, section 21 of the Act states that, despite anything in the Act, no period may be counted as a period of physical presence for the purpose of this Act during which a person has been, under any enactment in force in Canada, (a) under a probation order; (b) a paroled inmate; or (c) confined in or been an inmate of any penitentiary, jail, reformatory or prison. Section 5 of the Act provides for a physical presence period of six years immediately before the date of the person's application for citizenship.
Therefore, a person who was under a probation order in the 6 years before the application, but is no longer on probation at the time of submitting the citizenship application may be eligible for citizenship, provided that when the time spent on probation is taken into account, the individual still has 1460 days of physical presence during the six year period. The online Physical Presence Calculator includes a section to enter any time spent serving a sentence (e.g. prison, penitentiary, jail, reformatory, probation and/or parole) and will notify the person that he or she is eligible to apply for citizenship if the person has 1460 days of physical presence after deducting time spent serving a sentence and absences. If the person has less than 1460 days, the calculator will display a future date when the person may be eligible to apply.
When completing the citizenship application form, it is recommended that the person respond "YES" to the applicable prohibition question at Section 8 on the application form and include an explanation in the box below the question to make a reference to the probation time having been included in the online physical presence calculation. To avoid unnecessary delays in processing the application, it is also recommended that a copy of the probation order be included when submitting the application.
We trust this information is helpful.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Inadmissibility finding outside of Canada and impact on temporary status inside Canada-REP-2017-0016
threads.question:
Good afternoon,
I have a question about impact of inadmissibility finding in PR application made outside of Canada on temporary status inside
Canada.
Fact scenario: an individual is currently resident in Canada on a valid work permit. They applied for Permanent residence as a FSW outside of Canada and recently received a negative decision. The application was denied on basis of misrepresentation (s.40) due to alleged use of unauthorized representative; as such, there is a finding of inadmissibility and a five-year bar.
The applicant's work permit/temporary status in Canada is still valid -in order to continue using it, does the applicant need to now apply for a TRP? or can they continue on this work permit and only apply for the TRP when they file for a WP extension?
Thank you,
中 and Cizenship Caneda
Lnomdn
threads.answer:
Dear Ms.
Thank you for your patience while we prepared our response to your question of January 4 regarding a Temporary Resident Permit. Please see our replies to your questions below.
Question 1: Does the applicant need to now apply for a TRP?
Response 1: When there is a finding of misrepresentation on an application outside Canada under Section 40 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the foreign national is both inadmissible for five years and ineligible to apply for permanent residence for five years, as noted in Section 40(3) of the IRPA.
The foreign national does not automatically cease to be a temporary resident. The five-year ineligibility for applying for permanent residence does not apply to applications for temporary residence. However, if a foreign national is determined to be inadmissible and is in Canada, enforcement action may be initiated by IRCC or CBSA which could result in a removal order being issued.
According to Section 209 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), a work permit becomes invalid either when it expires or when a removal order made against the holder becomes enforceable.
If a foreign national is inadmissible but has a reason to travel to, or remain in, Canada that is justified in the circumstances, they may apply for a temporary resident permit (TRP). To be eligible for a TRP, the need to enter, or stay in, Canada must outweigh the health or safety risks to Canadian society, as determined by an immigration or a border services officer.
Question 2: Can they continue on this work permit and only apply for the TRP when they file for a WP extension?

threads.answer:

The Citizenship Act determines who is a Canadian citizen, including those who are citizens by virtue of being born outside Canada to a Canadian parent. threads.subject: Intra-company transfer work permit question-REP-2017-0275-
threads.question:
To whom it may concern; I understand that a worker applying for an intra-company transfer (ICT) work permit to Canada to work in a subsidiary, branch of affiliate office must have one complete year of work experience (i.e. 365 days) out of the previous three years with the parent company from outside of Canada to qualify for an ICT work permit.
Question: Does an employee qualify to apply for an ICT work permit if the employee has been paid by the parent company from outside of Canada but the employee has worked for one year only within Canada as a “trainer’ on a visitor record for the parent company abroad? Does the one year of employment with the parent company have to take place outside of Canada? If so why?

threads.answer:
Good day,
Question:
Does an employee qualify to apply for an ICT work permit if the employee has been paid by the parent company from outside of Canada but the employee has worked for one year only within Canada as a “trainer" on a visitor record for the parent company abroad? Does the one year of employment with the parent company have to take place outside of Canada? If so why?
Response: One of the requirements to be eligible to apply under the ICT work permit is to provide a confirmation that the foreign national has been employed (via payroll or by contract) continuously (full-time, not accumulated part-time) by the enterprise outside Canada, in a similar full-time position, for at least one year within the three-year period immediately preceding the date of initial application. The fact that the foreign national has never worked for the company outside Canada would not
constitute a "transfer” from the enterprise outside Canada to the parent company in Canada.
In addition, the foreign national must be transferred to a position in an executive, senior managerial, or specialized knowledge capacity. It is also part of the requirements that they were occupying a similar full-time position for the enterprise outside Canada. For more information please consult the instructions for Canadian interests -Significant benefit-Intra-company transferees or NAFTA-Intra-company transferees

threads.answer:
Good day,
This is in response to your enquiry of March 10th regarding the definition of part-time studies.
The International Student program gives flexibility to designated learning institutions to define "full time studies" and "part time studies" in the context of their institutions. Thus, each institution determines the minimal course load required for a student to be considered as having full-time status or a part-time status.
That being said, for the purposes of permanent resident programs such as Express Entry, the definition of full time studies is more quantified. The definition presented in the Express Entry profile is in line with the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations section 83(2), which explains that when awarding adaptability points (as part of the Comprehensive Point System) to an applicant in the Foreign Skilled Worker stream "full-time study means at least 15 hours of instruction per week during the academic year, authorized under a study permit or under section 188, at a secondary or post-secondary institution in Canada that is recognized by the provincial authorities responsible for registering, accrediting, supervising and regulating such institutions, including any period of training in the workplace that forms part of the course of instruction." This standardized definition is used to quantify applicant's time spent in studies in order to award them up to 5 points for elements defined in IRPR 83(1)(b) and 83(1)(b.1). Thus, for the purposes of an express entry application, less than 15 hours of instruction per week during the academic yearis considered a part-time study.

threads.answer:
Good day,

Visa-exempt foreign nationals who have been issued a temporary resident permit (TRP) are not authorized to hold an eTA, as they have been found to be inadmissible to enter Canada. If a TRP is granted, it will allow the foreign national to be able to board a flight to enter Canada. eTA's are not issued alongside a TRP.
Visa-exempt foreign nationals who have been issued a TRP by an overseas office to permit travel to Canada will be able to board a plane to Canada, so long as their TRP document remains valid and they have the appropriate travel document (e.g. a passport) in their possession.
A traveller issued a TRP at a port of entry does not require an eTA to enter Canada. An individual in possession of a TRP and who is in Canada can remain in Canada under the condition described in the TRP.

Question:

While the job title is printed on the work permit, it is the National Occupational Code (NOC) that we assess against when issuing the work permit and conducting the inspections.
