threads.answer:
Dear Ms.
Thank you for your questions on implied status. Please see our responses to your questions below.
Question: Will this person therefore have implied status to continue working until a decision is made on the open work permit application?
Response: Regulation 201 allows foreign nationals to apply for a renewal of their work permit only if the application is made before their work permit expires. Regulation 186(u) allows foreign nationals to work without a work permit if they continue to comply with the conditions set out on the expired work permit, and a decision on the renewal of their application has not yet been made. R183(6) requires that they continue to meet the conditions that were in place when the application for extension was submitted.
A temporary resident who holds a valid work permit and submits an application in Canada for another work permit is considered to be 'renewing.' A renewal of a work permit can be for a new employer, same employer or an open work permit.
For example, an International Experience Canada participant who nearly reached the validity period of their 24-months working holiday open work permit and received an offer of employment from a new employer to work in a different LMlA exemption. If the foreign national applied for a new work permit before their lEC open work permit expires, they may continue working without a permit but under the conditions of their previous valid work permit (e.g., open employer, open occupation) until the decision is made on the renewal application and the new work permit issued. Also, if a foreign national held an employer-specific work permit at the time of the renewal application, they may continue working with the same employer until a decision is made on their new application. They may not work for the new employer while on implied status as that would be a different condition.
We trust this information will be of assistance.

threads.answer:
Good day,
This is in response to your enquiry from March 15th regarding expiry of study permit – 90 days after completion of a study program:
If a foreign national was given a study permit, there is an expiry date marked on the document. This is the expiry date of your temporary resident status in Canada.
The duration of the validity of a study permit corresponds to the length of the program of study plus 90 days following program completion. The program of study is considered complete when you receive a notification in writing of program completion from your school.
As per subsection R222(1), a study permit becomes invalid upon the first to occur of the following days:
(a) the day that is 90 days after the day on which the permit holder completes their studies,
(b) the day on which a removal order made against the permit holder becomes enforceable, or
(c) the day on which the permit expires. If your study permit has expired and you have not applied for an extension, or if you did not respect one of the conditions on your permit or you have studied without a required permit, you have committed an offence under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. You may be subject to an admissibility hearing that could lead to removal from Canada. However, if you wish to stay in Canada after your status has expired you may apply for restoration of status within the 90 days following your loss of status. If not, you have to leave Canada. It is illegal to remain in Canada beyond the validity of your status in Canada. It is illegal to work without a required work permit. It is illegal to study without a required study permit. For information on temporary resident status or extending your stay in Canada as a student, please refer to our instruction guide: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/information/applications/guides/5552ETOC.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/information/applications/guides/5552ETOC.asp) Regards,

QUESTION: What is then the purpose of auditing an "employer" who is not paying the wages, who will not have the control, direction and the power to hire/fire the foreign worker?
RESPONSE: The 'employer' for the purposes of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations is the entity that creates the need for the foreign workers presence in Canada. Employer does not have to be a 'direct hire' but can also be contract of service situations.
There are more conditions imposed under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations than simply ensuring that the wages stated in the offer are paid. For further information please see After hiring a temporary worker : Your responsibilities for a list of the conditions imposed. For your ease of reference they are copied below.
comply with the conditions and time limits outlined in the temporary worker's work permit; you are legally responsible for ensuring that these conditions are met, so make sure you are familiar with them; remain actively engaged in the business that submitted the offer of employment for as long as the temporary worker is employed; comply with all federal, provincial and territorial employment laws, including laws about recruiting workers; provide the temporary worker with a job in the same occupation that was listed in the offer of employment; provide the temporary worker with wages and working conditions that meet or are better than those listed in the offer of employment;
- make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of physical, sexual, psychological and financial abuse; keep any documentation related to the hiring and employment of the temporary worker for a period of six years after the work permit is issued; and attend any inspection and provide all requested documentation or information. An inspection will review all of these conditions.

threads.subject: IRCC's Policy on Holding Two Work Permits Simultaenousely-REP-2017-0422-
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam:
Background: A person has an open work permit until She has been working for "Employer A" in
That same person received a job offer from "Employer B" with an LMIA. The worker applies for and receives an LMIA-stream work permit valid until The "Employer B" is also located in
I am seeking an expert opinion on the IRCC's formal policy on having two or more work permits simultaneously. No decisive information on this matter can be obtained from the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act or the Regulations.
and has a pending nomination application before the province.
Lnfomonedion
Two employers being in the same city, the worker can fulfill terms of the employment with the "Employer A" and "Employer B". The worker receives a nomination letter from the province and is eligible for LMIA exempt work permit under R 204 (c).
Questions:
1) Does IRCC allow or prohibit holding two valid work permit simultaneously, given that the terms of both employments are met and complied?
2) Does issuance ofLMA-stream work permit automatically invalidate the open work permit?
3) Will this person be allowed to apply for an LMIA-exempt work permit based on the nomination and the province's 204(c) support letter? (i.e. Does the valid LMIA-stream work permit make this person ineligible for R 204 (c) work permit?)
As no sections of the Act or the regulation, guidelines, or manuals address the issue in the above mentioned circumstances, I resort to the Immigration Representative inbox.
I would greatly appreciate your reply and comments on my inquiry.
Best Regards,
threads.answer:
Good day,
QUESTION: 1) Does IRCC allow or prohibit holding two valid work permit simultaneously, given that the terms of both employments are met and complied? RESPONSE: There is no legal bar to a temporary resident holding two valid work permits simultaneously.
QUESTION: 2) Does issuance ofLMA-stream work permit automatically invalidate the open work permit? RESPONSE: No, the issuance of one work permit does not automatically invalidate a previously issued work permit. Section 209 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations specifies when a work permit becomes invalid.
QUESTION: 3) Will this person be allowed to apply for an LMIA-exempt work permit based on the nomination and the province's 204(c) support letter? (i.e. Does the valid LMIA-stream work permit make this person ineligible for R 204 (c) work permit?) RESPONSE: Each work permit application is based on the information provided by the foreign national for that application. A temporary resident may legally hold more than one work permit at a time if the processing officer is satisfied that the person meets the requirements of the program they are applying under.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox on the subject of CRS points assigned for a Canadian educational credential
Per section 30 (1) of the Ministerial Instructions, the points that are to be assigned for a Canadian educational credential are the following:
- (a) 0 points, if the foreign national has a secondary school educational credential;
- (b) 15 points, if the foreign national has an eligible credential from a one-year or two-year post-secondary program; and
- c) 30 points, if the foreign national has o (i) an eligible credential from a post-secondary program of three years or more, o (ii) an eligible credential from a university-level program at the master's level or at the level of an entry-to- practice professional degree for an occupation listed in the National Occupational Classification matrix at Skill Level A for which licensing by a provincial regulatory body is required, or o (iii) an eligible credential from a university-level program at the doctoral level.
(2) Points are to be assigned under subsection (1) only for the eligible credential corresponding to the highest level of education for which the foreign national meets the requirements of subsection (3).
(3) Points are only assigned under subsection (1) if, for the purpose of obtaining the credential, the foreign national
- (a) studied in Canada at a Canadian educational institution;
- (b) was enrolled in full-time study or training for at least eight months; and
- (c) was physically present in Canada for at least eight months.
For the purpose of this section, the following are not eligible credentials:
- (a) credentials obtained in a study or training program in which the study of English or French as a second language amounted to more than half of the program;
- (b) credentials obtained in a study or training program in which distance learning amounted to more than half of the program; or
- (c) credentials obtained in a study or training program while receiving a scholarship or fellowship that stipulated that the recipient return to their home country to apply the knowledge and skills gained In order for your client to be assigned points for his degree in Canada, you must demonstrate by answering questions in the
Express Entry system that the above-mentioned criteria are met. We strongly suggest you review your responses to the education questions in the system.

Dear Matthew LeBaron,
Thank you for bringing this information to our attention. We are currently in the process of consulting with our provincial colleagues on required documents. We will be reporting the information to the group responsible for updating instruction guides and forms when our consultations are complete. Any determined discrepancies will be corrected as soon as possible.
In the meantime, we recommend applicants continue to ensure they use the proper application and indicate for which type of work permit they are applying. As your questions pertain to provincial nominees, it is important to distinguish the two Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) exemptions available for provincial nominees.
The two LMIA exemptions are:
1. R204(c)-LMIA exemption code T13, Federal – Provincial/Territorial agreements.
Eligibility requirements include: the Offer of employment to a foreign national exempt from a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) form [IMM 5802] and proof the employer has paid the employer compliance fee; a copy of the nomination letter from the provincial or territorial government that confirms that the foreign national has been nominated for permanent residence by the province (if the nomination is expired, a copy of the acknowledgement letter confirming that CiC received the permanent residence application while the nomination was still valid); and a statement from the province that it has determined that all factors required for the issuance of a work permit under paragraph R204(c) as per its agreement with Canada have been met, identifying the occupation and employer information. The required factors include:
a. that the nominated individual is urgently required by the provincial-based employer who has made the foreign national a job offer in that province or territory (it should be noted that self-employed persons are therefore not eligible for this type of work permit, given the lack of employer-employee relationship),
b. that the job offer is genuine and the job offer will create economic benefits or opportunities,
c. that the employment is not part-time or seasonal, and
d. that the wages and working conditions of the employment would be sufficient to attract and retain Canadian citizens.
2. R205(a)- LMIA exemption A75 Bridging Open Work Permit (BOWP) This exemption applies to provincial nominees inside Canada who are pending a decision on their permanent residence applications.
Eligibility requirements include that the foreign national must:
- be currently in Canada;
- have valid status on a work permit that is due to expire within the next four months;
- be the principal applicant on an APR under the FSWC, the CEC, the FSTC, the PNC (see note below), or one of the two caregiver classes;
- have completed one of the following APR stages:
o their electronic application for permanent residence (e--APR) submitted under Express Entry has passed the R10 completeness check; or o they have received a positive eligibility assessment on their paper APR submitted by mail under one of the economic classes above;
- have applied for an open work permit;
- have paid the work permit processing fee and the open work permit holder fee; and
- have provided, as applicable, evidence (e.g., nomination certificate) that their provincial nomination is unrestricted.
Note: Foreign nationals in the Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) are eligible for a BOWP ONLY if they have provided a copy
of the nomination letter issued by the nominating province or territory along with their application and there is no indication that employment restrictions exist as conditions of the nomination.

Question: Section 29(2)(a)(iii) of the Ministerial Instructions reads:
o(iii) the foreign national holds a valid work permit issued under the circumstances described in

threads.answer:
Dear Ms
Thank you for your question regarding implied status. Please see below for our response.
Question: Will this person therefore have implied status to continue working until a decision is made on the open work permit application?
Response: Regulation 201 allows foreign nationals to apply for a renewal of their work permit only if the application is made before their work permit expires. Regulation 186(u) allows foreign nationals to work without a work permit if they continue to comply with the conditions set out on the expired work permit, and a decision on the renewal of their application has not yet been made. R183(6) requires that they continue to meet the conditions that were in place when the application for extension was submitted.
A temporary resident who holds a valid work permit and submits an application in Canada for another work permit is considered to be 'renewing.' A renewal of a work permit can be for a new employer, same employer or an open work permit.
For example, an International Experience Canada participant who nearly reached the validity period of their 24-months working holiday open work permit and received an offer of employment from a new employer to work in a different LMlA exemption. If the foreign national applied for a new work permit before their lEC open work permit expires, they may continue working without a permit but under the conditions of their previous valid work permit (e.g., open employer, open occupation) until the decision is made on the renewal application and the new work permit issued. However, if a foreign national held an employer-specific work permit at time of renewal application, they may continue working with the same employer until a decision is made on their new application. They may not work for the new employer as that would be a different condition.
We trust this information will be of assistance.

threads.subject: Employer of record-Offer of Employment (International Mobility Program) - request for clarification-REP- 2017-0576
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam,
I am reaching out to you regarding an important question which I am unable to get a consistent response on from different CBSA POE Supervisors and officers so I was hoping you could provide some insight.
In the NAFTA context when a US company would like to send a professional to perform specific work for a client in Canada
and Cizenship Caneda
(assuming the US citizen qualifies under one of the NAFTA occupations), which entity/company should be listed on the Offer of Employment (and details completed via employer portal) if the control of the worker (and salary) during his/her assignment in Canada will remain with the US employer? I received different information when I called various POEs and some CBSA officers indicate that they won't accept an application from a US company, no matter what, and that only the Canadian entity/client must submit the offer of employment; some say that it would be OK for a US company to complete the request and the Offer of Employment as long as there is evidence of the contract with Canadian client and evidence of US employee's employment in the US. I can't seem to find anything in the manual to confirm that either scenario would be acce ptable although the actual NAFTA provision indicates that a NAFTA professional must be employed by a Canadian entity. However, I am aware of quite a few situations where US companies have signed contracts with Canadian clients and the client in Canada is refusing to complete any information regarding the offer of employment as they do not consider “employing" the US national worker (since they do not pay him, nor do they have any control over his job duties, or have ability to fire him, etc.). Therefore, they insist that the US company should complete the offer of employment and request the Work Permit for their US national workers to allow them to complete the assignment in Canada.
Your assistance and guidance in this regard would be very much appreciated as there appears to be no consistent approach to these situations. I believe it is critical to know for accuracy and compliance reasons.
Thank you for your kind attention to this communication and I hope to hear from you at your earliest convenience.
Many thanks.
Best regards,
threads.answer:
Good day,
QUESTION (1): which entity/company should be listed on the Offer of Employment (and details completed via employer portal) if the control of the worker (and salary) during his/her assignment in Canada will remain with the US employer?
RESPONSE(1) : The 'employer' for the purposes of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations is the entity that creates the need for the foreign workers presence in Canada. Employer does not have to be a 'direct hire' but can also be contract of service situations.
The following information is available in the Employer Portal Enrollment Guide:
Who needs to complete an offer of employment
If there is more than one company involved in hiring the temporary worker
An offer of employment must be submitted for any temporary worker coming to Canada to work for a specific employer who does not need a Labour Market Impact Assessment. In some cases there is more than one employer or company involved in hiring the temporary worker. The employer who needs to submit the offer in these cases depends on the employment situation. There are two types of employment situations:
1. Contract of service: When a Canadian company hires a temporary worker directly, or accepts a transfer of a temporary worker from a foreign company. The temporary worker, usually, but not in all cases, would be on the Canadian company payroll and part of its human resources.
2. Contract for service: When a Canadian company contracts a foreign company, and the foreign company provides an employee to the Canadian company to fulfill the contract.
If you are a Canadian company that hires a temporary worker directly, or you accept a transfer from a foreign company, your company is the only employer. You must complete and submit an offer of employment. If you are a Canadian company that contracts the services of a foreign company, you must complete and submit the offer of employment, not the foreign company. This is because it is your Canadian company that is creating the need for the temporary worker to enter Canada. You must submit the offer even if:
- the temporary worker is, and will stay, an employee of the foreign company, and/or
- the foreign company is paying the temporary worker's wages.
Note: Read the Employer Portal user guide to find out how a Canadian company should fill out the offer of
employment when a foreign business or organization is involved in employing the temporary worker.
QUESTION(2): However, I am aware of quite a few situations where US companies have signed contracts with
ndn Canadian clients and the client in Canada is refusing to complete any information regarding the offer of employment as they do not consider “employing” the US national worker (since they do not pay him, nor do they have any control over his job duties, or have ability to fire him, etc.). Therefore, they insist that the US company should complete the offer of employment and request the Work Permit for their US national workers to allow them to complete the assignment in Canada.
RESPONSE (2): The Canadian entity is the entity that controls the work place in Canada, since the majority of the conditions imposed are under the purview of the Canadian entity, they must be the entity providing the offer of
employment that is required by the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations. Although, the Canadian entity
may not pay the foreign worker, they do have the ability to refuse access to their premises and depending on the contract of service can dictate what the foreign worker is to do when on their premises.
There are more conditions imposed under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations than simply ensuring
that the wages stated in the offer are paid. For further information please see After hiring a temporary worker: Your responsibilities for a list of the conditions imposed. For your ease of reference they are copied below.
comply with the conditions and time limits outlined in the temporary worker's work permit; you are legally responsible for ensuring that these conditions are met, so make sure you are familiar with them; remain actively engaged in the business that submitted the offer of employment for as long as the temporary worker is employed; comply with all federal, provincial and territorial employment laws, including laws about recruiting workers;
provide the temporary worker with a job in the same occupation that was listed in the offer of employment; provide the temporary worker with wages and working conditions that meet or are better than those listed in the
offer of employment;
make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of physical, sexual, psychological and financial abuse; keep any documentation related to the hiring and employment of the temporary worker for a period of six years after the work permit is issued; and attend any inspection and provide all requested documentation or information.
In addition, for many of the Labour Market Impact Assessment exemptions there must be a Canadian entity who provides the offer of employment in order to meet the requirements of the LMIA-exemption. For example-NAFTA requires both a Canadian and American entity involved in a contract. If the offer of employment is submitted by the American entity then it will never meet the requirements of the NAFTA LMIA-exemptions because there is no Canadian employer.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.question:
Good Morning,
My name is
I have the following question that needs your kind input, thank you.
A minor of 16-year old, a PR holder, has been accompanying her Canadian mother outside of Canada. Accompanying her Canadian mother outside of Canada has been enabling the minor to meet the residency obligation to keep her PR status. My question are:

threads.answer:
Greetings,
A minor applying for the grant of citizenship must meet the following under 5(2) of the Citizenship Act: Grant of citizenship
(2) The Minister shall grant citizenship to any person who is a permanent resident within the meaning of subsection 2(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and is the minor child of a citizen, if
(a) an application for citizenship is made to the Minister by a person authorized by regulation to make the application on behalf of the minor child;
(b) the person has, subject to the regulations, no unfulfilled conditions under that Act relating to his or her status as a permanent resident;
(c) in the case of a person who is 14 years of age or over at the date of the application, he or she has an adequate knowledge of one of the official languages of Canada; and
(d) in the case of a person who is 14 years of age or over at the date of the application, he or she demonstrates in one of the official languages of Canada that he or she has an adequate knowledge of Canada and of the responsibilities and privileges of citizenship. threads.answer:
Good day,
Any period of employment during which time the foreign national was engaged in full-time study will not be included in calculating work experience under the Canadian Experience Class (CEC), nor will it count for the purposes of points assigned under the Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS). This includes any Canadian work experience that is gained while a student is on an academic break or a co-op term.
Work experience that is gained after a student has completed their studies, but before they are issued a post-graduate work permit, may qualify as valid Canadian work experience under the CEC or the CRS if the applicant can satisfy an officer that they were not engaged in full-time studies during that time (e.g. proof of completion of full-time study in combination with evidence of skilled work over the same period). To ensure that the CRS points are awarded properly, the applicant must indicate No' when asked if studying full-time when entering this work experience in their Express Entry profile and application.

FW: Additional duties to IMP Work Permit holder-REP-2017-1697
Please find the response to your question below.
Question
I am wondering what the procedure is to “amend" or add additional job duties (up to 50% more) – and remuneration-to a foreign national with an already issued work permit through a LMIA exemption (C44)
Answer
It is important that the foreign national hold a work permit that accurately reflects the job that they are doing in Canada; and, that they are actually doing the job for which the work permit authorizes them to do [see Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) 183(1)(b) and 185]. It is also important that the Offer of Employment be filled out completely and accurately before it is submitted to IRCC [IRPR 209.11], that the National Occupation Code (NOC) indicated on the Offer of Employment is the correct one for the job and duties the foreign national will be/is doing.
Providing additional duties, thereby increasing weekly hours, and a salary that is higher salary to the foreign worker than the salary indicated on the Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC after the work permit was issued would not require the foreign national to obtain a new work permit. Typically, a foreign worker does not need a new work permit unless there has been a change to the conditions that affect the worker – i.e. employer, occupation or location. Or, if the change in working conditions negatively impacts the worker, such as reduction in hours or salary, then a new Offer of Employment and a new work permit would be required before the change takes effect, otherwise the employer risks being found non-compliant with the original job offer submitted to IRCC.
Several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer by the IRPR on issuance of a work permit based on an offer of employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works; provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the
IRPR.
The employer cannot amend duties, hours or salary information in the Offer of Employment that was submitted to IRCC after the work permit has been issued to the foreign worker.

The regulatory amendment to raise the age limit for dependent children from under 19 to under 22 years of age came into force on October 24, 2017. The higher age limit applies to applications for permanent residence received on or after October 24th, 2017.

Multiple-step permanent resident applications have two steps required for the principal applicant:

This provincial nominee application is the first step of the principal applicant's process, therefore the child's age is 'locked-in' at 20 years old. If the principal applicant submits an application for permanent residence on or after October 24th, 2017, and if at that time the person's child continues to be single (not married/not in a common-law relationship), that child may be eligible to be included in the permanent resident application as a dependent child.

Thank you for sending us your question.
Arizona – Set Aside Conviction pursuant to Title 13-907
As you may be aware, the Saini test represents the essential elements required to equate a foreign pardon to a Canadian record suspension “pardon”.
The second part of the Saini test compares the aim, content and effect of the Arizona law to that of Canada's record suspension.
Title 13, section 907 of the Arizona Penal Code, reads as follows:
Setting aside judgment of convicted person on discharge; application; release from disabilities; exceptions
A. Except as provided in subsection D of this section, every person convicted of a criminal offense, on fulfillment of the conditions of probation or sentence and discharge by the court, may apply to the judge, justice of the peace or magistrate who pronounced sentence or imposed probation or such judge, justice of the peace or magistrate's successor in office to have the judgment of guilt set aside. The convicted person shall be informed of this right at the time of discharge.
B. The convicted person or, if authorized in writing, the convicted person's attorney or probation officer may apply to set aside the judgment.
C. If the judge, justice of the peace or magistrate grants the application, the judge, justice of the peace or magistrate shall set aside the judgment of guilt, dismiss the accusations or information and order that the person be released from all penalties and disabilities resulting from the conviction except those imposed by [..]
In Arizona, one may apply to have their conviction “set aside” upon fulfillment of the conditions of probation or sentence and discharge by the court. This is intended to release the individual from all penalties and disabilities resulting from the conviction. As set out in the aforementioned legal opinion, this is similar to the aim of Canada's record suspension as both laws do not effectively erase the conviction but rather seek to ensure that the conviction no longer reflects adversely on an applicant's character.
The legislation is very brief in content as it does not provide details concerning the application process and eligibility provisions beyond the completion of the sentence, but the wording does imply that the decision to grant the application is discretionary as in Canada. The recent changes to Canadian legislation allow for further similarities as certain offences deem an individual ineligible for conviction relief in both jurisdictions. However, there is no designated conviction-free period as there is in Canada where the prescription period is 5 or 10 years of good behaviour depending on the offence. There is also no indication that the Arizona courts can revoke a set aside if the individual is convicted of a subsequent offence, they are no longer of good standing or, the application contained false statements; this discretion is available to the National Parole Board which can revoke a record suspension on any of the aforementioned grounds.
What is significantly different between the two laws is the effect as the Canadian legislation strictly limits access to the record of conviction (removes it from CPIC, etc.) whereas, in Arizona, the charge and conviction remain fully accessible to anyone searching an individual's record where wording is added to indicate the conviction was set aside. A conviction that has been set aside may still be used to deny certain kinds of employment (if the job relates to the conviction), permits, certificates, licenses and can also be used in future criminal cases. In addition, the legislation does not permit the offender to deny the conviction if asked on a job application. This differs from Canadian legislation as suspended records that are in the custody of federal agencies are kept separate and apart from one's primary criminal record and information pertaining to such records will not be disclosed without the specific approval of the Minister of Public Safety. In addition, the CRA states that no employment application form, within the federal authority, may ask any question that would reveal a suspended record.
I will, however, note that solely for sexual offences listed in the schedule 1 to the CRA, information regarding ones criminal record will be available in certain circumstances regardless of the suspension. Consequently, one's suspended record may be disclosed only if that person wishes to work with children or vulnerable persons, and this is with the individual's written consent for disclosure.
A record suspension does not ensure that either municipal or provincial agencies will not disclose the record as the CRA applies only to records kept at the federal level. However, many provincial and municipal agencies will cooperate by restricting the disclosure of the records once they are notified of the suspension.
Given these difference, I find the aim, content and effect of the foreign legislation to be too dissimilar to a Canadian record suspension to be deemed equivalent. As such, the essential requirements provided by the Saini test have not been satisfied for us to recognize the set aside.
We trust that this information will be useful to you.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Good morning Mr.
Question: CETA chapter 14 allows non-Canadian vessels to be used for feeder services, empty container replacements, and dredging services. However, CETA remains mute on the issue of work permits. Do all personnel aboard such vessel require a work permit under the new regime, or are they exempt from obtaining work permits for all three of the services allowed under the new regime?
Answer: As per our program delivery instructions on R186(s), the Coasting Trade Act defines coasting trade “as the carriage of goods
or passengers by ship.. from one place in Canada... to any other place in Canada... either directly or by way of a place
outside Canada". When a vessel or ship meets the criteria which defines coasting trade as outlined in the Coasting Trade Act, the ship will require a coasting trade license (CTL). For officers, if a ship holds a CTL, it is usually an indication that work permits will likely be required for the foreign crew members as the license is indicative of the fact that the vessel is involved in cabotage (meaning the domestic transportation of goods and services) activities within the domestic labour market
Under the Canada-European Union (EU) Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), ships registered in an EU member state and engaged in the following operations are exempt from the requirement to obtain a Coasting Trade Licence
(CTL):
Feeder services between the Ports of Halifax and Montreal Repositioning empty containers Dredging services
Although the EU registered ship is exempt from the need to obtain a CTL, it does not mean that the ship is not engaging in cabotage activities within the domestic labour market. Therefore, foreign crew members working onboard vessels engaged in cabotage would likely still require work permits. The CETA only grants an exemption from the CTL requirement, it does not exempt these foreign crew members from the requirement to obtain a work permit.
Please note that we are currently in the process of updating our program delivery instructions on this subject.
If you have any further questions, please do not hesitate to ask.

Good afternoon,
Question
On the topic of salary, if the employer gives a significant raise (e.g. 40%) would that be a concern for an IMP work permit compliance inspection?
Answer
It is important that the foreign national hold a work permit that accurately reflects the job that they are doing in Canada; and, that they are actually doing the job for which the work permit authorizes them to do [see Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) 183(1)(b) and 185]. It is also important that the Offer of Employment be filled out completely and accurately before it is submitted to IRCC [IRPR 209.11], that the National Occupation Code (NOC) indicated on the Offer of Employment is the correct one for the job and duties the foreign national will be/is doing.
Providing a salary that is higher salary to the foreign worker than the salary indicated on the Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC after the work permit was issued would not require the foreign national to obtain a new work permit. Typically, a foreign worker does not need a new work permit unless there has been a change to the conditions that affect the worker – i.e. employer, occupation or location.
However, several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer by the IRPR on issuance of a work permit based on an offer of employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works; provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the IRPR.
The employer cannot amend benefit information in the Offer of Employment that was submitted to IRCC after the work permit has been issued to the foreign worker.
Proactive notification to IRCC of inconsistencies surrounding working conditions, including salary and benefits, are not required under the International Mobility Program. However, the employer who provided the offer on which the work permit is based is still responsible for ensuring that the wages and benefits are consistent with what was stated in the offer of employment. Employers may be inspected on the conditions listed above and, therefore, they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not. The employer must keep all documents related to any changes from the original Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC.
Employers who have concerns that they are not meeting conditions of the Offer of Employment can use the Voluntary Disclosure process (see bottom of page After hiring a temporary worker).
Typically, any substantial change from the Offer of Employment must be justified as per subsection 203(1.1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). An officer may find that a change in an employee contract that increases the salary is justified under R203(1.1) in that it is similar to a change in the provisions of a collective agreement. In addition, an increase in wages may result in a finding that the employer did not provide “substantially the same" wages if the increase would have affected the ability of the foreign national to qualify for the LMlA-exemption.
Wages under the International Mobility Program must meet the minimum wage requirement in the province of employment as per the condition to meet federal or provincial laws. Wages paid that are higher than those in the offer of employment, it may indicate a change in duties that would mean a different occupation than offered.
In cases where the employer has promoted or otherwise changed the foreign worker's duties, the foreign worker must receive a new Offer of Employment and work permit prior to implementing the change.
If a new work permit for the promotion or change in occupation has not been previously approved and the temporary foreign worker is found to be working in an occupation other than what was stated on the Offer of Employment, this may constitute non-compliance by the employer.
Foreign workers are also subject to other federal (such as ESDC who leads the Temporary Foreign Workers Program) and provincial or territorial legislative and regulatory requirements. Employers should also meet those requirements for compliance purposes.]
We trust this information will be useful to you.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Answer
While the job title is printed on the work permit, it is the National Occupational Code (NOC) that we assess against when issuing the work permit and conducting compliance inspections. There are usually many different titles associated to a single NOC code. As long as the duties, education requirements, salary, etc. of the occupation continue to match the NOC code then there should be no requirement for changing the work permit, and therefore, no requirement to submit a new offer of employment through the Employer Portal.

The employer is required [R209.2(1)(b)] to retain all documents related to the employment of the foreign worker for up to six years after the date of issuance of the work permit, including details about the title change, to ensure information can be provided to an IRCC officer in the event of an inspection.

Hello,
Thank you for your question
Several conditions are imposed automatically on the employer by the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) on issuance of a work permit based on an offer of employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the
province in which the foreign national works;
provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the IRPR.
Typically, a foreign worker does not need a new work permit (nor is a new Offer of Employment required to be submitted) unless there has been a change in employer, occupation or location.
After a work permit has been issued to the foreign worker, IRCC does not require proactive notification of changes that are part of the regulatory imposed conditions on the employer, such as wages, working conditions, location, etc.
However, the regulations state that the employer must keep all documents pertaining to the employment of the foreign national for six years beginning on the first day of employment, including any documentation supporting the termination of employment. If there are any changes to the information that differs from what was provided in the Offer of Employment, then the employer will (if asked during a compliance inspection) have to provide the documentation that justified the change as per subsection R203(1.1).
The Voluntary Disclosure mechanism was put in place to allow employers who found themselves to be non-compliant with the conditions outlined under R203(1) to inform IRCC. Disclosure of a termination of employment would not be necessary unless the relevant provincial/territorial guidelines were not followed.
More information is available on our website at the following link:
After hiring a temporary worker – voluntary disclosure and form [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/work/employers/hire-after.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/work/employers/hire-after.asp)
We hope this information is helpful.

Question: What about in cases where the temporary worker becomes a permanent resident? If the permanent resident is in possession of a valid work permit, i.e. they landed before the expiry of their current employer specific work permit, does the employer need to withdraw the offer?
Response:
If an employer pays the $230 compliance fee and submits the offer of employment through the Employer Portal, the offer can be withdrawn and the fee refunded only if the work permit has not yet been issued to the foreign national.
Once the work permit has been issued to the foreign national and the offer of employment is matched to the work permit, it is no longer possible to withdraw the offer of employment. If a temporary worker becomes a permanent resident before the expiry of their work permit, the employer does not need to withdraw the offer.
The employer is responsible for adhering to the conditions of the International Mobility Program for the duration of the work permit. You can read more about employer responsibilities here.
If the worker leaves their position, the employer should retain any pertinent documentation which relates to compliance with the imposed conditions. Employers are required to retain all documents to substantiate the accuracy of information provided in the Offer of Employment and to demonstrate their compliance with the conditions set out in paragraphs R209.2(1)(a) and (b) from the first day of the associated work permit issuance to six years thereafter.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Good day,
Thank you for your question regarding departing and returning to Canada after an extension is filed.
If your current temporary resident status is still valid you can apply for an extension of your stay. For any permit, you should always apply at least 30 days before your current status expires. Your original temporary status as a visitor, student or worker continues under the same conditions until your application is finalized and you have been notified of the decision.
You can leave Canada and return, as long as your Temporary Resident Visa (TRV) or Electronic Travel Authorization (eTA) is still valid. If your TRV or eTA is expired, you will have to apply for and receive a new one before you leave. A valid TRV or eTA does not guarantee entry to Canada. All foreign nationals must undergo an examination at the port of entry by a Border Services Officer of the Canada Border Services Agency, to determine if they are admissible to Canada. If the officer believes there is reason to refuse your re-entry, you will not be able to re-enter Canada. The officer at the port of entry may ask you for a copy of your extension application, the fee payment receipt, and any other document to prove you applied for an extension.
A temporary resident with implied status who has left Canada may be allowed to re-enter Canada as a temporary resident, pending a decision on the renewal of their application to study or work in Canada, provided they are TRV-exempt, as per section R190, or on a multiple-entry visa. They may not resume work or study in Canada until their application for renewal has been granted.
Regards,

Hello,
Thank you for sharing your suggestions about the Employer Portal with us.
The Canadian organization that hires a temporary worker directly, or accepts a direct transfer from a foreign company, will be considered the only employer for the purpose of the International Mobility Program. That employer should complete and submit an offer of employment using the Employer Portal and pay the employer compliance fee.
In some cases there may be more than one organization involved in the entry of the temporary worker to Canada. If a Canadian organization contracts the services of a foreign organization and that organization is providing an employee to fulfill the contract, and this employee is remaining as an employee of the foreign company, then the Canadian organization should still complete and submit the offer of employment and pay the employer compliance fee not the foreign organization. This is because it is the Canadian organization that is creating the need for the temporary worker to enter Canada and will be responsible for some of the regulatory conditions imposed on employers when having a foreign national come to work in Canada, such as remaining actively engaged as a business, complying with federal or provincial labour laws, and providing a safe workplace.
These conditions [R209.2(1)(a)(i-iv)] state that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works; provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph
72.1(7)(a) if the IRPR.
Guidance is provided in the Employer Portal User Guide on how to enter information about wages and benefits, when it is another entity that is responsible for that area.
In any case, IRPR 209.11(1) suggests that the entity that must submit the Offer should be the entity who is employing the worker in Canada. Regardless of who submits the offer, whoever submits the offer is responsible for being the contact if there is a compliance inspection. And, according to R209.4(1) and (2), they must be available to answer questions and provide documents (i.e. payroll, timesheets) and be on hand for any on-site inspections.
We hope this information is helpful.

Bonjour Mme
Questions: Afin de rencontrer les critères requis pour le code de dispense A75, serait-il possible pour ce candidat d’obtenir une offre d’emploi de lui-même ou de la part d’un de ses associés? Subséquemment, serait-il problématique que le nom de la personne ressource apparaissant dans le portail soit le nom du candidat lui-même?
Réponse : Le code de dispense C11 s’applique pour les entrepreneurs ou les travailleurs autonomes devant d’établir au Québec et qui ont un certificat de sélection du Québec (CSQ) à titre d’entrepreneur ou de travailleur autonome. Il semble que ce code pourrait être plus approprié par rapport à la situation que vous décrivez si le candidat répond aux critères d’admission.
Pour être admissible à un permis de travail dispensé de l’étude d’impact sur le marché du travail sous le code d’exemption C11, l’étranger doit :
avoir un CSQ valide à titre d’entrepreneur ou de travailleur autonome; faire l’objet d’une demande d’entrée hâtive formulée par le ministère de l’Immigration, de la Diversité et de l'Inclusion (MIDI); avoir reçu l’un ou l’autre des documents suivants : Oun numéro d’offre d’emploi; o une autorisation de la Direction générale de l’orientation du programme d’immigration de présenter le formulaire Offre d’emploi à un ressortissant étranger dispensé d’une étude d’impact sur le marché du travail (EIMT) [IMM 5802]. Pour en savoir plus, voir Permis de travail pour un employeur précis avec dispense de l’étude d’impact sur le marché du travail; avoir acquitté les frais relatifs à la conformité de l’employeur- les travailleurs autonomes sont considérés comme leur propre employeur et doivent donc acquitter les frais
Si le candidat ne répond pas aux critères pour C11, il ne peut pas être son propre employeur sous A75. L’intention de la dispense sous A75 est de permettre aux titulaires de permis de travail présents au Québec de présenter une demande de renouvellement ou de prolongation de leur autorisation de travailler au Canada, sans que leur employeur ne soit tenu d’obtenir une étude d’impact sur le marché du travail (ElMT). Cette dispense ne vise pas les entrepreneurs ou les travailleurs autonomes. Response: It is true that the Canadian company is creating the need for the foreign worker to come to Canada, and will be providing the work location in accordance with federal and provincial or territorial labour laws, and therefore, should submit the offer of employment to IRCC; however, at this time there is no regulation that makes this an obligation.
Given the above, can you please confirm that in the offer of employment section on wages and benefits the alternative compensation section can be completed to simply state that the individual is on the payroll of the foreign company as the Canadian client does not have access to the applicant's payroll and benefit records or information.
Response: Correct. Guidance in the Employer Portal User Guide states that the employer' that submits the offer should provide as much detail as possible in the Alternative Compensation Scheme field/section about the wage and benefit source and arrangement.
Please note: The offer of employment is only for the assessment of a work permit for immigration purposes and is not intended to establish the standard ‘employee/ employer' relationship as normally understood in the labour force.
In addition can you confirm that should the offer of employment be selected for a compliance review that the Canadian client will be exempt from providing information regarding payroll and benefits information for this individual?
Response: No. IRCC does not currently allow for multiple employers (i.e. to submit the offer of employment), however this policy is currently under review.
The current policy is that whoever submits the offer of employment is responsible, as per the regulations under section 209 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, for cooperating in the event a compliance inspection is conducted. The inspectors will consider the employer on the Offer as the “employer of record”. That means that they will be contacted and asked to provide information or documentation that would be assessed against what was indicated on the offer submitted to IRCC – AND they could be held liable for any findings of non-compliance. This would go for the foreign company as well if they submitted the offer.
So, for example, if the Canadian company submitted the offer which indicated very clearly and concisely that the foreign contractor was employing the foreign worker, and paying X amount in wages and providing specified benefits, then the compliance inspectors would request that the Canadian company obtain, or get the foreign company to send, the required payroll and other employment/contract information that would show that the foreign national is getting paid what they were told, while in Canada. If the foreign company refused to cooperate with the Canadian company, this would place the Canadian company at risk of being found non-compliant with the regulatory conditions.

'employer' inside the International Mobility Program.
The Interpretations, Policies and Guidelines (IPGs): Determining the Employer/Employee Relationship-IPG-069 provided by the Canada Labour Program under Employment Standards clarifies that all statutes have particular policy goals, so it is possible that a worker may be held to be an "employee" for one law, but not for another. The Supreme Court of Canada made it clear that courts and tribunals must take into account the particular policy objectives of the statute when deciding if a person has employee status [Pointe-Claire (City) v. Quebec (Labour Court), [1997] 1 S.C.R. 1015].
The Temporary Resident Program Delivery Instructions (Glossary) currently defines employer as a person, firm, corporation, contractor, or other association or organization in Canada which: Indicates the intention to have an employer-employee relationship with a person who is a temporary foreign worker, and, Has an employer-employee relationship with respect to employees, as indicated by the fact that it may hire, fire, pay,

Under 185(b) of IRPR, a foreign worker only requires a new work permit if there has been a change in employer, occupation or location; if the foreign worker submits an application for the employer's name to change it would be considered a new work permit and he/she would pay the $155 processing fee while the employer would be responsible to pay the $230 compliance fee.
If the employer intends to change the name of the business, it might be in the best interest for affected workers to submit applications to renew their work permits to reflect the new employer. Having the correct employer's name on the work permit will ease future contacts with both provincial and federal governments since the FW will not have to explain the name change each time.
Alternatively, if the decision is made to NOT request to change the name on the WP until it is necessary for the FW to file an application to get an extension of the WP (and change conditions), then the employer could avoid having to pay the Employer Compliance Fee. In this case, the employee(s) should be provided with a letter signed by the employer confirming the name change; this is to ensure that, should the foreign national be required to present their work permit at any time-up until the expiry of the existing work permit-they will have the documentation to link the two employer names.

Dear Mr.
To answer your question. Under Express Entry, self-employed work experience regardless of the applicant's presence in Canada, will be evaluated as foreign skilled work experience. Per section 23 and 24 of the Express Entry Ministerial Instructions, points are assigned for combinations of foreign work experience and either official language proficiency or Canadian work experience, provided that the foreign work experience is work experience that
(a) is acquired by a foreign national outside Canada in one or more occupations listed in Skill Type 0 Management Occupations or Skill Level A or B of the National Occupational Classification matrix;
(b) consists of full-time work experience, or the full-time equivalent for part-time work experience, with one or more employers;
(c) is acquired within the 10-year period preceding the day on which points are assigned to the foreign national under section 23 or subsection 24(1); and
(d) is remunerated by the payment of wages or a commission. Requirements
(2) In order to be assigned points under section 23 or 24 for their foreign work experience, a foreign national
(a) must specify in their expression of interest the four-digit code in the National Occupational Classification that corresponds to each of the occupations they have engaged in while accumulating their foreign work experience; and
(b) must have performed the actions described in the lead statement for the occupation as set out in the occupational descriptions of the National Occupational Classification, as well as a substantial number of the main duties, including all essential duties, as set out in the National Occupational Classification. In other words, Yes. An applicant that has at least 1 year of self-employed work experience would qualify to meet the minimum entry criteria for the Federal Skilled Worker (FSW) program, if he/she meets the aforementioned requirements above. In reference to IRPR s. 215(1)(f)(iii): can this provision be relied upon for a FN to be able to apply for a study permit inside of Canada once they have completed a prerequisite course of less than 6 months in length? As outlined in the PDI discussing letters of acceptance (under conditional letter of acceptance), a prerequisite program is one outlined in a conditional letter of acceptance indicating that the student will be able to register at the DLl once this program is completed. The prerequisite program may be taken at a DLl or non-DLl, as long as it satisfies the requirements set out by the DLI which issued the conditional letter of acceptance. Good afternoon,
Your understanding is accurate. An applicant could enter Canada under the GSS exemption for either_30 days in a 12 month
period OR 15 days once every 6 months (but not both).
Applicants can only benefit from these short-term exemptions if the necessary amount of time has elapsed since their last short-term exemption was granted. Consecutive uses are not permitted. Example: If a foreign national entered Canada under the 15-day work permit exemption and is required to work in Canada for another 15 days, they will not be eligible to renew their stay as a temporary worker. Six months must pass before foreign nationals are eligible to use the 15 day exemption again. The following scenarios provide guidance as to when foreign nationals can benefit from short-term work permit exemptions if they have already used another short-term exemption:
1. If foreign nationals benefited from the 15-day exemption, when may they be granted from the same exemption again? They may be granted a subsequent exemption if they have not been granted a short-term work permit exemption
in the last 6 months.
2. If foreign nationals benefited from the 15-day exemption, when may a foreign national be granted a 30-day exemption or 120-day exemption? They may be granted a 30-day or 120-day exemption once 12 months have elapsed since the date they
were granted the 15-day exemption.
3. If foreign nationals benefited from the 30-day exemption, when may they be granted the same exemption again? They may be granted a 30-day exemption again if they have not been granted a short-term work permit exemption
in the last 12 months.
4. If foreign nationals benefited from the 30-day exemption, when may they be granted a 15-day exemption or 120-day exemption? They may be granted a 15-day exemption once six months have elapsed since the 30-day exemption was granted.
They may be granted a 120-day exemption once 12 months have elapsed since the 30-day exemption was granted.
Hope this helps.

Thank you for your question, we hope the information below is helpful.
Question: Can the employer simply agree to reduce the employee's hours without first filing a new Offer of Employment for an LMIA exempt work permit through the Employer Portal?
Response: Under the International Mobility Program employer compliance regime, the employer is required to provide the temporary worker with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same or better than those indicated in the offer of employment. Working conditions include non-wage related remuneration benefits and entitlements such as hours of work.
Several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer by the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) on issuance of a work permit based on an offer of employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works; provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the
IRPR.
Employers may be inspected on these conditions and they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not.
In order to reduce the hours of work for a temporary worker – and remain compliant with regulatory conditions-the employer can submit a new offer of employment as well as pay the $230 compliance fee. The worker must then apply for a new work permit using the new offer of employment number.
Alternatively, since foreign workers generally only are required to obtain a new work permit when either the employer or job or location changes, proactive notification to IRCC of salary and hours of work changes is not required under the International Mobility Program. The employer who provided the offer on which the work permit is based is still responsible for ensuring that worker is getting what was stated in the initial offer submitted to IRCC, therefore, if employers have concerns that they are not meeting conditions, they can use the Voluntary Disclosure process (see bottom of page After hiring a temporary worker) which is taken into consideration by the inspectors when assessing penalties for any violations of the conditions.
Sincerely,

threads.answer:
Good day,
QUESTION: In a case where the work permit based on a dual intent LMIA was issued for less than two years due to the expiry of the individual's passport, is it possible to request the balance of the maximum duration of two years with the original dual intent LMIA once the foreign worker who is named on LMIA has renewed his/her passport?
RESPONSE: Yes, a limited passport expiry date then obtaining a new passport is the only situation where the LMIA may be reused. For further information please see: Temporary Foreign Worker Program: Labour Market Impact Assessment validity and suspension, and duration of employment, the relevant section is copied below for your reference.
Passport expiry effect on duration of work The expectation is that CIC or CBSA officers will issue a work permit for the duration of work indicated in the LMIA. However, in cases of passport expiry, a work permit may be issued for a shorter duration than identified in the LMlA. For example, if the LMIA work duration is two years but the temporary foreign worker's passport will expire in one year, the officer will issue a one-year work permit.
In cases of passport expiry only, provided the initial LMlA and work permit application were received before the assessment expiry date, temporary foreign workers will be able to renew their existing work permits without obtaining a new LMlA. That is, while the assessment expiry date of the LMlA has passed, the temporary foreign worker met the initial time frame for application and his work permit can therefore be extended for the duration outlined in the initial LMIA, provided the passport has been renewed accordingly. To assist officers processing the extension, CIC and CBSA officers are asked to record reasons in the GCMS Case Notes view tab when a work permit is issued for a shorter duration than is indicated in the LMlA.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Q. How does a non-Canadian employer, sending a employee to Canada pursuant to a services contract with a Canadian client, complete the online system?

Who needs to complete an offer of employment
If there is more than one company involved in hiring the temporary worker
An offer of employment must be submitted for any temporary worker coming to Canada to work for a specific employer who does not need a Labour Market Impact Assessment. In some cases there is more than one employer or company involved in hiring the temporary worker. The employer who needs to submit the offer in these cases depends on the employment situation. There are two types of employment situations:
1. Contract of service: When a Canadian company hires a temporary worker directly, or accepts a transfer of a temporary worker from a foreign company. The temporary worker, usually, but not in all cases, would be on the Canadian company payroll and part of its human resources.
2. Contract for service: When a Canadian company contracts a foreign company, and the foreign company provides an employee to the Canadian company to fulfill the contract.
nmigration, Réfugiés Informat dosd A omionct If you are a Canadian company that hires a temporary worker directly, or you accept a transfer from a foreign company, your company is the only employer. You must complete and submit an offer of employment.
If you are a Canadian company that contracts the services of a foreign company, you must complete and submit the offer of employment, not the foreign company. This is because it is your Canadian company that is creating the need for the temporary worker to enter Canada. You must submit the offer even if:
- the temporary worker is, and will stay, an employee of the foreign company, and/or
- the foreign company is paying the temporary worker's wages.
Note: Read the Employer Portal user guide to find out how a Canadian company should fill out the offer of
employment when a foreign business or organization is involved in employing the temporary worker.
If both companies are Canadian
If there are two Canadian companies involved in the offer of employment, the employer of record must submit the offer of employment. The employer of record is the company that will make sure both companies involved meet the conditions of employing a temporary foreign worker. Find out more about these conditions and your responsibilities as an employer.
In all cases, the employer of record must be involved in hiring the temporary worker. This can include setting up the details of the job they will do and overseeing their work.
If you are a foreign company
Foreign employers should only use the Employer Portal when there is:
- no contract with a Canadian company and
- no Canadian entity involved in the employment scenario.
Examples include:
- a self-employed entrepreneur, like a provincial nominee, coming in to sell at a trade show. If the temporary worker is self-employed, the business name should be the temporary worker's name, or
- crew on ships coming to the Arctic on a “significant benefit to Canada” exemption.
When you enrol and are asked Is this a Canadian Organization?, choose No, then answer the questions about your foreign company. Enter your company's federal registration number in the business number field.
If you are coming to Canada to incorporate a new business, you will need a nine-digit Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) business number. If you do not yet have a CRA business number, you will not be able to use the Employer Portal to submit your offer. Email us with the following information to find out what to do:
- your full name, date of birth and place of birth as listed on your passport
- your country of citizenship
- your business name, if known
- your business contact address, if known

After completion of their program, Student Permit holders can continue to work off-campus for a maximum of 20 hours per week until the SP becomes invalid (90 days afternotification of program completion).

Students who are not eligible to apply for a PGWP may continue to work off-campus for a maximum of 20 hours/week until the SP becomes invalid (90 days after notification of program completion).

threads.question:
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
Bonjour,
Voici mes questions :
1) Un travailleur étranger admis au Canada pour une période de 2 ans à ce titre, peut-il suivre des cours universitaires crédités pendant une session universitaire qui est de 4 mois, par exemple la session d’automne 2017, et par la suite, après une période d’arrêt, par exemple de 4 mois, suivre un ou d’autres cours universitaires crédités pendant une autre session universitaire, par exemple la session d’été 2018, sans permis d’études durant son séjour ou doit-il obtenir un permis d’études pour cette 2º session?
2) Un travailleur étranger admis au Canada pour une période de 2 ans à ce titre, peut-il suivre des cours universitaires crédités pendant une session universitaire qui est de 4 mois, par exemple la session d’automne 2017, et suivre un ou d’autres cours universitaires crédités pendant une session universitaire successive, par exemple la session d’hiver 2018, sans permis d’études durant son séjour ou doit-il obtenir un permis d’études pour cette 2º session?
Notez que dans les deux situations, le travailleur étranger n’obtiendra pas de diplôme ou de certificat, car il suivra ces cours à titre d’étudiant libre à chacune des sessions universitaires.
Merci pour votre réponse.
Salutations cordiales,
and Citizenship Caneda
threads.answer:
Bonjour,
Réponse :
Un étranger doit obtenir un permis d’études pour entreprendre des études ou des cours de formation universitaires ou professionnelles ou autres dont la durée est de plus de six mois dans un établissement d"enseignement désigné (EED) au Canada. Les activités suivantes ne sont pas considérées comme étant des études et n’exigent pas de permis d’études au sens de la Loi sur l’immigration et la protection des réfugiés (LIPR) :
- les cours préscolaires (prématernelle);
- les cours d’intérêt général ou d’autoperfectionnement;
- l’apprentissage à distance;
- les cours suivis à titre d’auditeur (généralement des cours théoriques que l’on suit sans obtenir des crédits la capacité d'obtenir rétroactivement des crédits).
En général, les étrangers au Canada qui ne possèdent pas de permis d’études et qui souhaitent s’inscrire ultérieurement à un autre cours ou programme d’études doivent présenter une demande à l’extérieur du Canada et obtenir un permis d’études de la manière habituelle (p. ex. à un bureau canadien des visas à l’étranger). Les étrangers qui ne possèdent pas de permis d’études ne peuvent obtenir une prorogation de leur séjour autorisé à titre de visiteur simplement pour terminer un cours de courte durée ou un programme de moins de six mois qui se poursuivrait au-delà de la période de séjour autorisée initiale. L’alinéa R188(1)c) n'a pas été prévu pour permettre aux étrangers de suivre des cours de courte durée, l’un après l’autre, en prolongeant simplement leur statut de résident temporaire et obtenir ainsi un certificat ou un diplôme sans jamais avoir eu un permis d’études. (IRCC) reconnaît que les visiteurs et les travailleurs étrangers de long séjour peuvent s’inscrire à des cours ou des programmes d’études occasionnels d’une durée de six mois ou moins à tout moment pendant leur séjour au Canada.
ll est donc recommandé qu’un étranger soit encouragé à présenter une demande de permis d’études pour un cours ou un programme d’études de courte durée s’il prévoit faire une demande pour un autre programme par la suite ou travailler sur le campus de l'université ou du collège qu’il fréquente à plein temps. L’article R215 prévoit une dispense visant à permettre à certains étrangers de présenter une demande de permis d'études après leur entrée au Canada.
Voir: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/francais/ressources/outils/temp/etudiants/qui.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/francais/ressources/outils/temp/etudiants/qui.asp)
Cordialement,
La boîte aux lettres des représentants en immigration

Please kindly confirm if the 12 months of full-time skilled work experience in Canada under the Canadian Experience Class must be continuous. For example, if an applicant works 7 months full-time, and then takes 4 months off, and then resumes the job for another 5 more months full-time, and all of these occurs in the 3 years before he/she applies, will the applicant still meet the minimum 12 months full-time work experience requirement?

threads.answer:
Good day,

Work experience does not need to be continuous under the Canadian Experience Class (CEC). Breaks in employment are acceptable provided the individual can demonstrate that they have acquired at least 12 months of full-time, or the equivalent in part-time, skilled work experience in Canada within the three years before they apply. threads.answer:
Good day,
QUESTION: Due to the date entered for an expired passport, the IMM5710 work permit will not validate. Is it acceptable to upload the form with a dummy expiry date and include the explanation in the Representative's submission letter in the online portal?
RESPONSE: Generally, as per subsection 52(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), a foreign national seeking to become a temporary resident must hold a travel document that is valid for the period authorized for their stay. In other words, the applicant must have a valid passport in order to submit the application for an extension of their work permit and remain in Canada. The validity of the work permit cannot exceed the validity of the passport.
Furthermore, paragraph 10(2)(d) of the IRPR states that the application shall include a declaration that the information provided is complete and accurate.
Therefore, applicants are not able to apply to extend their work permits with an expired passport.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox
