threads.question:
Dear Officer:
A number of our clients have asked for clarification on the Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) points amendments effective November 19, 2016 as outlined in the Ministerial Instructions Respecting the Express Entry System: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/department/mi/express-entry.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/department/mi/express-entry.asp)
1. To obtain 50 CRS points for NOC O, A, B jobs, the applicant requires a Qualifying Offer of Arranged Employment (aka "valid job offer"). One requirement for having a valid job offer is "your current employer made you an offer to give you a full-time job for at least one year if you are accepted as a permanent resident." The way this requirement is worded effectively requires an employment contract with at least an 18 month term from date of eAPR submission in order to cover the six month published processing standard for Express Entry and still have one year remaining once the applicant becomes a PR. The difference between an 18 month and 12 month contract is a concern for certain project-based industries, e.g. Visual Effects and Animation. For an applicant already working in Canada for the employer listed on their work permit, is it acceptable for the employment contract to be valid for one year from the date of eAPR submission rather than the date the applicant becomes a PR?
2.For LMlA-exempt work permit holders working for the employerlisted on their work permit, one requirement for having a "valid job offer" is "have one year of full-time work experience (or an equal amount of part-time work) for that employer".
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
a. Does this full-time work experience need to be in the same NOC the applicant is employed in at the time of the eAPR? If not, does this work experience need to be at a particular NOC level?
b. Does this full-time work experience need to be continuous? E.g. would six months of full-time work experience, followed by an employment break, followed by another six months of full-time work experience for the same employer be acceptable?
3. In the Ministerial Instructions Respecting the Express Entry System, Sections 15(7)(b) and 19(8)(b) relating to CRS points for Canadian work experience specify that "a period of self-employment... is not to be included in calculating a period of work experience." These Ministerial Instructions do not mention self-employment in relation to foreign work experience or a Qualifying Offer of Arranged Employment.
a. Can self-employment be included when calculating CRS points for foreign work experience?
b. Can self-employment be included when calculating CRS points for Qualifying Offer of Arranged Employment?
c. Can self-employment be included when calculating Arranged Employment points under the Federal Skilled Worker Selection Factors?
Thank you kindly,
Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Hello
Thank you for your email correspondence to 's Immigration Representatives mailbox.
You will find below the responses to your questions:
1. Question: For an applicant already working in Canada for the employer listed on their work permit, is it acceptable for the employment contract to be valid for one year from the date of eAPR submission rather than the date the applicant becomes a PR? Response: No. In the case of a fixed term contract, if an employer is not ready to support the permanent resident application of a candidate by offering a job offer of at least one year, then the candidate will not receive points for arranged employment. The intent of the change to a job offer duration of at least one year was to be more facilitative to certain types of employers who could not enter into indeterminate contracts. If the job offer has a fixed term, the end date must be at least one year from the date of PR issuance. That being said, IRCC recognizes that operational needs may change after a candidate() becomes a PR and does not require employers to keep their employees for a full year. If an employer is concerned about indicating a specific termination date on the letter of offer, they can continue to extend indeterminate job offers to their employees. This would meet the requirements of the Mls and the Regulations.
2.Question a) Does this full-time work experience need to be in the same NOC the applicant is employed in at the time of the eAPR? If not, does this work experience need to be at a particular NOC level? Response: No. As per subsection 29(2)(a)(ii) of the Ministerial Instructions, there solely exists the requirement for the foreign national to have acquired work experience for the same employer who is now offering a job going forward, but it is not a requirement of the Mls that the foreign national must be in the same occupation as they were when the work experience was acquired. The work experience must be at a NOC level 0, A or B. Question b) Does this full-time work experience need to be continuous? E.g. would six months of full-time work experience, followed by an employment break, followed by another six months of full-time work experience for the same employer be acceptable? Response: Yes, as stated in section 29(2)(iii) of the Ministerial Instructions, the foreign national must have worked for the employer listed on their work permit and have accumulated at least one year of full-time work experience, or the equivalent in part-time work, over a continuous period of work for that employer.
3.Question a) Can self-employment be included when calculating CRS points for foreign work experience? Response: Yes, provided that it meets the requirements of sections 25(1) and (2) of the Ministerial Instructions, as follows:
(1) For the purposes of sections 23 and 24, foreign work experience is work experience that
(a) is acquired by a foreign national outside Canada in one or more occupations listed in Skill Type 0 Management
Occupations or Skill Level A or B of the National Occupational Classification matrix;
(b) consists of full-time work experience, or the full-time equivalent for part-time work experience, with one or more
employers;
(c) is acquired within the 10-year period preceding the day on which points are assigned to the foreign national under
section 23 or subsection 24(1); and
(d) is remunerated by the payment of wages or a commission.
Requirements
(2) In order to be assigned points under section 23 or 24 for their foreign work experience, a foreign national
(a) must specify in their expression of interest the four-digit code in the National Occupational Classification that
corresponds to each of the occupations they have engaged in while accumulating their foreign work experience; and
(b) must have performed the actions described in the lead statement for the occupation as set out in the occupational
descriptions of the National Occupational Classification, as well as a substantial number of the main duties, including all essential duties, as set out in the National Occupational Classification.
Question b) Can self-employment be included when calculating CRS points for Qualifying Offer of Arranged Employment?
Response: Yes, indicating an applicant is self-employed would not preclude them from claiming arranged employment in Express Entry. However, it will disqualify them from the Canadian Experience Class.
Question c) Can self-employment be included when calculating Arranged Employment points under the Federal Skilled Worker Selection Factors?
Response: Yes, provided that the offer of arranged employment meets the requirements of R82(2) of IRPR, as well as the definition of R82(1) of IRPR, as follows: arranged employment means an offer of employment that is made by a single employer other than an embassy, high commission or consulate in Canada or an employer who is referred to in any of subparagraphs 200(3)(h)(i) to (iii), that is for continuous full-time work in Canada having a duration of at least one year after the date on which a permanent resident visa is issued, and that is in an occupation that is listed in Skill Type 0 Management Occupations or Skill Level A or B of the National Occupational Classification matrix.
The requirements of R82(2) to be awarded points for a valid offer of employment depend on the applicant's circumstances, and are summarized in the instructions found here under Applications received on or after January 1 2015.
We trust this information will assist you.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: CDN work permit-C20 - Extension-REP-2017-0760
threads.question:
Dear IRCC Officer,
Please advise if there it is possible to extend a C20 application within Canada. What are the eligibility requirements for an extension? Would a company just need to confirm that the reason for the initial continues to exists? What type of supporting documentation is required? Is there a limit to the time the work permit may be extended? I greatly appreciate your response to this request.

Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Good day,
QUESTION (1): Please advise if there it is possible to extend a C20 application within Canada.
RESPONSE (1): Under sections 199 and 201 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, a work permit holder may apply for a renewal (extension) of their work permit in Canada if they do so before the expiry of their present work permit. This information is available in our Help Centre: Can I apply to extend a work permit from inside Canada? QUESTION (2): What are the eligibility requirements for an extension?
RESPONSE (2): The eligibility requirements are the same for the extension as they were for the initial work permit. The employer and the foreign worker must continue to meet the reciprocity requirements.
QUESTION (3): Would a company just need to confirm that the reason for the initial continues to exists?
RESPONSE (3): Yes, the reciprocal agreement/ arrangement would have to be ongoing for the requirements of C20 to continue to be met for the extension.
QUESTION (4): What type of supporting documentation is required? Is there a limit to the time the work permit may be extended?
RESPONSE (4): You would have to provide the same supporting documentation as for the initial work permit, ensuring that it
is updated for the new work permit duration requested.
For your future information there are answers to most frequently asked question in the Help Centre.

threads.answer:
Good day,
QUESTION: Could you please indicate whether those citizens of Romania who no longer require a TRV to enter Canada may apply for a work permit at the port of entry, or if they must apply through a visa office?
RESPONSE: A Romanian citizen in possession of an eTA is not visa-exempt. Therefore, they do not meet the requirement of R198 (application for work permit on entry). R198 states that the foreign national must be exempt under Division 5 of Part 9 from the requirement to obtain a temporary resident visa. The new eTA for Romanian citizens who formerly held a Canadian TRV or presently hold a US visa is not described in R190 (Division 5 of Part 9) and therefore they must apply for and obtain their work permit prior to their arrival in Canada.
Regards,

threads.answer:

Question:
If a Canadian company is duly registered to do business in the United States, has an address in the United States, has a Federal Employer Identification Number (FEIN) and files a tax return in the United States as a company having a trade or business` in the United States, but does not have "permanent establishment`` in the United States, are we correct in understanding that the Canadian company can transfer an employee who has been working solely in the United States for the American division of the Canadian company to Canada?

The change in the definition of dependent child, from under 19 to under 22, only comes into force on October 24, 2017. For permanent resident applications that are submitted before that date, there are no provisions for the principal applicant to include a child between the ages of 19 and 21 on the basis that the age of dependent child is scheduled to change in the near future.
The age of a child of a Convention Refugee (CR) applicant for permanent residence (PR) is locked in on the date that the applicant's refugee claim was received. If IRCC receives a PR application for the CR prior to October 24, 2017,the current definition of dependent child would apply -a 20-year old child would not qualify. threads.subject: Implied status-different Work Permits-REP-2017-0833
threads.question:
I have had this situation come up in a number of cases, and want to make sure I’m giving the right advice. Client is in Canada on either a PG-WP, or an IEC-WP (working holiday), marries a Canadian, and an Inland Sponsorship and Open WP applications are filed. If their original WP expires before the new Open WP is issued, I know they still have status, but can they still work during that gap?
I found this in the FAQ, but it talks about Study v Work Permit, not 2 different types of WP:
I have applied for a new work permit. Can I stay in Canada if my work permit expires?
Yes. You can stay in Canada, and may be able to keep working, under what's called implied status. That means the law implies you are a temporary resident. The implied status lasts until Citizenship and Immigration Canada (CIC) decides on your new permit application. However, you must respect the following requirements:
If you applied for another work permit
You must stay in Canada and meet the conditions of your original work permit. If you applied for a work permit extension before your work permit expired, you can keep working under the same conditions as your existing permit until CIC decides on your application unless you have applied to extend your stay under another category.
If you applied for a different kind of permit
You cannot do any of the activities allowed by the original work permit. For example, you may have come to Canada as a worker and then applied for a study permit. If so, you must stop working once your work permit expires. After that, you cannot work or study until you get a new permit.

Les certificats de police sont requis pour le demandeur et tous les membres de la famille qui l'accompagnent âgés de 18 ans ou plus, et doivent être fournis pour chaque pays ou territoire (sauf le Canada) dans lequel les demandeurs ont passé au total six

Good day,

Police Certificates are required for the applicant and all accompanying family members who are 18 years of age or older, and must be provided for each country or territory (except Canada) in which the applicants have spent a total of six (6) months or more since the age of 18. The total amount of time spent in the country or territory does not have to be consecutive (in a row). For example, if an applicant lives in Canada but commutes back and forth to the USA on a daily basis for 6 months or more, the applicant would require a Police Certificate from the USA.
Police Certificates are also required whether or not they had an established residential address during that time.

threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your question on clinical laboratory workers who may require a medical examination.
Question:
Would you have guidelines to determine whether a medical exam is required? For example, here are a number of questions we
have relating to the subject:
- is the medical exam required only in cases where there are direct contacts with a patient?
- would laboratory technicians working on the fabrication of medication to be sent to patient be required to do the exam even though they do not see patients?
- would quality assurance workers, testing medication for quality with sample that do not return to the lab and are not sold to patients be required to do the exam?
- would sales representatives visiting medical clinic with samples be required to do the exam?
Answer:
Certain foreign nationals must pass the medical examination prior to working in Canada. As per R30(1)(a)(ii), the medical examination is required for the protection of public health; not only for a vulnerable portion of the population. For example, the medical examination detects and prevents the transmission of communicable diseases such as tuberculosis. Different factors need to be taken into account when reviewing the tasks of a worker; e.g. direct contact with patients and/or medication to be distributed to the general public, working in a confined laboratory with other personnel members, etc.
Scenarios
- is the medical exam required only in cases where there are direct contacts with a patient? No. Although a foreign working in an occupation that has direct contact with a patient does require a medical examination, it is not the only factor in determining whether the medical examination is required or not.
- would laboratory technicians working on the fabrication of medication to be sent to patient be required to do the exam even though they do not see patients? Yes. Since the medication will be distributed for patients to take, then a medical examination is required in order for a work permit to be approved, as long as all other requirements are met.
- would quality assurance workers, testing medication for quality with sample that do not return to the lab and are not sold to
and Cizenship Canedaot Citoyenneté Canada Lnfomanduvduon patients be required to do the exam? No. If the medication that the worker is testing is not intended for distribution or to be returned to a laboratory where it would be handled by other personnel members, then a medical examination is not required.
- would sales representatives visiting medical clinic with samples be required to do the exam? Are the samples sealed and remain sealed during the sales transaction? If so, then a medical exanination would not be required. Please note that our answers based on the limited information provided on each scenario. In order to determine whether or not a medical examination is required, all tasks that will be performed by each occupation must be clearly defined. We trust this information is helpful. threads.answer:
ImmigrationKepresentatives
Good day,
QUESTION: Could you explain if a franchising agreement between a Canadian company (registered in Canada and has active business operations in Canada) and a company outside Canada (registered and has active business operations outside Canada) could be used as a basis for an application for a Temporary Resident Visa (TRV) to enter Canada as a Business Visitor – Intra-company trainee?
RESPONSE: Intra-company transferees are required to obtain work permits for work they will perform in Canada. Franchises are not considered a qualifying relationship unless you can prove that both Canadian and foreign franchise are a parent, subsidiary, branch or affiliate business relationship with the other.
Business visitors are work permit exempt and must meet the requirements for R187 in order to qualify as such.
Please review the information on Business visitors (portions copied below for ease of reference) at International Mobility Program: Authorization to work without a work permit-Business visitor [R186(a)]
General crite ria
- There must be no intent to enter the Canadian labour market (i.e., no gainful employment in Canada).
- The activity of the foreign worker must be international in scope (i.e., that is, there is the presumption of an underlying cross-border business activity, e.g., after-sales service).
- There is the presumption of a foreign employer, as o the primary source of the worker's remuneration remains outside Canada; the principal place of the worker's employer is located outside Canada; o the accrual of profits of the worker's employer is located outside Canada.
Trainers and trainees
Paragraph R187(2)(b) also covers persons entering Canada to provide familiarization or training services to prospective users or to maintenance staff of the establishment after installation of specialized equipment purchased or leased outside Canada has been completed. It also covers intra-company trainers and trainees.

Answer :
The policy intent on short-term work permit exemption is that the periods of work have to be consecutive (30 consecutive days in 12 months). Applicants would still be allowed to leave and enter Canada; however, any travel outside of Canada after the start date of their work in Canada will not add days to the exemption. Once the work starts, the days will be counted consecutively, regardless of whether the person is working after or not or whether they were in Canada or not. Moreover, upon return to Canada, it will be the responsibility of the foreign national to demonstrate to an officer that their original period of work has not elapsed. The officers' guidance on short-term work permit exemption will be updated to add that the periods of work have to be consecutive.
Upon request, border services officers (BSOs) may issue a visitor record authorizing the foreign national to work.
We trust this information is helpful.
Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Dear Ms.
Normally, the request for the Schedule A should appear in the portal as soon as you link the application to your representative account.
Schedule As can be submitted without an ink signature through the Client or Representative Portals because-when any document is submitted this way-there is an additional electronic signature process built into the portal, which is linked to a credential such as an individual's GCKey. Documents submitted through our Web Form require an ink signature because a submission through the web form does not involve providing the same kind of secure electronic signature.
Therefore, we are unable to accept an electronically signed Schedule A without an ink signature through the Case Specific Enquiry form.
It is true that you cannot upload a printed, and then rescanned, Schedule A, through the portal. This is because scanned documents (as they are effectively a "photocopy" of a piece of paper) do not contain "in the background" (ie. within the PDF file) the client information which a saved, validated PDF form has. The portal will not accept a scanned PDF because this data is missing.

threads.subject: ESL Student-PGWP & Spousal Work Permit-REP-2017-1213
threads.question:
My client is studying ESL at on a study permit. She will not be eligible to obtain a degree, diploma or certificate upon completion. The program is full-time and one year long, and her study permit reflects this. I have two questions:
1. Can she apply for a Post Grad Work Permit upon completion? I assume not.
2. While she is studying can her spouse apply for a spousal work permit?
Best,
threads.answer:
Hello
This is in response to your enquiry sent on July 11 regarding language studies, post-graduation work permits and spousal work permits.
Question 1:
Can she apply for a Post Grad Work Permit upon completion? I assume not.
Answer: As per the PDl on the Post-Graduate Work Permit Program, only graduates of programs which confer degrees, diplomas or certificates are eligible. In addition, they must have graduated from a program at a designated learning institution (DLI) which has been designated by the province or territory in which it is located as eligible for the program.
As the program in your example does not confer degrees, diplomas or certificates, it would not be eligible for the Post-Graduate Work Permit Program.
Question 2: While the principal applicant is studying, can her spouse apply for a spousal work permit?
Answer: Accompanying spouses or common-law partners of foreign students are eligible for an open work permit (some restrictions may be imposed depending on whether a medical examination has been passed ) under the C42 labour market impact assessment (LMlA) exemption [R205(c)(ii)], if their spouse or common-law partner is a study permit holder and a full time student at: a public post-secondary institution, such as a college, university, or CEGEP in Quebec; a private post-secondary institution that operates under the same rules and regulations as a public institution and receives at least 50 percent of its financing for its overall operations from government grants (currently, only private college-level educational institutions in Quebec qualify); or
- a Canadian private institution authorized by provincial statute to confer degrees.
Specific programs of study are not currently listed (or excluded) under this LMIA exemption. As a result, a spouse of a study permit holder undertaking ESL studies on a fulltime basis at an eligible institution would still be eligible for an open work permit under C42.
I hope that this information is helpful to you. If you have any further enquiries, you may contact us at .
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Lonely Canadian sponsorship-REP-2017-1362
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam,
We are in the process of preparing an application for a client (a Canadian citizen who does not have any other family members – parents, siblings, children, aunts/uncles, nephews/nieces who are Canadian citizens/permanent residents/registered Indians in Canada) to sponsor her adult daughter for permanent residence in Canada. Based on our review, we have determined that the package to use is Sponsoring of adopted children and other family [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/information/applications/family.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/information/applications/family.asp). However, the document checklist noted [IMM5287] does not require the sponsor to provide proof of being a lonely Canadian in support of her application.
Are we to just simply do a family tree? Is there another form required?
Please advise.
Thank you,
threads.answer:
Ms.
Thank you for your question.
Immigration and Refugee Regulations 117 (h) provides the opportunity to reunify a single, unattached person who is either a permanent resident of Canada or who is a Canadian Citizen, who has no close family member or relative in Canada, together with a family member who lives outside of Canada.
Evidence that may be provided by the sponsor as proof that she is alone in Canada may include documents such as tax returns, insurance policies, home ownership or a rental agreement. Please note the applicant may also provide any other credible documentation as proof that she is alone and have no other members of the family class who she can sponsor. An officer will review the documentation and if necessary seek clarification from the applicant.
The applicant should also provide proof of relationship between the sponsor and her daughter. This can take the form of a birth certificate, baptismal certificate or any other credible documentation.
For more information about the documentation our Department accepts and how our Department assesses relationships,
please review the online manual, Processing Members of the Family Class, OP 2.
Note that the guidance offered on-line and in these email responses is for reference only and our Department's officers assess each application on an individual basis.
Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: 'New" admission when returning to Canada from the U.S. or when referred back by I.N.S. - REP-2017-1322
threads.question:
Dear Officer,
Please clarify the following:
If a temporary resident who has a valid work permit in Canada, leaves Canada to go to the U.S. (and the U.S. only) is admitted to the U.S. and then returns to request a modification to his or her work permit (e.g. change of place of employment or employer) at a Canadian port of entry, is the return considered a new "admission" to Canada or rather a continuation of the earlier authorized period of admission as a temporary resident?
If the same temporary foreign worker travels to the U.S./Canada border but is referred back to the Canadian port of entry by the INS, is that a new "admission"? Can the temporary foreign worker be denied re-admission to Canada?
If possible, please refer to any relevant statute, jurisprudence or section of a manual or the IRCC website that may permit a deeper and more detailed comprehension of your response.
Thank you in advance for your anticipated reply to this question.
Sincerely,
Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Dear Mr.
Question:
If a temporary resident who has a valid work permit in Canada, leaves Canada to go to the U.S. (and the U.S. only) is admitted to the U.S. and then returns to request a modification to his or her work permit (e.g. change of place of employment or employer) at a Canadian port of entry, is the return considered a new "admission" to Canada or rather a continuation of the earlier authorized period of admission as a temporary resident?
Response:
The foreign national's return is considered a new “admission" to Canada.
Every time a foreign national seeks entry to Canada, the border services officer must be satisfied that the foreign national meets all the admissibility requirements. In addition, a foreign national who holds a valid work permit, and who wishes to change their conditions or renew their work permit may be eligible to apply for a work permit after entering Canada in Canada, pursuant to section 199(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations.
Foreign nationals may have specific conditions imposed on them with the work permit. These conditions may include not authorized to work at any other location'. If this condition is imposed and a location is specified then the worker would need a new work permit (including a new offer of employment in case of an LMIA-exempt work permit) in order to change locations. The applicant, in such case, may be eligible to apply to change their work permit conditions. The Application to Change Conditions or Extend Your Stay in Canada as a Worker can be found on the IRCC website.
Question:
If the same temporary foreign worker travels to the U.S./Canada border but is referred back to the Canadian port of entry by the INS, is that a new "admission"? Can the temporary foreign worker be denied re-admission to Canada?
Response:
Same as above.
We trust this responds to your question.
Regards,

and Cizenship Canedaot Cioyenneté Canada

Hello
Apologies for the delay in responding.
In general, a self-employed person means someone who has relevant experience who would be able to be self-employed in Canada and contribute to Canada's economy in one of the eligible areas.
In terms of performance, "world class” normally refers to those who are known internationally. However, it also identifies persons who may not be known internationally, but perform at the highest levels in their discipline and is intended to include those who have the ability to compete in athletics either through performance at a world-class level or the ability to be self-employed in a discipline, as in the case of figure skaters or coaches.
As to whether or not this includes athletes in the ASEN Para Games, in the end, the decision is left to the discretion of the officer who must consider an applicant's experience, intent and ability to create their own employment in Canada. This also includes a person's financial assets, as a measure of intent and ability to establish economically in Canada, as there is no minimum investment for a self-employed person. The capital required depends on the nature of the work. Applicants must have sufficient funds to create an employment for themselves, to support themselves and their family members. They must show that they have been able to support themselves and their family through their talents, and that they would likely continue to be able to do so in Canada.

Dear Sir/Madam:
I have a question regarding study permits and working off campus for students enrolled in an English language Foundation program.
Section 186(v)(ii) states that a foreign national may work in Canada without a work permit if they are the holder of a study permit and the program in which they are enrolled is a post-secondary academic, vocational or professional training program, or a vocational training program at the secondary level offered in Quebec, in each case, of a duration of six months or more that leads to a degree, diploma or certificate.
However, IRCC's website also notes that individuals who are studying English or French as a second language cannot work off campus without a work permit. (see here: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/study/work-offcampus.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/study/work-offcampus.asp))
My question is, can a foreign national, who is issued a letter of acceptance from a designated learning institution (DLI) that states the individual is enrolled in a vocational program, (and is issued a four year study permit that notes that he is allowed to accept employment off campus), work off campus if he/she is currently enrolled in a one year, full time English Language

threads.answer:
Hello

Question: If an applicant has worked 52 weeks, but some of the weeks were part-time (let's say 15 hours per week) and some weeks were 90 hours per week, can we add all the hours together and if we reach 1560 hours an applicant will be eligible?
Response: For the purpose of meeting the eligibility requirement of work experience for CEC in accordance with Ministerial Instructions, the maximum hours calculated for the weeks the candidate worked full time would be 30 hours, the hours worked in access of 30 in any one week will not count toward the 1560 hours required to meet eligibility. For example, all weeks the candidate worked more than 30 hours of work, the system will calculate as 30, and all other weeks would be added based on the information given. Additional information could be uploaded to show the actual hours worked by week if you think this would best illustrate how the person met the 1560 requirement.
Please note that if your client is invited to apply based on a system calculation that you consider to be early, you may want to decline that invitation until the hours required are met.

threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives mailbox. We trust that you will find the answer to your question below of assistance.
Question: I have a question with regard to doctors in Canada applying for PR through Express Entry. Although all doctors in Canada are, for tax purposes, considered "self-employed”, having to invoice a health authority for their work as opposed to being on payroll, I would like clarification that a doctor with an LMIA and work permit naming a specific health authority for which they can work (for example, the Fraser Health Authority), would not be considered “self-employed" for IRCC purposes. The work permit dictates they can only work for one health authority, but because of the structure of our medical system, mandates that they bill for their work rather than being put on a hospital's payroll.
Answer: IRCC officers consider the following factors in determining whether an applicant is considered an employee or self-employed:
- the degree of the worker's control or autonomy in terms of how and when work is performed, and the method(s) used to do the work;
- whether the worker owns and/or provides tools and equipment to accomplish the work;
- the degree to which the worker has to perform the work personally and whether the worker has the option of subcontracting work or hiring others to help and assist with completing the work;
- the degree of financial risk assumed by the worker, including whether the worker is required to make any investment in order to complete the work or provide the service and whether the workeris free to make business decisions that affect his/her ability to realize a profit or incur a loss (as opposed to the opportunity to earn commissions or other productivity bonuses); and
- any other relevant factors, such as written contracts. The onus is on the applicant to satisfy the officer that an employee-employer relationship exists as part of the eligibility requirement. Please note that an applicant may choose to request a ruling from the CRA to have their specific employment status determined. Such a ruling will state whether, in the view of the CRA, a worker is an employee or self-employed, and whether or not that worker's employment is pensionable or insurable. A worker may request a ruling by sending a letter or completed Form CPT1, Request for a Ruling as to the Status of a Worker under the Canada Pension Plan and/or the Employment Insurance Act to their tax services office. This ruling may thereafter be submitted to IRCC to supplement a PR application.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Caring for Children pathway-REP-2017-0535

Hello,
Does work experience under NOC 4411 obtained on an open work permit qualify for the Caring for Children pathway?

threads.answer:
Dear
Apologies for the delay in responding, we appreciate your patience.
Yes, an applicant with an open work permit working in a caregiver occupation may qualify to apply for permanent residence under the Caring for Children Class provided the applicant meets all the requirements for permanent residence. Please note that the onus is on the applicant to provide evidence to demonstrate that they meet the requirements of the Caring for Children Class and that they have performed the duties listed in the NOC 4411 job description.
In addition, in lieu of a LMIA, the officer assessing the application may rely on other documentation to ensure that the full-time employment offer was bona fide (ie. employer paid wages at the rate required for that occupation and provided the required benefits and workplace insurance) for the full two years. In order to assess whether the employment offer was fair and genuine, a written contract between the employee and employer, signed in advance of the work period must outline the list of duties to be performed, the employment conditions as well as details about mandatory benefits, wages, workplace safety insurance coverage, hours of work, sick and vacation leave and any other conditions of employment. The officer assessing an application for permanent residence may request additional documentation or information in order to be satisfied that the employment offer was fair, genuine and that it met all mandatory requirements. For example, the officer assessing the application may request additional information from the employer such evidence that he/she has sufficient income to justify hiring a caregiver and pay the required wages/benefits as well as evidence that the Federal, Provincial/Territorial Income Tax Deductions, Employment Insurance premiums and the Canada Pension Plan contributions have been transferred to the Canada Revenue Agency.
Payments can be made through a caregiver recruiting agency, however, the onus would be on the applicant to satisfy the officer that they meet all of the requirements.

threads.subject: Diplomats-extensions as regular temporary residents in Canada-REP-2017-1377
threads.question:
Hello,
I am looking for guidance on whether a person who is a diplomat can make an application for a regular work permit/study permit while inside Canada to Vegreville. Or if they would need to make that application to a visa office.
The attached guidelines seem to indicate this may be a possibility as long as they receive a no objection letter from the embassy/consulate?

threads.answer:
Hello
This is in response to your August 7th enquiry regarding the process to regularize a diplomat's status after the end of their diplomatic posting in Canada.
Question: I am looking for guidance on whether a person who is a diplomat can make an application for a regular work permit/study permit while inside Canada to Vegreville. Or if they would need to make that application to a visa office.
Response:
Regulation R199(i) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations provides foreign nationals with the authority to apply for a work permit after entering Canada by submitting their work permit application to CPC-Vegreville if they hold a written statement from Global Affairs Canada (GAC) stating that it has no objection to the foreign national working at a foreign mission in Canada.
Diplomats (or foreign representatives) may apply for a regular work permit or study permit after their posting is completed. They are subject to the regular procedures for applying for a work permit or applying for a study permit.
When applying online, they should use the Application to change conditions, extend your stay or remain in Canada as a Student or as a Worker as they are eligible to apply for an extension to their temporary resident status from within Canada. The GAC non-objection letter can also be attached as part of their submission. Their application will be processed at CPC-Vegreville and no further changes in the existing protocol will be necessary.
Question: The attached guidelines seem to indicate this may be a possibility as long as they receive a no objection letter from the embassy/consulate? Specifically if a diplomat's official post will end, how would they go about extending their status in Canada as a regular student/worker.
Response: The attached guidelines pertain to family members of foreign representatives wishing to remain in Canada after the principal employee's departure for purposes of continuing their education. As per instructions in section 4.5 of the attached Guidelines:
4.5 Inland Application for Study Permits: Family members having obtained the "No Objection" Note or Letter must subsequently apply for an extension of their temporary residence status in Canada and the study permit, and pay the related fee. Application forms (which accompany the "No Objection" Note or Letter) can be submitted inland to the Case Processing Centre-Vegreville, Alberta.
If the diplomat's official post will end, they are subject to the regular work or study permit application processes.
We trust this information will be of assistance.
Thank you,

threads.question:
CMB-IMP-Investigations / RDC-PMI-Enquetes (CIC)
Our firm represents a number of Canadian employers who employ foreign nationals who have been transferred to Canada under the Intra-company transferee category for senior managerial positions. In a number of these situations, the employer may want to enhance benefits after the senior manager has been working in Canada such as providing a car and paid accommodations that was not set out in the Offer of Employment filed. In order to ensure compliance, please advise whether the employer should file a new offer of employment in support of a new work permit that includes these enhanced benefits, or whether the employer should file the voluntary disclosure form IMM 5964. Please also clarify what the employer should do if they wish to make the enhanced benefits of a car and paid accommodation retroactive to the date that the work permit was issued. Thank you for your assistance.
and Cizenship Canedaot Citoyenneté Canada
L'information divulguée en vertu de l oi sur laccés à Tinfomation
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your enquiry and please accept our apologies for the delay in responding.
Question
Regarding providing enhanced benefits (car and paid accommodations) to the Intra-company transferee that were not indicated in the Offer of Employment, please advise whether the employer should file a new offer of employment in support of a new work permit that includes these enhanced benefits, or whether the employer should file the voluntary disclosure form IMM 5964.
Answer
The employer cannot amend benefit information in the Offer of Employment that was submitted to IRCC after the work permit has been issued to the foreign worker.
Providing enhanced benefits to the foreign worker after work permit issuance would not require the foreign national to obtain a new work permit. Typically, a foreign worker does not need a new work permit unless there has been a change to the conditions that affect the worker-i.e. employer, occupation orlocation.
Under the International Mobility Program, several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer (the employer who submitted the Offer of Employment) by the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) on issuance of a work permit based on an Offer of Employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must:
- be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works; provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the IRPR. In the circumstances of providing enhanced benefits such as you mentioned, proactive notification is not required under the International Mobility Program. However, employers may be inspected on the conditions listed above and they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not. The employer must keep all documents related to any changes from the original Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC. Employers who have concerns that they are not meeting conditions of the Offer of Employment can use the Voluntary Disclosure process (see bottom of page After hiring a temporary worker). More information about compliance inspections can be found at Employer Compliance Inspections.
Citoyenneté Canada
Thank you,

threads.subject: [CPD-2017-0684] FW: Policy Clarification-Citizenship Eligibility-REP-2017-1356
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam:
Please provide clarification, with regards to eligibility for citizenship, on treatment of time spent outside of Canada for international students on overseas exchange programs with participating Canadian colleges and/or universities, when the newly
passed amendments to the Citizenship Act fully take effect.
Question: Will international students, who become permanent residents of Canada, be able to count time as a half day for each day spent
overseas as an Exchange Student with a participating Canadian college/university who grant/award their
certificate/diploma/degree at the end of their program of study?
Best Regards,
Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Greetings,
The amendments to the Citizenship Act as a result of the passing of Bill C-6, maintain that physical presence inside Canada is the primary requirement to meet the residence requirement.
Provisions of Bill C-6 expected to take effect in the fall of 2017, state that applicants may count each day they were physically present in Canada as a temporary resident or protected person before becoming a permanent resident as a half-day toward meeting the physical presence requirement for citizenship, up to a maximum credit of 365 days. The client must be physically present in Canada in order to be eligible.
Time spent outside of Canada as a permanent resident that may be considered as equivalent to time physically present in Canada to meet the citizenship residence requirement remains unchanged under 5(1.01), 5(1.02) and 5(1.03) of the Citizenship Act.
Therefore, international students who are not yet permanent residents will not be eligible to count time outside of Canada on exchange programs as time that is equivalent to physical presence inside Canada. If however, the client is a permanent resident and meet the definitions under 5(1.01), 5(1.02) or 5(1.03) of the Citizenship Act, they may be allowed to use that time towards their residence requirement on their citizenship application.
Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your email. Regarding visa requirements, all Brazilian citizens require a temporary resident visa to travel to Canada. As you are most likely aware, the following change for Brazilian citizens came into effect on May 1, 2017.
Beginning May 1, 2017, Brazilian, Bulgarian and Romanian citizens are eligible to apply for an eTA if they are traveling to Canada by air and:
Have held a Canadian visa in the past 10 years, or ●hold a valid United States (U.S.) nonimmigrant visa (NIV)
If foreign nationals from these three countries do not meet the eligibility requirements listed above, they must then be in possession of a valid temporary resident visa (TRV) to travel to or transit through Canada. While nationals of Brazil, Bulgaria and Romania who meet the eligibility requirements of eTA expansion can apply for an eTA, they may still apply for, obtain, and travel with a temporary resident visa (TRV). As eTAs are only valid for air travel to or transit through Canada, all Brazilian, Bulgarian, and Romanian nationals travelling by land, sea, and rail must be in possession
of a valid TRV.
Generally speaking, if a foreign national already has a valid visa in their passport, it is not necssary to issue a new visa when a study or work permit is approved, even if the visa category is different. However, the validity date of the exisiting visa (if it will expire in the near future) may impact a visa officer's decision to issue a new one.
Without all of the case information before us, we cannot say definitively why the officer issued a new visa in one situation but not in another.
Thank you,

Please find a response to your questions below.
Scenario: International student completes four-year bachelor's degree from Canadian university. Then completes an 8-month master's program.
Question: Is the student eligible to apply for a post-graduate work permit, and if so, is the student eligible to obtain a 3 year PGWP?
Answer:
Who is eligible to participate?
To obtain a work permit under the PGWPP, the applicant must meet the following requirements:
have a valid study permit when applying for the work permit; have continuously studied full time in Canada (i.e., studies must have taken place at a Canadian educational institution) and have completed a program of study that is at least eight months in duration; have completed and passed the program of study and received a written notification from the educational institution indicating that they are eligible to obtain a degree, diploma or certificate. The educational institution must be one of the following: 0 a public post-secondary institution, such as a college, trade or technical school, university or CEGEP (in Quebec); O a private post-secondary institution that operates under the same rules and regulations as public institutions; O a private secondary or post-secondary institution (in Quebec) offering qualifying programs of 900 hours or longer leading to a díploma of vocational studies (DVS) or an attestation of vocational specialization (AVS); or Oa Canadian private institution authorized by provincial statute to confer degrees (i.e., bachelor's degree, master's degree, doctorate), but only if the student is enrolled in one of the programs of study leading to a degree, as authorized by the province, and not in just any program of study offered by the private institution.
Applicants must apply for a work permit within 90 days of receiving written confirmation (e.g., an official letter or transcript) from the educational institution indicating that they have met the requirements for completing their program of study. Calculation of the 90 days begins the day the student's final marks are issued or the day formal written notification of program completion is received, whichever comes first.
Other considerations
Work permit issuance and validity
Issuance
Work permits issued under the PGWPP are LMIA-exempt, may be open and may be valid for up to three years, depending on the duration of the program of study. They are normally issued by the Case Processing Centre in Vegreville (CPC-V). However, by virtue of sections R197 and R198, work permits under the PGWPP may also be issued by POEs or visa offices overseas. For administrative purposes, it is more facilitative to refer clients to apply online or on paper to the CPC-V.
When work permits are being issued by POEs or visa offices overseas, officers should ensure that the appropriate fields and screens in the Global Case Management System (GCMS) and the Field Operations Support System (FOSS) are populated.

Validity
Work permits issued under the PGwPP may be valid for up to three years. When determining the length of a post-graduation work permit that can be issued, officers should consider the program length as confirmed by the DLI in the written confirmation of program completion (e.g., an official letter or transcript).Regularly scheduled breaks (e.g., regularly scheduled winter and summer breaks) should be included in the time accumulated toward the length of the work permit.
Examples:
If the duration of the program of study is at least eight months but less than two years, the duration of the work permit should coincide with that of the program of study as confirmed by the DLl in the written confirmation of program completion*(e.g., an official letter or transcript).Regularly scheduled breaks (e.g., regularly scheduled winter and summer breaks) should not be subtracted from the length of the post-graduation work permit. If the duration of the program of study is two years or longer as confirmed by the DLl, the duration of the work permit should be three years. Regularly scheduled breaks (e.g., regularly scheduled winter and summer breaks) should not be subtracted from the length of the post-graduation work permit. If a student obtained a one-year degree, diploma or certificate from an eligible institution in Canada after having obtained, within the prior two years, another degree, diploma or certificate from an eligible institution in Canada, the duration of the work permit may be up to three years.
*Officers may issue three-year work permits to individuals who complete a master's degree in Canada when the DLl has confirmed in the written confirmation of program completion (e.g., an official letter or transcript) that the degree is 16 to 23 months in duration and does not include regularly scheduled breaks.

Thank you for your question.
Answer to question 1-
While the job title is printed on the work permit, it is the National Occupational Code (NOC) that we assess against when issuing the work permit and conducting compliance inspections. There are usually many different titles associated to a single NOC code. As long as the duties, education requirements, salary, etc. of the occupation continue to match the NOC code then there should be no requirement for changing the work permit, and therefore, no requirement to submit a new offer of employment through the Employer Portal.
As per the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act Regulations (IRPR), a foreign worker is only required to obtain a new work permit when the employer, work location or occupation changes.
The employer is required [R209.2(1)(b)] to retain all documents related to the employment of the foreign worker for up to six years after the date of issuance of the work permit, including details about the title change, to ensure information can be provided to an IRCC officer in the event of an inspection.
For more information, see the section "Occupation, Wages and Working Conditions" in the Employer Compliance Inspections page on the IRCC website.
Answer to question 2-
lEC has specific rules about participations. If the foreign national has participated in one category (12 months of the 24 months) and the employer promoted the foreign national to a new position (different NOC), a new work permit would be required (this will count as a new participation to lEC). However, lEC program does not allow the foreign national to continue to participate in the same category twice. As such, the foreign national must either submit their name to participate in lEC in a different category (from Young Professional to Working Holidays, for example) or the employer must obtain an LMIA unless the foreign national is exempt from LMIA requirements under a different category /LMIA exemption. For more info, see the section Program requirements specific to each country or territory on the IRCC web page.
In terms of employer compliance with the International Mobility Program, it is important that the foreign national hold a work permit that accurately reflects the job that they are doing in Canada; and, that they are actually doing the job for which the work permit authorizes them to do [see Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) 183(1)(b) and 185]. It is also important that the Offer of Employment be filled out completely and accurately before it is submitted to IRCC [IRPR 209.11], that the National Occupation Code (NOC) indicated on the Offer of Employment is the correct one for the job and duties the foreign national will be/is doing.
Providing a salary that is higher salary to the foreign worker than the salary indicated on the Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC after the work permit was issued would not require the foreign national to obtain a new work permit. Typically, a foreign worker does not need a new work permit unless there has been a change to the conditions that affect the worker – i.e. employer, occupation or location.
However, several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer by the IRPR on issuance of a work permit based on an offer of employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works; provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the
IRPR.

The employer is required /R209.2(1)(b) to retain all documents related to the employment of the foreign worker for up to six years after the date of issuance of the work permit, including details about the title change, to ensure information can be provided to an IRCC officer in the event of an inspection.

While a marriage where one or both parties were not physically present is considered an “excluded relationship” under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, possible options are available to a Canadian citizen who would like to sponsor a foreign national they married by proxy, telephone, fax, internet or similar means.

QUESTlON: Please advise whether the foreign worker could be permitted to work across Canada, or if they should have the work permit amended to positively state permission to work across Canada (i.e. "Employment Location: Unknown" or "Remarks: Canada Wide Work Permit")
RESPONSE: If the condition is not written on the work permit (i.e. imposed) then technically the worker may work anywhere in Canada, however, the employer must be careful that moving the employee's location does not affect the condition regarding working condition' and that the LMIA-exemption would also apply in the different location.
In the case of an LMIA-exempt work permit, there are two different sets of conditions involved – those imposed on the employer based on the offer of employment, and those imposed on the worker as per the work permit.
Employer conditions: location' is normally considered as part of the condition that the employer must provide the ‘same working conditions.’ The change in work location can't be less favourable to the employee. In addition, the location can't be changed if the location was part of the LMIA-exemption requirement/justification (e.g. provincial nominees). IRCC does not require proactive notification of changes, but it is required that the employer maintain any documentation regarding the changes and provide it as justification at time of inspection. Employers who believe that they are not meeting conditions can use the Voluntary Disclosure process.
Worker conditions: the foreign national may have specific conditions imposed on them with the work permit. These conditions may include not authorized to work at any other location'. If this condition is imposed and a specific location is specified then the worker would need a new work permit (including a new offer of employment in case of an LMIA-exempt work permit) in order to change locations.
For future situations we do provide the following instruction to assist employers in providing accurate information in the Employer Portal User Guide: Physical job location Enter the location where the temporary worker will be working.

Dear I
Question:
If someone on a post graduate work permit were to apply for the Francophone Mobilité work permit, before the expiry of their PGwP, would they have implied status as a worker?
Response:
Regulation 201 allows foreign nationals to apply for a renewal of their work permit only if the application is made before their work permit expires. Regulation 186(u) allows foreign nationals to work without work permit if they have continued to comply with the same conditions as set out on the expired work permit, in the event that they submitted an application before their work permit expires [R201(1)], and a decision on the renewal of their application has not yet been made. This section applies to all work permit renewals that qualify under R201.
A temporary resident who holds a valid work permit can submit an application in Canada to extend their stay and work for a new employer, the same employer or apply for a different type of document, for example, visitor or student.
Working under R186(u) is available to all work permit holders who apply under R201 regardless of what initial work permit was issued under. R186(u) allows the temporary resident to continue working without a permit; but R183(6) requires that they continue to meet the conditions that were in place when the application for extension was submitted. In your case, the applicant is on a post graduate work permit (PGWP), if they apply for a Francophone Mobilité permit before their PGWP open work permit expires, they may continue working without a permit but under the conditions of their previous valid work permit (e.g., open employer, open occupation) until the decision is made on the renewal application and the new work permit issued. However, if they held an employer-specific work permit at time of renewal application, they may continue working with the same employer but they may not work for the new employer as that would be a different condition until a decision is made on their new application.
Please note that applicants on implied status who leave Canada before a decision is made on the new work permit-would not be able to resume work until a decision is made.
Applicants who are applying to change their authorization in Canada (e.g., from work to study) cannot benefit from the R186(u) provision because they did not apply under R201 to renew their conditions. However, they may benefit from R183(5) [extension of period authorized for stay provision]. They can stay in Canada as temporary residents (visitors) until a decision is made on their application.

the same NOC and duties-REP-2017-1538
Hello and thank you for your query,
Question
Can you please advise about situations where employers would want to raise the salary of an LMlA-exempt foreign worker (by 10-15% - e.g., through a research grant) and provide non-wage benefits, such health insurance and a housing subsidy, that had not been identified in the Offer of Employment. Having perused your relevant policy, I understand that the employer will not need to submit a new Offer of Employment and a new WP application would not be necessary-so long as the additional remuneration and benefits do not indicate a substantive change in the worker's duties (thereby taking the worker outside of the approved NOC profile).
Is my understanding correct?
Answer
You are correct. Providing an increase in salary as well as enhanced benefits to the foreign worker after work permit issuance would not require the foreign national to obtain a new work permit. Typically, a foreign worker does not need a new work permit unless there has been a change to the conditions that affect the worker – i.e. employer, occupation or location.
Under the International Mobility Program, several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer (the employer who submitted the Offer of Employment) by the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) on issuance of a work permit based on an Offer of Employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works; provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than
- those set out in that offer;
make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the
IRPR.
The employer cannot amend benefit information in the Offer of Employment that was submitted to IRCC after the work permit has been issued to the foreign worker.
Proactive notification to IRCC of salary changes, and additional non-wage benefits, is not required under the International Mobility Program. However, the employer who provided the offer on which the work permit is based is still responsible for ensuring that the wages and benefits are consistent with what was stated in the offer of employment. Employers may be inspected on the conditions listed above and, therefore, they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they
met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not. The employer must keep all documents related to any changes from the original Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC.
Employers who have concerns that they are not meeting conditions of the Offer of Employment can use the Voluntary Disclosure process (see bottom of page After hiring a temporary worker).

Reply:
Yes, non-unionized employers are precluded from using the C14 LMlA exemption. If the foreign national is not unionized, they would not qualify for an exemption under C14. In these cases, the majority of workers are unionized Canadians and the employment of foreign nationals performing essential work on the production is important to the production occurring in Canada and securing the Canadian jobs.

1.The position is unionized. Proof of unionized work not only protects the direct employment of Canadians, but demonstrates that the employment of foreign nationals performing essential work on the production is important to the production occurring in Canada and securing the Canadian jobs. For example, if digital media/visual effects positions are not unionized, the temporary foreign worker cannot access this LMIA exemption.
2. The relevant union or guild has no objections. We strongly encourage applicants to submit a letter from the relevant union or guild with their applications along with any other supporting documentation.

This is in response to your October 18th enquiry regarding your question about implied status and ability to work.
As per subsection 186(u) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, [http://laws-](http://laws-) lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/sor-2002-227/page-35.html, “a foreign national may work in Canada without a work permit until a decision is made on an application made by them under subsection 201(1), if they have remained in Canada after the expiry of their work permit and they have continued to comply with the conditions set out on the expired work permit, other than the expiry date". Since subsection 201(1), [http://laws-](http://laws-) lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/regulations/sor-2002-227/page-38.html, refers to work permit renewals, implied status does not apply when the work permit holder submits an application for a study permit.
Therefore, a work permit holder applying for a study permit while the work permit is expired does not have implied status on the work permit.
If the work permit is still valid for a few months and while it's still valid and the person applies for a study permit, the person can work during the original validity period of the Work Permit.

To clarify, a Visitor Record (VR) and the stamp placed in a foreign national's passport at a port of entry are two different things. A VR is an actual document (IMM1097) that is issued to a foreign national when an officer is of the opinion that their stay should be documented. The stamp in the passport is a record of the foreign national's entry into Canada. If there is no date written below the stamp in the passport, R183(2) would apply in that the period of authorized stay is 6 months.
As an example, super visa holders are eligible for a two-year visit on their initial stay only. A Border Services Officer of the Canada Border Services Agency, will stamp the super visa holder's passport and write a date two years out on their initial entry.
Section 183 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations details the conditions on temporary residents.
Ultimately Border Services Officer at the POE have the authority to determine the length of time that a temporary resident may remain in Canada.

A sponsor who is sponsoring a parent or grandparent must meet the minimum necessary income requirements for each of the three years immediately preceding the date of the application. The minimum necessary income requirement is equal to the Low Income Cut offs (LICOs) plus 30%, taking into account the number of family members for whom they are or will be financially responsible for, including family members of the principal applicant as described in R1(3).

Dear Mr
We apologize for the delay in our answer.
Question:
l’m seeking guidance as to what IRCC considers to be a “service contract” for the purpose of obtaining a T23 work permit. For example, can a Canadian employer directly hire a Korean engineer (assuming licensing issues are not at play) as an
Citoyenneté Canada
employee of the Canadian business? In other words, can there exist an employee/employer relationship between the Korean engineer and Canadian company?
Response:
A service contract corresponds to a contract for services that is an arrangement whereby one party agrees to perform certain specific work stipulated in a contract for another party. There is no employee/employer relationship.
In your example, in order to meet the requirements of the Korea-Canada FTA, the Canadian employer could hire a Korean engineer that is self-employed as an independent professional in order to fulfill a pre-arranged service contract granted by the Canadian employer. The Korean engineer would not become an “employee" of the Canadian employer. The engineer would come to provide a service that is directly linked to the service contract.
Question:
Perhaps another way of framing the question is “how broadly or narrowly is the concept of ‘service contract' interpreted?" Is an employment agreement (which is essentially a contract for services) an acceptable relationship in this case?
Response:
An employment agreement would correspond to a contract of service where there is an employer/employee relationship. A contract of service does not fall under this FTA.
The service contract (or contract for services) must be between the Korean company (or independent professional) and the Canadian company to provide a pre-arranged service contract. An employment agreement would not fall under the definition of a pre-arranged professional service which means a professional service to be provided in the territory of the other Party, the terms of which have been determined and documented prior to the entry of the professional into the territory of the other Party.
Question:
In the context of other FTAs (eg. NAFTA), an employee/employer relationship can exist as long as there is evidence of pre-arranged professional services. Is this also the case for “independent professionals” under the Korea agreement?
Response:
No, the Professionals category under the Korea-Canada FTA is different than the Professionals category under NAFTA.
Under the Korea-Canada agreement, an independent professional means a self-employed professional who seeks to
engage, as part of a service contract granted by an enterprise or a service consumer of the other Party, in an activity at a professional level. The professions are limited to architect, engineer, management consultant and veterinarian.
We trust this respond to your questions.
Regards,

For the purposes of IRPR section 222(1)(a), a study permit becomes invalid 90 days after the day on which the permit holder completes their studies and is graduated by their learning institution. Question:
We are considering offering a full-time faculty position to an individual who is a Palestinian Refugee born in Lebanon, who holds valid travel document for a Palestinian refugee born in Lebanon. He does not have a passport and is currently living and working in the U.S. If we were to obtain an LMIA (based on ESDC requirements) can he apply for a work permit as a temporary foreign worker using his travel document?
Response:
The foreign national may use their valid travel document in lieu of a passport to enter Canada as a foreign worker. It should be noted that the foreign national must meet all the eligibility and admissibility requirements.
Question: Is he also eligible to apply for Permanent Residence in Canada using the travel document and without a passport (assuming he meets the requirements of either the FSWP or CEC)?
Response:
Yes, the foreign national would be able to apply for permanent residence through in express entry with a valid travel document, if invited to apply. The travel document must show proof of status (citizenship or residency), as well as photo identification. The travel document must be issued by a government and include applicant's name, photo, date of birth, document number, and the issue and expiry dates, if applicable. A travel document is used only by individuals who cannot obtain a passport.

Who needs to complete an offer of employment If there is more than one company involved in hiring the temporary worker An offer of employment must be submitted for any temporary worker coming to Canada to work for a specific employer who does not need a Labour Market Impact Assessment. In some cases there is more than one employer or company involved in hiring the temporary worker. The employer who needs to submit the offer in these cases depends on the employment situation. There are two types of employment situations:
1. Contract of service: When a Canadian company hires a temporary worker directly, or accepts a transfer of a temporary worker from a foreign company. The temporary worker, usually, but not in all cases, would be on the Canadian company payroll and part of its human resources.
2. Contract for service: When a Canadian company contracts a foreign company, and the foreign company provides an employee to the Canadian company to fulfill the contract.
If you are a Canadian company that hires a temporary worker directly, or you accept a transfer from a foreign company, your company is the only employer. You must complete and submit an offer of employment. If you are a Canadian company that contracts the services of a foreign company, you must complete and submit the offer of employment, not the foreign company. This is because it is your Canadian company that is creating the need for the temporary worker to enter Canada. You must submit the offer even if:
- the temporary worker is, and will stay, an employee of the foreign company, and/or the foreign company is paying the temporary worker's wages.
In the situation your described, the Canadian entity would be the contracting company with a contract of service with the Mexican company. It is not required that the Canadian entity pay the wages of the foreign national. Instructions for completing that section of the offer of employment can be found in the Employer Portal User Guide
However, please be advised that the wages paid while the foreign worker is in Canada must comply with the applicable Provincial laws regardless of whether the wage is paid by the foreign entity or the Canadian entity.

Question: Would there be an issue if the foreign worker was paid through commission vs a flat fee?
Response:
As per subparagraph 203(1)(e)(i) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) the employer must provide the foreign national with substantially the same working conditions and wages, but not less favourable, than what was offered in the original Offer of Employment. It does not matter if the employer decides to pay the foreign national through commission or a flat fee as long as it was clear in the Offer of Employment how the foreign national would be paid.
Any substantial change from the Offer of Employment must be justified as per subsection 203(1.1) of the IRPR. Please note that wages under the International Mobility Program must meet the minimum wage requirement in the province of employment as per the condition to meet federal or provincial laws.
Proactive notification of salary changes are not required under the International Mobility Program (Led by ). However, this information may be requested along with justification for the salary change when the foreign worker applies for an extension of their work permit or a new foreign worker applies for a work permit for the same employer.
Foreign workers are also subject to other federal (such as ESDC who leads the Temporary Foreign Workers Program) and provincial or territorial legislative and regulatory requirements. Employers should also meet those requirements for compliance purposes.
For more information you may consult the instructions After you hire a temporary worker.

Réponse : Le 15 juin 2014, le code de dispense de l'étude d’impact sur le marché du travail (ElMT) C30 a été remplacé par les codes C31, C32 et C33.
Le code de dispense C32 (programme d'enseignement coopératif pour les étudiants étrangers de niveau postsecondaire) vise les étudiants étrangers qui ont l’intention d'occuper un emploi constituant une partie essentielle d'un programme postsecondaire de formation générale, théorique ou professionnelle offert par un établissement d’enseignement désigné (EED) au Canada. L'emploi ne peut constituer plus de 50 % de la durée totale du programme d’études. Si l’institution d’enseignement déclare que l'ATE est une partie essentielle du programme, alors une dispense C32 est requise. La lettre d’acceptation remise par l'EED doit indiquer clairement que le travail constitue une partie essentielle du
programme postsecondaire de formation générale, théorique ou professionnelle et que tous les participants sont tenus
de travailler afin d’obtenir leur diplôme ou certificat.
