Dans ce cas-là, les clients ont deux options :
A) Travailler hors campus sans permis de travail pour un maximum de 20 heures par semaine pendant la session et à temps plein pendant les congés réguliers (R186v).
Pour être admissibie, ils doivent :
détenir un permis d’études valide; être étudiant à temps plein inscrit dans un établissement d'enseignement désigné; être inscrit à un programme postsecondaire de formation générale, théorique ou professionnelle, ou à un programme de formation professionnelle de niveau secondaire offert au Québec; être inscrit à un programme d’une durée d'au moins six mois qui mène à l’obtention d’un diplôme ou d’un certificat; continuer de respecter les conditions de son permis d’études, ainsi que les conditions d’accès au travail hors campus (p. ex., ne pas travailler plus de 20 heures par semaine au cours d’une session régulière).
B) Soumettre une demande de permis de travail sous le programme Expérience international Canada sous la catégorie Coop/Stage qui permet de travailler à temps plein afin d’acquérir une expérience de travail reliée à son domaine d'études tout en effectuant un placement coop ou un stage à l'étranger. During the course of processing an application an officer may request additional information from applicants. In some circumstances an officer may request information to demonstrate that an applicant and their spouse have been separated. Please refer to 'IP8: Spouse or Common-law partner in Canada Class' found here: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/englisH/resources/manuals/ip/ip08-eng.pdf](http://www.cic.gc.ca/englisH/resources/manuals/ip/ip08-eng.pdf), for further information, including the following:
"Evidence of separation from the spouse may include
- a separation agreement; a signed formal declaration that the marriage has ended and that the person has entered into a common-law relationship;
- a court order regarding custody of children; and documents removing the legally married spouse(s) from insurance policies or wills as beneficiaries..."
As noted in the list above, a signed formal declaration may be one of the pieces of information provided by an applicant to demonstrate that a marriage has ended. However it is not in and of itself always deemed to be sufficient. Each application is assessed on its own merit separately by an officer who will determine when further information is required. Other factors such as family law in the country outside of Canada also play a role in this decision to request more information.
The IMM 5604 form (Declaration from non-accompanying parent/guardian for minors immigrating to Canada) is not sufficient to establish proof of custody.
When assessing the custody issue regarding a child, officers rely on the local authority with jurisdiction to determine legal custody to determine the legitimacy of the documents provided in support of a child application for permanent resident in Canada while always being concerned with the best interest of the child. In Canada, jurisdiction regarding custody issues rest with the provinces.
Custodial matters can be complicated and are assessed on a case by case basis and it is at the officer's discretion to seek more information to make a determination on the case. If the parent and child are seeking to remain in Canada permanently, the accompanying parent should be in possession of official documentation verifying that the non-accompanying parent has no claim to custody nor any objection to the removal of the child from the country of origin. Unless a Court order or official document had been issued with the explicit details or the custody arrangement, we cannot confirm that the IMM 5604 is sufficient as proof of custody.

Good afternoon,
Thank you for consulting with the Immigration Representatives Mailbox.
On November 21, 2014, the Governor in Council approved changes to the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and the Immigration Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), bringing into force amendments relating to the consequences for misrepresentation.
Previously, the consequence for misrepresentation was a two-year period of inadmissibility. With the changes described on November 21, 2014, the consequence is now a five-year period of inadmissibility and a ban on applying for permanent residence for the same period of time (five years). The period of inadmissibility (five years) begins on the date of the refusal letter for overseas applicants and begins once the the removal order is enforced for in-Canada applicants. It is important to check in with the Canada Border Services Agency prior to departing Canada to ensure the removal order is enforced and recorded as such.
The ban does not apply to applications for temporary residence; the procedures for inadmissible persons applying for temporary residence remain the same (i.e., if the person is inadmissible, they may be considered for a temporary resident permit (TRP) where warranted).
The Parole Board of Canada has the authority to grant and or issue a record suspension (formerly known as “pardons”) who have been convicted in Canada of an offence under an Act of Parliament. The Immigration Refugee Citizenship Canada officers do not counsel applicants about record suspensions. Only once a record suspension is issued to the applicant will the IRCC officer review the totality of the information before them in order to take a fulsome decision on the application for temporary or permanent residency.

The employer mitigated the situation by filing a new offer for the consultant's next visit to Canada.
Answer:
In the case of a LMIA-exempt, employer-specific work permit, several conditions are imposed automatically on the employer by the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) on issuance of a work permit based on an offer of employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works; provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the IRPR.
Under the IMP Employer Compliance Regime, employers may be inspected on these conditions and they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not. It is required that the employer maintain any documentation and provide evidence when requested to do so as part of an inspection.
Each work permit is issued based on the Offer of Employment provided. Once the work permit is issued the employer must meet the conditions in that offer until the end of the work permit
Employers who have concerns that they are not meeting the regulatory conditions can use the Voluntary Disclosure process (see bottom of page After hiring a temporary worker.
We strongly encourage all employers who think they may have violated an International Mobility Program (IMP) condition to submit a voluntary disclosure form, even if they believe they have mitigated the issue. The purpose of employer voluntarily disclosing is to encourage them to comply with the program conditions through self-monitoring. However, please note that disclosures are not meant to remove the employer's regulatory obligations.
Voluntary disclosures are beneficial to employers because:
IRCC may determine that the disclosure is not considered a violation, which results in no penalty; and if IRCC finds the potential violation may be considered non-compliance then initiates an inspection to assess the potential violation and makes a non-compliant determination, the disclosure may reduce the penalty calculation by 4 points if the disclosure is accepted by IRCC (i.e., the disclosure is complete/not missing information related to the potential violation, it's timely, it's voluntary/no other enforcement action or inspection is underway, etc.).
Depending on the number of points the employer has accumulated as a result of the violation, the penalty may end up being reduced to a warning letter.
Conversely, if IRCC initiates an inspection and the employer had not voluntarily disclosed before-hand and makes a non-compliance determination, the penalty could be more severe (e.g., an Administrative Monetary Penalty and/or a program ban).

Response:
Applicants can only benefit from these short-term exemptions if the necessary amount of time has elapsed since their last short-term exemption was granted. Consecutive uses are not permitted. They may be granted a subsequent exemption if they have not been granted a short-term work permit exemption in the last 6 months. If foreign nationals benefited from the 15-day exemption, when may a foreign national be granted a 30-day exemption or 120-day exemption? They may be granted a 30-day or 120-day exemption once 12 months have elapsed since the date they were granted the 15-day exemption. If foreign nationals benefited from the 30-day exemption, when may they be granted the same exemption again? They may be granted a 30-day exemption again if they have not been granted a short-term work permit exemption in the last 12 months.

Question: 1) is a TFW (with a valid work permit) who is leaving a position in Canada obligated to inform IRCC or CBSA that he will no longer be working for his current employer? If so, please advise how one can advise IRCC or CBSA? Please also advise if a TFW wishing to leave a position in Canada (or who is terminated) is required to relinquish his work permit at the port of entry?
Response: No, the TFW who terminates employment prior to the expiry date of their work permit is not obligated to advise IRCC or CBSA or to relinquish the work permit at the port of entry.
Question: 2) Is the employer of a TFW who wishes to fire or who is taking a position outside of Canada obligated to inform IRCC or CBSA? If so, please advise how they may do so.
Response: The employer can fire a TFW that does not carry out the duties agreed to in the contract, they can give the employee the required notice or pay in lieu of notice. For more information, contact your provincial or territorial labour standards board. Under the International Mobility Program, each work permit is issued based on the Offer of Employment provided. Once the work permit is issued the employer must meet the conditions in that offer until the end of the work permit. If the employer changes the offer – e.g. the job offer was for three years, and now the employer cannot provide employment for a period of one year during the validity period of the work permit, then this is considered to be not meeting the conditions of the Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC.
IRCC does not require proactive notification of changes to the Offer, but it is required that the employer maintain any documentation and provide evidence regarding the change and provide it as justification when requested to do so as part of an inspection.
Employers who believe that they are not meeting conditions can use the Voluntary Disclosure process (see bottom of page After hiring a temporary worker).
If the employee decides to take a position outside of Canada refer to answer at Question 1.

Answer #3b:
As per the program delivery instructions, spouses or common-law partners of full-time students may qualify for an open work permit under the C42 Labour Market Impact Assessment, if the study permit holder is full-time student at a designated learning institution (DLl) in Canada, which includes: a public post-secondary institution, such as a college, university, or CEGEP in Quebec; a private post-secondary institution that operates under the same rules and regulations as a public institution and receives at least 50 percent of its financing for its overall operations from government grants (currently, only private college-level educational institutions in Quebec qualify); or a Canadian private institution authorized by provincial statute to confer degrees.

Question 1
Since the offer of employment will be submitted by the Canadian company, as per IRCC instructions, what company must apply for / be listed on the permit as the employer of record? The US company or the Canadian company?
RESPONSE: The entity which makes the offer of employment is the entity that requires the foreign national's presence in Canada. In this situation, it would be the Canadian company as they are considered the employer for the purposes of the IRPR and will have the conditions imposed on them. It is not possible to have one entity submit the Offer of Employment and the work permit issued to another. The Canadian company must complete and submit the offer of employment through the Employer Portal.
Please refer to the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) which refer to an offer of employment as the basis for the work permit issuance.
The term ‘employer'is defined as:
.... a person, firm, corporation, contractor, or other association or organization in Canada which:
Indicates the intention to have an employer-employee relationship with a person who is a temporary foreign worker, and, Has an employer-employee relationship with respect to employees, as indicated by the fact that it may híre, fire, pay, supervise, or otherwise control and direct the employee in the material details of how their work is to be performed.
Regulation 200(1)(c)(ii.1) stipulates that an offer of employment is required to issue a work permit
As such, it is the Canadian entity who requires the presence of the foreign national to 'perform that work' and therefore is the one making the 'offer of employment'. This leads to subsection 209.11(1) of the IRPR that came into effect in February
2015. This is the section that links the 'offer of employment' to the employer for the purposes of the IRPR.
209.11 (1) An employer who has made an offer of employment to a foreign national referred to in subparagraph 200(1)(c)(ii.1) must, before the foreign national makes an application for a work permit in respect of that employment, provide the following information to the Minister by means of the electronic system that is made available by the Department for that purpose:
(a) their name, address and telephone number and their fax number and electronic mail address, if any;
(b) the business number assigned to the employer by the Minister of National Revenue, if applicable;

Dear Ms.
Question:
I would appreciate if you could provide confirmation that implied status allows a person to continue working under the conditions of an expired work permit when the pending application is filed;
a. Under a different category and where the conditions of each permit are the same (i.e. Open Spousal Work Permit (OSWP) to Bridging Open Work Permit (BOWP).
b. Under a different category where the conditions of each permit are not the same (i.e. OSWP/Post Graduate Work Permit to LMIA-based or LMIA-exempt employer-specific WP). Response: A temporary resident who holds a valid work permit and submits an application in Canada for another work permit is considered to be 'renewing.'A renewal of a work permit can be for a new employer, same employer or an open work permit. Working under R186(u) is available to all work permit holders who apply under R201 regardless of what initial work permit was issued under. R186(u) allows the temporary resident to continue working without a permit; but R183(6) requires that they continue to meet the conditions that were in place when the application for extension was submitted. For example, an International Experience Canada participant who nearly reached the validity period of their 24-months working holiday open work permit and received an offer of employment from a new employer to work in a different LMIA exemption. If the foreign national applied for a new work permit before their lEC work permit expires, they may continue working without a permit but under the conditions of their previous valid work permit (e.g., open employer, open occupation) until the decision is made on the renewal application and the new work permit issued. However, if they held an employer-specific work permit at time of renewal application, they may continue working with the same employer but they may not work for the new employer as that would be a different condition until a decision is made on their new application. Applicants who are applying to change their authorization in Canada (e.g., from work to study) cannot benefit from the R186(u) provision because they did not apply under R201 to renew. However, they may benefit from R183(5} [extension of period authorized for stay provision]. They can stay in Canada as temporary residents (visitors) until a decision is made on their application. Good day,
QUESTION(S): In the situation of a wife who has been determined a Convention refugee by the RPD in Canada and where the husband has been determined by the ID to be inadmissible to Canada
1. Can she choose not to include her husband in her PR application and will she still qualify for PR? In other words, her husband's inadmissibility will not prevent her from becoming a PR?
2. If she includes her husband in her application, will she be disqualified from PR because of his inadmissibility?
In response to the first question, as per the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations section 10(2), the application for permanent residence should contain all family members of the applicant, whether accompanying or not. Protected persons must list all family members living inside and outside Canada on their application for permanent residence.
Protected persons may choose to remove a family member from their application any time up to the point of being granted permanent residence. The individual who is “removed" from the application will not be granted permanent residence or issued a visa as a result of the application. The processing fee for that person will not be refunded once processing of the application has commenced.
Since the removal of a family member from the application will not change the fact that the family member has been listed in compliance with R10(2)(a), that family member may be sponsored in the future, provided that the individual remains otherwise eligible for inclusion in the family class at the time that the sponsorship application is submitted.
In cases where an included family member was never determined to be a protected person and wishes to be severed from the principal applicant's application (for example, the principal applicant has left Canada), they should be instructed to apply for permanent residence under humanitarian and compassionate considerations. Included family members who are not protected persons are subordinate applicants, and the validity of their application is entirely dependent on the granting of permanent resident status to an eligible protected person (applicant).
Source: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/perm/protect/family.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/perm/protect/family.asp)
Further to the second question, Convention refugees or protected persons, and the family members included in their application for permanent residence, may be granted permanent residence unless they are inadmissible under the following provisions: A34, A35, A36(1), A37 or A38(1)(a) or (b). The inadmissibility of a family member has no bearing on the admissibility of a protected person.

application be filed? or a new offer filed through the Portal?
RESPONSE: A new work permit is only required where there is a change in the conditions imposed on the employer or the employee. The information provided in the offer of employment become the conditions (wages, occupation and working conditions) imposed on the employer upon issuance of the work permit.
Employers should be aware that there are separate conditions imposed directly on the foreign worker and that changes to occupation, location, etc may not be allowed on the specific work permit.
Proactive notification of salary changes are not required under the International Mobility Program (Led by ). Increases in salary are not usually less favourable than’the salary provided in the offer of employment, and therefore would not require a change in the conditions. However, if the change in salary is accompanied by a change in the employee's occupation or additional duties that are outside of the National Occupation Classification (NOC Occupation) specified on their work permit, this would require a new offer and work permit.
The employer must keep all documents pertaining to the employment of the foreign national for six years beginning on the first day of employment. If there are any changes to the information that differ from what was provided in the Offer of Employment, then during an inspection, the employer will have to provide the documentation that justified the change as per subsection R203(1.1).
Employers who believe that they are not meeting conditions can use the Voluntary Disclosure process.

In regards to your inquiry, an applicant is not required to meet the settlement funds requirement if he/she is currently authorized to work in Canada AND has a gualifying offer of arranged employment. Note* A work permit on its own is not a job offer, even if it is an LMIA-exempt work permit. We understand the issue of whether or not settlement funds are required can seem complicated. Consequently we have tried to simplify the issue by providing you with an overview of the various scenarios below. Please keep in mind that CEC applicants are not required to provide proof of settlement funds in their eAPR. Other exemptions granted within programs are based on the type of work permit issued. So, for example, if an applicant applies under the PNP program, the exemption would be granted depending on whether or not they meet MEC for either FSW, FSTP or CEC and on the type of work permit issued.
Under the Federal Skilled Worker Program (FSWP) and the Federal Skilled Trades Program (FSTP), all applicants must meet the settlement funds reguirement, with the exception of applicants who meet one of the following scenarios:
Scenario Notes Applicant is currently working in Canada on a work permit that was issued based on a positive Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMiA) and has a valid job offer 1 See Note 1 from an employer in Canada. Applicant is currently working in Canada on an LMIA-exempt work permit that was issued in accordance with paragraph R204(a) or R204(c) and has a job offer 2 See Note 2 (with or without an LMIA) from an employer in Canada. Applicant is currently working in Canada as an intra-company transferee (ICT) under the General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS) on a LMIA-exempt work 3 See Note 3 permit that was issued in accordance with paragraph R205(a) and has a job offer (with or without an LMIA) from an employer in Canada.
Note 1: The requirements for a job offer to be considered valid are slightly different according to the program. Under the FSwP, a job offer is considered to be valid if it is for continuous, paid, full-time work that is for one year (permanent), non-seasonal and in Skill Type 0 or Skill Levels A or B of the 2011 National Occupational Classification (NOC) matrix, and if it meets one of the following two conditions:
The employer making the job offer has a positive LMIA, or The applicant is currently working in Canada in a NOC 0, A or B job on a work permit that was issued based on a LMlA; is working for the employer listed on the work permit; is authorized to work in Canada when submitting their application and when the visa is issued; and the employer has made the applicant a full-time job offer if accepted as a permanent resident.

While under the FSTP, a job offer is considered to be valid if it is made by up to two employers, for continuous, paid, full-time work that is for at least one year in a skilled trade occupation (job that starts with 72, 73, 82, 92 or 632 and 633 in the 2011 National Occupational Classification (NOC) matrix), and if it meets one of the following two conditions:
The employer making the job offer has a positive LMlA, or The applicant is currently working in Canada in a skilled trade job on a work permit that was issued based on a LMlA; is working for an employer listed on the work permit; is authorized to work in Canada when submitting their application and when the visa is issued; and the employer has made the applicant a full-time job offer if accepted as a permanent resident in a job that is in the same three digit level of the NOC as the current job.

Hello and thank you for your questions related to the short term work permit exemptions.
Questions 1:
Under the 30 day exemption, can a foreign national leave and re-enter under the same exemption during the same 30 day period? For example, if a foreign national seeks entry on September 1st, can they leave on September 5th and return on September 10th and remain in Canada until September 30th?
Response:
Yes, a foreign national may leave and re-enter Canada under the same exemption during the same 30-day period; however, the number of consecutive days of work cannot be extended beyond the initial number of days. The authorized work period begins on the first day of work indicated in the employment offer and ends in 30 days (or in 15 days). The onus is on the foreign national to demonstrate that they are still eligible to use the short-term exemption (30 days) and are still admissible to Canada.
Question 2:
Can a foreign national use both the 15 and 30 day exemption in the same year? For example, can a foreign national enter for 15 days in September 2017 and then 16-30 days in October 2017? If yes, then is it correct to say that the foreign national can re-use the 15 days exemption after six months (i.e. March 2018) and the 30 days exemption after 12 months, (ie. October 2018?)
Response:
A foreign national may use the 15-day short term exemption once every 6 months (in the example provided, the foreign national may re-use the15-day exemption in March 2017) and the 30-day exemption once every 12 months.

Based on the information provided, it is unclear if the mother is in Canada or not. New Ministerial Instructions came into force on January 1, 2017 to support the implementation of a new Randomized Selection Intake process for the parents and grandparents program (PGP). In order to sponsor parents and grandparents, the sponsor must first be selected under the Randomized Selection Intake process. If a potential sponsor is not randomly selected to apply to sponsor their parent/grandparent, they will have the opportunity to submit a new Interest to Sponsor form when the program reopens.
Applicants in the family class who's sponsors are found ineligible to sponsor may request humanitarian and compassionate consideration if they have selected to continue processing the application to overcome the requirement to have an eligible sponsor. However, this applies to cases where an application to sponsor has already been submitted. Ministerial Instructions with respect to the processing of applications for a permanent resident visa made by parents or grandparents of a sponsor as members of the family class and the processing of sponsorship applications made in relation to those applications – states that “A request made under subsection 25(1) of the Act from outside Canada and that accompanies an application that was not accepted for processing under these Ministerial Instructions, will not be processed." This means that requests for humanitarian and compassionate consideration (H&C) for persons outside of Canada will not be accepted unless the sponsor was selected under the Randomized Selection Intake process and submitted a sponsorship application.
If the sponsor's mother is presently in Canada, she may submit an In-Canada application for permanent residence on H&C grounds to BRO-Vancouver as per the H&C instructions on the cic.gc.ca website: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/information/applications/handc.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/information/applications/handc.asp).
Alternatively, parents and grandparents can reunite with their loved ones in Canada by applying for a Super Visa. The Super Visa is a multiple entry visa issued for up to ten years that supports family reunification by allowing applicants to remain in Canada for up to two years without the need to renew their status. The Super Visa assists with the long-term sustainability of the PGP program by encouraging temporary residence as an alternative to entering the permanent residence queue.

Good day,
Your question concerns the situation where an applicant who intends to apply for permanent residence under the Family Class is married to the sponsor while still being legally married to his first wife, and the possibility of applying as a common- law partner.
Applications for permanent residence under the Family Class are based on the relationship with a sponsor who is either a Canadian Citizen or Permanent Resident of Canada. Applicants must be truthful and self-identify their marital status within an application. If an applicant is married to the sponsor, they are legally required to indicate that marital status on the application.
A permanent resident or a foreign national may be found inadmissible to Canada for misrepresentation pursuant to paragraph 40(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act “for directly or indirectly misrepresenting or withholding material facts relating to a relevant matter that induces or could induce an error in the administration of this Act." The consequence to the applicant for a finding of misrepresentation is a period of inadmissibility of five years.
Section 126 of the Act also states that every person who knowingly counsels, induces, aids or abets or attempts to counsel, induce, aid or abet any person to directly or indirectly misrepresent or withhold material facts relating to a relevant matter that induces or could induce an error in the administration of this Act is guilty of an offence.
Applicants must meet the requirements of the category under which they apply. Under paragraph 117(9)(c)(i) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations “a foreign national shall not be considered a member of the family class by virtue of their relationship to a sponsor if the sponsor or the foreign national was, at the time of their marriage, the spouse of another person". For Canadian immigration purposes, R117(9)(c)(i) excludes from recognition marriages that took place when the sponsor or spouse was married to another person.
We hope you find this information useful.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

1) There is an exemption for showing proof of funds for skilled worker applicants that are currently working in Canada. Is there a similar exemption for Start-up Visa applicants? All applicants must show that they have enough money to support themselves and any dependants, even if they are already in Canada. The reason for this is that, if they are working on their start-up venture, they would not be earning income to support themselves. Therefore, all applicants must provide proof that they have the money when they submit their application. The amount they will need depends on whether they are single or if they have a family, based on the LICO amounts on our website at: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/immigrate/business/start-up/eligibility.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/immigrate/business/start-up/eligibility.asp). Applicants must clearly demonstrate that they have sufficient and available funds to meet the requirements at the time the application is made, as well as when the application is finalized. The funds must also be available, transferable and unencumbered by debts or other obligations. In addition, if they want to work on their start-up before they are granted PR status, they would have to apply for a Start-Up visa work permit which actually requires them to have 52 weeks of funds. For more information, please go to our website at: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/work/prov/business.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/work/prov/business.asp) The applicant's family includes: their spouse or partner, their dependent children and their spouse's dependent children. It also includes a spouse or dependent children who are permanent residents or Canadian citizens or dependants that are non-accompanying.

- Bank statement(s) or deposit book(s) of applicant (and spouse) that show accumulated savings. documents that show property or capital payable to the applicant (such as stocks, bonds, debentures, treasury bills, etc.) or
- Documents that guarantee payment of a set amount of money, which are payable to the applicant (such as bankers’ drafts, travelers cheques or money orders).

Please see our Program Delivery Instructions on Foreign workers: Work Permits for Start-up Business Class permanent resident visa applicants.
To be eligible for a Start-up Business Class Work Permit, the following requirements must be met:
the applicant must intend to reside in a province or territory other than Quebec; an Offer of Employment to a Foreign National Exempt from a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) [IMM5802] has been completed by foreign national as ‘self-employed' and the form and employer compliance fee have been submitted to CIC; a Commitment Certificate must have been issued by a designated entity indicating that the work permit applicant is “essential” and there are urgent business reasons for the applicant's early entry to Canada (i.e. section 8.0 of the Commitment Certificate is completed); and letter of support linked to a Commitment Certificate has been issued by a designated entity the applicant must have sufficient funds to meet the low income cut off for their family size for 52 weeks.
Applicants must show that they have sufficient funds to support themselves and their family members. The funds are to pay the cost of living for the applicant and their family during the first start up year when there may be little to no income from the start-up business.
Spouses and common-law partners of Start-up Business Class work permit holders may apply for an open work permit based on their status as a spouse or common-law partner of a high skilled worker (LMlA Exemption C41). This is why the proof of funds for the size of the family is required, regardless of whether they are accompanying or not.

This is in response to your inquiry regarding studies/training while on a work permit:
Foreign nationals are required to obtain a study permit for engaging in academic, professional, vocational or other education or trainingthat is more than six months in duration at a designated learning institution (DLl) in Canada.
As per paragraph R188(1)(c), foreign nationals may enter Canada or remain in Canada without a study permit to attend a course or program of study of six months' duration or less. This exemption helps to facilitate access to short-term courses, regardless of their subject matter. The course or program of study may be part-time or full-time and should be completed within the period authorized upon entry (i.e., up to six months).
(IRCC) recognizes that foreign workers may engage in occasional studies or programs of study lasting six months or less during their stay in Canada.
It is recommended that foreign nationals be encouraged to apply for a study permit for a short-term course or program of study if they intend to apply for another program afterwards or work on the campus of the university or college at which they are a full-time student. Section R215(1)(c), provides an exemption to allow certain foreign nationals (i.e., valid work permit holders) to apply for a study permit after entry to Canada.
For more information, please see our program delivery instructions on when a study permit is required: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/students/who.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/students/who.asp)

As detailed in R215, a foreign national may apply for a study permit after entering Canada if they:
(a) hold a study permit;
(b) apply within the period beginning 90 days before the expiry of their authorization to engage in studies in Canada under subsection 30(2) of the Act, or paragraph 188(1)(a) of these Regulations, and ending 90 days after that expiry;
(c) hold a work permit;
(d) are subject to an unenforceable removal order;
(e) hold a temporary resident permit issued under subsection 24(1) of the Act that is valid for at least six months;
(f) are a temporary resident who

Response for sending. Please close item.
If the foreign transferer plans to now have the U.S. entity pay the wage of the intra-company transferee, this would not require the foreign national to obtain a new work permit. A foreign worker does not need a new work permit unless there has been a change to the conditions that affect the worker, such as —employer, hours worked, wages paid, occupation or location.
Since there is no change in the job, the Canadian entity is still considered the primary employer.
As you know, several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer by the immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) on issuance of a work permit based on an offer of employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works; provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the IRPR.
Employers may be inspected on these conditions and they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not.
Proactive notification of salary changes is not required under the International Mobility Program. However, the employer who provided the offer on which the work permit is based is still responsible for ensuring that the wages paid are what was stated in the offer of employment regardless of the source of the pay. Employers who have concerns that they are not meeting conditions of the offer of employment can use the Voluntary Disclosure process (see bottom of page After hiring a temporary worker).
Furthermore, if the employer who provided the offer on which the work permit is based wishes to ensure that the situation is very clear in case an inspection occurs, they may choose to submit a new offer of employment reflecting the new wage situation in the alternate compensation scheme' field of the Employer Portal AND have the worker obtain a new work permit based on the new offer of employment.
However, regardless of who is paying the wage, the primary employer will always be responsible for ensuring that the worker is paid what was offered in the Offer of Employment for which the work permit was issued.

REP-2017-0177
Dear Ms.
Question:
If an individual residing outside of Canada submits an application for a Working Holiday work permit under the International Experience Class program, are there any rules or regulations that prevent that individual from travelling to Canada as a visitor while the work permit application is in process at an overseas visa office?
Response:
There are no rules or regulations that prevent an individual from travelling to Canada as a visitor while they have a work permit application in process. However, they must meet all the requirements to enter Canada as a visitor depending on their country of nationality (visa, eTA). In addition, foreign nationals who seek to enter Canada temporarily must satisfy an officer that they:
•intend to return to their home country and will not try to remain in Canada;
- have enough money to cover travel costs and support themselves while in Canada;
- do not intend to work or study in Canada unless they have a permit to do so;
- do not have a criminal record or are not a security risk; and are in good health (or have completed a medical examination, if required).
The applicant must keep in mind that the border services officer may question the true purpose of their visit to Canada given that they have a work permit application in process.
In the event that the applicant is in Canada as a visitor and the application under International Experience Canada (IEC) is refused, the applicant will not be authorized to work in Canada and will have to comply with any conditions imposed at the port of entry (POE).
If the application under lEC is approved, the applicant will need to present their letter of introduction at a POE, which means they will have to exit Canada if they entered Canada as visitor. They'll need this letter of introduction to receive a work permit under International Experience Canada when they enter Canada and show it to a border services officer at the port of entry (airport, land border, etc.). The letter does not guarantee entry into Canada or guarantee a work permit.

Question: is it possible to apply for PR under the new pathways and either include an open bridging work permit application in that same package, or apply separately but without a letter from IRCC confirming receipt of the PR application (we would include instead a copy of the PR application and proof of filing)?
Response: The applications are submitted separately -first the application for PR, and once the Acknowledgement of Receipt letter has been received, an application for a bridging open work permit may be submitted. Since the introduction of online applications, submitting two applications together is now only accepted in very rare situations, which do not include the scenarios about which you are enquiring.
As per the Program Delivery Instructions on applying for a Bridging Open Work Permit, an application for permanent residence must have already been submitted under one of the following classes: •Federal Skilled Worker Program, Canadian Experience Class, Federal Skilled Trades Program, Provincial Nominee Program, Caring for Children Class, or Caring for People with High Medical Needs Class.
Additionally, the applicant must: currently be in Canada, have valid status on a work permit that is due to expire within four months include a copy of the Acknowledgment of Receipt letter as a supporting document.
If the permanent resident application is not complete, the bridging open work permit application will be refused and the processing fees will not be refunded.
As per the work permit application, an applicant must first determine whether they will apply on-line or on paper.
If the applicant has not yet applied for permanent residence and is therefore not eligible for a bridging open work permit, regular work permit application procedures apply. Please visit our website for further information on applying for a work permit.
Finally, if the applicant's work permit has expired within the past 90 days, they may be eligible to apply for restoration of status.
We trust this information will be of assistance.

Hello,
Thank you for your question, we hope the information below is helpful.
Question: Can the employer simply agree to reduce the employee's hours without first filing a new Offer of Employment for an LMIA exempt work permit through the Employer Portal?
Response: Under the International Mobility Program employer compliance regime, the employer is required to provide the temporary worker with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same or better than those indicated in the offer of employment. Working conditions include non-wage related remuneration benefits and entitlements such as hours of work.
Several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer by the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) on issuance of a work permit based on an offer of employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works; provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the IRPR.
Employers may be inspected on these conditions and they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not.
In order to reduce the hours of work for a temporary worker – and remain compliant with regulatory conditions-the employer can submit a new offer of employment as well as pay the $230 compliance fee. The worker must then apply for a new work permit using the new offer of employment number.
Alternatively, since foreign workers generally only are required to obtain a new work permit when either the employer or job or location changes, proactive notification to IRCC of salary and hours of work changes is not required under the International Mobility Program. The employer who provided the offer on which the work permit is based is still responsible for ensuring that worker is getting what was stated in the initial offer submitted to IRCC, therefore, if employers have concerns that they are not meeting conditions, they can use the Voluntary Disclosure process (see bottom of page After
hiring a temporary worker) which is taken into consideration by the inspectors when assessing penalties for any violations of the conditions.
Sincerely,

Hello
This is in response to your enquiry from August 10th regarding post graduate work permit program (PGWpp) eligibility and regularly scheduled breaks. Please see below answers to each of your question: Question 1: Are students eligible for a PGwP if they took a scheduled break, as defined in the section of the website applicable to off-campus work? Answer: Yes, full time students who took regularly scheduled breaks, as defined in the Off-campus work program delivery instructions, are still eligible to PGWPP. Question 2: If a student's break meets the definition of a scheduled break, but does not fall during a traditional period, such as if a student takes the winter semester off rather than the summer semester, would they be eligible for a PGWP? Answer: Yes, the regularly scheduled break is a break taken between academic sessions (such as winter/summer holidays) as determined by the DLl. Thus, it can be taken in summer or in winter if the DLl recognizes it as a scheduled break. Question 3: Is there a maximum number of scheduled breaks that may be taken during the course of the year in order for a student to still be considered eligible for a PGwP? Answer: The regularly scheduled breaks' schedule is determined by each DLI. Therefore, IRCC does not define a maximum number of scheduled breaks that may be taken during the course of the year. For PGWPP eligibility purposes, the student must hold a full-time status during the academic session prior to, as well as subsequent to their institution's scheduled break. However, as per the definition of the scheduled break, the length of the regularly scheduled breaks should not exceed five month during each calendar year. Question 4: What mechanism will be used to confirm whether a student has studied continuously, given that the PGWP application does not require transcripts where a letter from the institution indicating the completion of degree requirements is submitted? Answer: In case where the applicant did not provide a copy of their transcripts with their application for a PGWP, the processing officer has the discretion to contact the applicant or the designated learning institution to request a copy of the transcripts to inform their decision, if need be. I hope that this information is helpful to you. If you have any further enquiries, you may contact us at .

Hello,
This is in response to your inquiry regarding Restoration. As per program guidelines, if the foreign national has lost their temporary resident status and submits their application within 90 days of losing their status, they may not continue to work or attend school. However, the foreign national must continue to meet the requirements of their stay and meet all the conditions of their permit. In order to apply for restoration, the applicant must continue to meet all eligibility criteria for an extension of their permit. For example, applicants seeking a study permit extension, they must provide proof of acceptance or enrolment in a designated learning institution. For applicants seeking a work permit extension, they must provide a copy of their job offer letter from a prospective employer or offer of employment number. Please see the following links for more information on Restoration of Temporary Resident Status: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/visa/validity/restoration.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/visa/validity/restoration.asp) [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/study/study-extend.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/study/study-extend.asp)

Dear
Please note that where an employer believes that a foreign national is eligible for a LMIA exemption or a work permit exemption (e.g., business visitor), they can request an opinion from one of IRCC's International Mobility Worker Units (IMWU) if the foreign worker is from a visa-exempt country and is currently outside Canada. The opinion given by the Unit is considered by border services officers at the port of entry. Requests and supporting documentation must be submitted at least 30 days before the date of the worker plans to enter Canada. IMWUs contact information can be found here: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/work/employers/apply-who.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/work/employers/apply-who.asp).
The IMWU service cannot be used if the foreign worker that an employer wants to hire is not from a visa-exempt country or is already in Canada. In such a case, it is the visa officer reviewing the work permit application who will determine if an LMIA exemption or a work permit exemption applies to the situation.
Scenario 1 Questions and Answers:
1) Is my understanding correct? If not, how am I wrong? Your understanding is correct. Foreign nationals do not have to 'fill out forms' at port of entry as the work permit application is verbal. However, the employer is required to fill out IRCC's 'Offer of Employment' in advance.
2) Is the appropriate LMIA exemption code T11? (see here: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/work/unique/airline.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/temp/work/unique/airline.asp)) - We would recommend C13 (Emergency repair personnel or repair personnel for out-of-warranty equipment) or T23NAFTA Professional (if the mechanic is an Engineer) but not T11 unless they have the specific agreement.
3) Is exemption code C13 a possibility as well? Are there others? Yes, if the maintenance is required in order for aircraft to be certified to leave the ground, as this may be emergency repair. If maintenance can wait for plane to return to foreign country then it would not be considered emergency repair.
4) What are the requirements for entry, in terms of documentation? By Regulation, the employer must provide the Offer of Employment using the Employer Portal prior to the foreign national's work permit application and the foreign worker must obtain a work permit.
5) With respect to the comment we heard from our client, is it the case that work permits were not required at some point in the last few years? We can't comment on past individual cases. Every final decision on who enters Canada and with what specific authorization is done by Canada Border Services Agency based on the information presented to them at the time of entry.
6) Alternatively or in addition, is it the case that some mechanics may not be (or have been) required to obtain a work permit by individual border service officers (for instance, depending on the airport)? Again, we cannot comment on past individual cases.
7) Is there anything that can be done to streamline entry and processing of such mechanics on a airline-wide basis or otherwise? We would suggest that they provide an 'Offer of Employment' for a 12 month period indicating an estimated time in Canada (e.g. employee will travel to Canada for 1 -2 days every week,...) in the Alternative Compensation Scheme area.
Scenario 2 Questions and Answers:
1) May USA Carrier mechanics come to Canada on a temporary basis to perform repair work for CAD Carrier? - We would recommend reviewing T23 NAFTA professionals if the mechanic has an engineering degree or obtaining a Labour Market Impact Assessment. The impetus would be on the Canadian carrier to prove skills not available in Canada.
2) I assume a work permit would be required, but anticipate that the T11 exemption does not apply – would the C13 exemption be a possibility? Must we look to NAFTA rules? C13 would only really apply if the maintenance was an emergency repair or on out-of-warranty equipment. Admission under this category would only be permitted for a short duration (i.e. less than 30 calendar days). For the mechanics to qualify under NAFTA, they would be required to have pre-arranged employment with the Canadian carrier, as well as be in possession of a Baccalaureate, Licenciatura Degree or state/provincial license.
3) If it is possible, please describe how and what requirements must be met or arrangements must be made. More on how to apply under NAFTA can be found here and information about applying under the C13 exemption can be found here.
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

FW: Validity of Work Permits-Multiple Work Permits -REP-2016-1698-
Please find response below to your question on validity of Post Graduate Work Permit.
Question: If a foreign worker is working on a valid Post Graduate Work Permit and then simultaneously obtains an LMIA based work permit, does the Post Graduate Work Permit remain valid until its expiry. For example, if the foreign worker quits their job, can then remain in Canada and find new employment based on their still valid Post Graduate Work Permit?
Response: Yes, the Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) remains valid until its expiry. The post-graduation work permit is an open work permit. This means that the permit holder can work in any occupation anywhere in Canada, and change employers. Please note that the foreign worker may not work for an employer on the ineligible employers list. (see [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?gnum=512&top=15](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/helpcentre/answer.asp?gnum=512&top=15))

Good afternoon,
Thank you for your query to the Immigration Representatives mailbox. Please see the response to your question below.
QUESTION:
Section 183(5) of the IRPR seems to contemplate this, but it is not clear whether the open work permit portion of the SCLP application will qualify as an application for “an extension of the period authorized for their stay”. Is this meant to cover only VR holders who are applying for another VR, or would an open work permit application be considered to satisfy this section as well?
ANSWER:
A foreign national who submits the IMM 5710 Application to change conditions or extend my stay in Canada – Worker is in effect submitting two applications in one. The foreign national is applying under section 181 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) for an ‘extension of their status' and an application under section 200 for a work permit as they meet the requirement of who can apply from within Canada under R199.
If submitted prior to the expiry of their present status, this combined application has two effects:
1) should a decision not be made on the ‘application' under R181 prior to the expiration of their present status, the foreign national will be allowed to remain by operation of law (implied status) under R183(5), and
2) the application for work permit under R200 allows for the issuance of an open work permit on approval.
Kind regards,
The Immigration Representatives mailbox

FW: When is the ITA requirement needed-REP-2017-2317
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives mailbox. We hope that you will find the answer to your question below of assistance.
Question: Is the individual obligated to decline the ITA, because they did not meet the CRS points at the time of the ITA? OR may the individual continue to submit the eAPR within the 90 day period, once that passage of time means the individual subsequently earns those extra Canadian work experience points?
Answer: When the Comprehensive Ranking System triggers an invitation to apply early, officers will look for evidence that the job is continuing or if the required work experience was obtained before the time of application. The onus remains on the applicant to demonstrate they meet the criteria under which they were invited to apply. A letter of explanation may assist the officer with the assessment of the applicant's work experience.
Please note that our calculation is based on monthly units, and we do not take into account days. When inputting work experience “From and To” dates, the system only asks for month and year for each entry. This results in some applicants being invited “early". That said, the date range is inclusive, meaning the month in the To date will count towards the calculation of full time equivalent units for that particular work experience entry. Example: Using the February 1st date, and assuming the candidate worked for a year (full-time and met relevant definition of work experience), the calculation would be as follows depending on whether To Date is set to January or February:
February 2016 - January 2017 = 12 months full-time equivalent duration February 2016 – February 2017 = 13 months full-time equivalent duration
In situations where the applicant completed or left the employment and the duration of that employment did not meet the criteria under which the candidate was invited to apply the candidate should decline the ITA and re-enter the pool.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Good day,
Based on the information that you provided, we understand that the candidate:
1. Completed their studies prior to coming to Canada to work under the AlESEC program.
2. Works in Canada under an employer-specific work permit, and has done so for at least one year.
3. This position is in a NOC A occupation.
4. The candidate is paid by the employer for the work that they have completed (ie. They are not receiving a stipend)
Based on the information that you have provided, it appears that the candidate would meet the following requirements for Canadian work experience to claim Comprehensive Ranking System Points and meet the qualifications of the Canadian Experience Class:
In order for work experience to be considered Canadian for the purpose of the Canadian Experience Class, a candidates skilled work experience must:
be in a job classified as skill type 0, or skill level A or B according to the 2011 National Occupational Classification, amount to at least one year of full-time (or an equal amount in part-time) in the previous three years, have been acquired with an employer in Canada (self-employment does not count), be an activity for which wages were paid or a commission was earned; be gained with the proper legal authorization (for example, as a documented worker with a valid work permit), and not be gained while studying on a student permit.
Please note that any period of employment during which time the foreign national was engaged in full-time study will not be included in calculating work experience under the Canadian Experience Class (CEC), nor will it count for the purposes of points assigned under the Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS). This includes any Canadian work experience that is gained while a student is on an academic break or a co-op term. If the candidate was engaged in full time study at the time of their work experience, they may be able to claim their work experience under the Federal Skilled Worker Program.
If the candidate has an offer of full-time employment from the employer that is on their work permit, they may be able to receive points for a valid job offer in the Comprehensive Ranking System. See the following link for more information: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/immigrate/skilled/exempt.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/immigrate/skilled/exempt.asp)

Good day,
Question: Once an individual has been issued a Work Permit under an LMiA exemption, if there are any changes to the job (for example, job position, title, salary, benefits, etc.), is there a way to inform of these changes?
Answer:
In the case of an LMiA-exempt work permit, several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer (the employer who submitted the Offer of Employment) by the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) on issuance of a work permit based on an Offer of Employment from that employer.
These conditions include that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works; provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the IRPR.
Employers may be inspected on these conditions and they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not.
Employer conditions: Each work permit is issued based on the offer of employment provided. Once the work permit is issued the employer must meet the conditions in that offer until the end of the work permit. If the employer changes the offer – e.g. for example, job position, title, salary, benefits – then a new offer of employment and a new work permit is required. For each offer there can be only one work permit that triggers the conditions on the employer (and condition on foreign national listed on work permit). If the employment changes and the employer wishes to change the conditions that apply to themselves (employer) then a new offer and a new work permit is required. The old work permit would only apply to the original offer and in the information listed in that offer.
IRCC does not require proactive notification of changes, but it is required that the employer maintain any documentation regarding the changes and provide it as justification at time of inspection. The employer is required to retain all documents related to the foreign worker for up to six years after the date of issuance of the work permit, including details about the title change, to ensure information can be provided to an IRCC officer in the event of an inspection.
Employers who believe that they are not meeting conditions can use the Voluntary Disclosure process.
More information can be found in the Employer Compliance Inspections page on the IRCC website-see the section "Occupation, Wages and Working Conditions:

Question:
A client recently obtained a work permit when he arrived in Canada. He holds an Ethiopian passport and continues to do so. Yet he was recently approved forcitizenship and will be obtaining a passport. He will not be able to be a citizen of both Ethiopia and due to Ethiopian law, and thus will return his Ethiopian passport.
As his work permit was issued under his Ethiopian passport, will the work permit need to be corrected to reflect his new country of citizenship, or is no change to country of citizenship on the WP necessary?. Would this be done via a new application or an application to Amend a temporary residence document (IMM 1436). It in fact turns out that IRCC did not issue the work permit as requested (it restricted to one location, whereas we asked for no location restriction). Could we correct that error and at the same time via said correction change the country of citizenship? Thank you.
Response:
Changes made to personal information after the client entered Canada will not be amended on the work permit (including citizenship). This information needs to match that of the passport. If the information on the client's passport has changed, they should apply for a new temporary resident document (i.e. a new work permit). To do so, they can submit the following form: Application to Change Conditions or Extend Your Stay in Canada (IMM 5710).
Please note that the IMM 1436 is only for changing clerical errors. Corrections will not be made for major changes to the client's employment situation (such as a change of location) unless a clerical error was made. For more information, please refer to Guide 5218.
The “Employer Location" field of the work permit must match the original Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) or the LMIA Exemption application submitted by the employer when the client first applied. If the “Employer Location" field does not match the LMIA/LMIA Exemption application submitted by the employer, than the client must apply for a new work permit (using the new passport).

Hello,
Thank you for your questions. Updated guidance regarding mergers and acquisitions will be available online shortly.
The main consideration for temporary workers who hold employer-specific work permits is whether the new organization can be seen to be a “successor in interest" employer, or, in the case of an acquisition, the same employer. Changes in ownership structure should not require a new LMiA or Offer of employment if the new organization assumes the previous owner's assets and liabilities (including those of the prior owner relating to the hiring and retention of temporary workers
e.g. where a “successor in interest" can be demonstrated). To establish a “successor in interest", the successor entity must demonstrate – in the event of an employer compliance inspection-that it has substantially assumed the interests and obligations, assets and liabilities of the original owner, and continues to operate the same type of business as the original owner. If the take-over organization is a “successor in interest" in that it has substantially assumed the interests and obligations, assets and liabilities of the original organization (wholly or partially), and continues to operate the same type of business as the original organization, then the take-over organization would remain the ‘employer' for the purpose of the existing work permit as well. The temporary worker is not obligated to obtain a new work permit, and will continue to be authorized to work in Canada for the duration of the period stated on the existing work permit, if: ●
the take-over organization meets the requirements that the LMIA-exempt work permit was issued under (e.g.,
qualifying relationship for intra-company transferee) or the take-over organization assumes the LMiA contract,
and
- the worker's employment conditions as per the original offer of employment, for example, the wage, duties, location, have not changed
If the take-over organization does not become a “successor in interest", that is, it does not assume all of the interests/obligations, assets/liabilities of the original organization, then a new LMiA or Offer of employment and new work permits are required for all temporary workers holding employer-specific work permits, and the employee should cease working for the take-over organization until a new work permit have been obtained. The new organization is responsible for ensuring that it only employs a foreign national in a capacity in which the foreign national is authorized under the IRPA to be employed, as per A124(1)(c).
Employers are advised to retain all documentation related to a merger or acquisition for six years. An inspection may be initiated from the first day of employment for which a work permit is issued up to a maximum of six years thereafter.
We hope this information is helpful.

Dear
We have consulted on your questions with our legal and policy experts. Thank you for your patience.
Your questions are highlighted with our responses below.
1) My understanding is that the Ministerial Instructions do not have authority to overrule legal statutes defined in IRPA and IRPR. The Minister has the authority to give expression of interest instructions that are more stringent than the Act or the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (the Regulations). Subsection 10.3(5) of the Act clarifies that instructions governing any matters related to the expression of interest scheme may provide for criteria that are more stringent than the criteria or requirements provided for in or under any other Division of the Act regarding applications for permanent residence.
2) Express Entry as described in the “Ministerial Instructions" is a process and it does not usurp the legal statute under IRPR 76(3) which grants a foreign national (FN) an option to submit an application for permanent residence (PR) to Canada if the FN cannot meet the point requirement under the FSWC but can prove that they can become economically established in Canada.
3) Therefore in my opinion the “Express Entry process” must provide an option to file an application for PR to Canada under IRPR 76(3). In my opinion the Express Entry process has an obligation to provide all options to file a PR application as defined in IRPA and IRPR. An expression of interest is not an application for permanent residence. A foreign national submitting an expression of interest through the Express Entry system is not an applicant for permanent residence. Rather, the purpose of the expression of interest is to allow IRCC to determine whether the candidate may be eligible to apply as a permanent residence. In their expression of interest, the candidate is not asked to provide documentation proving their eligibility, nor are they asked to pay any processing fees.
4) How and when will IRCC revise Express Entry to allow a FN to submit a PR application under IRPR 76(3) “substituted evaluation? How can a FN submit a PR application under IRPR 76(3) “substituted evaluation, until an actual revision is made to Express Entry? To be eligible to be invited to make an application as a member of a class subject to the expression of interest, a foreign national must meet the eligibility criteria that are set out at section 5 of the Ministerial Instructions for the Express Entry Application Management System. The eligibility criteria include meeting the requirements of the Federal Skilled Worker, Federal Skilled Trades, or Canadian Experience Class if the expression of interest were to be considered an application for a permanent resident visa.
Citoyenneté Canada
Substituted evaluation by officers cannot be used to determine whether the foreign national meets the eligibility criteria. Subsection 10.3(3) of the Act provides that the Minister is to use an electronic system to, among other things, carry out any applicable instructions governing any matters related to the expression of interest scheme and to determine whether the foreign national is eligible to be invited to make an application.
For greater certainty, subsection 5(2) of the Ministerial Instructions for the Express Entry Application Management System was recently amended, to clarify to officers the fact that they must not substitute their evaluation to the determination of whether or not the foreign national meets the criteria to be eligible to be invited to make an application.

Your Question: How can an FSWC PR application be filed under IRPR 76(3) since the Express Entry System does not allow for this option under Canadian Immigration law.
Answer: It is not possible to submit an application for permanent residence under any of the immigration programs now managed through Express Entry without being invited to do so as a candidate in the Express Entry pool.
Therefore, only those candidates who meet the eligibility criteria for entry into the Express Entry pool and who receive an Invitation to Apply from IRCC are able to apply through the electronic application for permanent residence (eAPR).
Substituted evaluation for FSW cannot be used to overcome a prospective candidate's failure to meet minimum entry criteria in the creation of an Express Entry profile. An Express Entry profile is not an application. There is no provision for substituted evaluation in the Ministerial Instructions governing the submission of an expression of interest (i.e. Express Entry profile) to immigrate to Canada.
This means that substitution of evaluation under IPRP 76(3) may only be considered in limited circumstances by an officer for applications made under Express Entry (i.e. a change in circumstance after an applicant has been deemed to meet the minimum requirements of the program to which they have been invited to apply and the requirements of section 11.2 of IRPA).

- Are applicants who have engaged in 24 months of full-time work in Canada and part-time studies in Canada on a study permit eligible? The applicant must demonstrate that they have obtained a total of at least 24 months of authorized full-time work experience in Canada within the 48 months before their complete application is received. Full-time work means at least 30 hours of paid work per week. Any periods of employment during which the applicant was engaged in full-time study will not be included when calculating the period of qualifying work experience. There is nothing to restrict an applicant from using work experience that was acquired while they were engaged in part-time studies on a valid study permit. It would be on the applicant to satisfy the officer that they were not engaged in full-time studies at the time the work experience was acquired. Good afternoon Thank you for submitting your query to the Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Please accept our apologies for the late response. Please find the responses to your questions below.
1) A certified translator refers to a member in good standing of a provincial or territorial organization of translators and interpreters in Canada, am I right? Yes, your interpretation here is correct.
2) A certified translation done by a certified translator who also provides a certified copy of the original document does not need a separate "certified true copy" of the original document done by a notary public any more, am I right? Yes, your interpretation is correct here also. For any document not in English or French, if it is translated by a certified translator, then they will also be able to produce a "certified copy” of the original document. In this case, the applicant would no longer be required to get a "certified copy" of the document from one of the 3 options listed in the guide.
3) Since a certified translator is allowed by IRCC to provide a certified copy of the original document, should "a certified translator" or " a member in good standing of a provincial or territorial organization of translators and interpreters in Canada" be added to the list of persons "who can certify copies" in the Guides to be consistent? The reason "certified translators" are not listed in the guide of "who can certify copies?" is because IRCC does not want to direct people to “certified translators" just for the purpose of having a "certified copy” of a document created. However, if they need a document translated in the first place, they can have it translated and create a "certified copy" in the same place from the same person without having to go to a notary public, commissioner of oaths, or commissioner of taking affidavits. The only time they would need to have a translation and "certified copy" generated in two different places is if the translator IS NOT a member in good standing of a provincial or territorial organization of translators and interpreters in Canada. In this case, the translator would do the translation, but they would need to have a "certified copy" made elsewhere from one of the 3 options listed in the guide. In other words, "certified translators" can create "certified copies" of the document they are translating, but cannot be used to certify copies of other documents which is why they are not included on the list of persons "who can certify copies." We hope this addresses your concerns. Sincerely, The Immigration Representatives Mailbox
