Please find below the response to your query.
Question
We have a client who has an employee that came to Canada as an Intra-Company Transferee. In that application, we confirmed that the foreign national would remain an employee of the US company, would remain on the US payroll, and would only travel to Canada intermittently as required to fulfill the conditions of his role. He is having a role change in the US that will no longer require him to come to Canada to work, though he will come periodically to attend meetings. It is a voluntary role reduction, and his salary, etc will be less. However, he will only enter Canada now to attend meetings.
There is no formal method for cancelling a work permit, so we ask if there is any proactive (steps) an employer should make in this situation, or is it something that if/when audited, it is addressed?
Answer
If the foreign national will no longer be an intra-company transferee-which is a job covered under the International Mobility Program that is exempt from the requirement for the employer to obtain a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) - and the job duties are changing and the salary is changing/decreasing, the foreign national may need to apply for a new work permit in order to be authorized to come to Canada. (There is no way to cancel an existing work permit; a new work permit can still be obtained, if necessary.) The employer will need to re-assess whether the new job duties in Canada requires a work permit or not, and if so, whether it requires an LMlA or is LMIA-exempt (which means the employer would need to submit a new Offer of Employment in the Employer Portal).
Authorization to work temporarily in Canada is given [IRPR 200.(1)(c)(ii.1)] based on the work permit application which stated the job the foreign national would be doing (National Occupation Code NOC), the employer, and the work location. A foreign worker does not need a new work permit unless there has been a change to the conditions that affect the worker – i.e. employer, occupation or location. Providing a salary that is different, i.e. lower, than the salary indicated on the Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC, after the work permit was issued would require the foreign national to obtain a new work permit and the employer to submit a new Offer of Employment (if the job has changed and the new job requires a work permit and an Offer of Employment).
It is important that the foreign national hold a work permit that accurately reflects the job that they are doing in Canada; and, that they are actually doing the job for which the work permit authorizes them to do [see Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations [183(1)(b) and 185].
As per 209.2(1) of the IRPR, several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer on issuance of a work permit based on an Offer of Employment from that employer.
and Citizenship Caneda
These conditions include that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province
in which the foreign national works;
provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the
IRPR.
The employer cannot amend benefit information in the Offer of Employment that was submitted to IRCC after the work permit has been issued to the foreign worker.
Proactive notification to IRCC of inconsistencies surrounding working conditions, including salary and benefits, are not required under the International Mobility Program. However, the employer who provided the offer on which the work permit is based is still responsible for ensuring that the wages and benefits are consistent with what was stated in the offer of employment. Employers may be inspected on the conditions listed above and, therefore, they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not. The employer must keep all documents related to any changes from the original Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC.
To clarify, in cases where the job has changed, the foreign worker must receive a new Offer of Employment and work permit prior to implementing the change. A new work permit may be required, and the foreign national will not be authorized to work in Canada in the new duties until a new work permit is obtained. Furthermore, if a random inspection is initiated for the first offer of employment, the inspection will still assess compliance for the entire period of the former work permit. If the employer was inconsistent in providing the foreign worker exactly what was stated in the Offer of Employment, then the employer will have to justify those differences with documentation i.e. how, why and when the job changed, and that a new work permit was obtained for the new job.
If a new work permit for the change in occupation has not been previously approved and the temporary foreign worker is found to be working in an occupation other than what was stated on the Offer of Employment, this may constitute non- compliance by the employer.
Employers who have concerns that they are not meeting conditions of the Offer of Employment can use the Voluntary Disclosure process (see bottom of page After hiring a temporary worker).
Foreign workers are also subject to other federal and provincial or territorial legislative and regulatory requirements. Employers should also meet those requirements for compliance purposes.
We hope that this information is helpful to you and once again please accept our apologies for the delay in responding to your query.
Sincerely,

threads.answer:
Dear
Thank you for your enquiry. Being on a peace bond does not prevent a person from being granted citizenship or from taking the oath of citizenship as long as the person is not subject to any other prohibitions outlined in the section 22 of the Citizenship Act.
Section 22 of the Act outlines situations that may prohibit a person from being granted citizenship or from taking the oath of citizenship. Specifically, Under paragraph 22(1)(a), a person is prohibited while the person is, pursuant to any enactment in force in Canada, i) under a probation order, ii) a paroled inmate, or iii) serving a term of imprisonment. Since a person on a peace bond in not under a probation order, a paroled inmate, or serving a term of imprisonment, a prohibition under 22(1)(a) would not apply. Under Subsection 22(2), a person is prohibited if the person has been convicted of an offence under the Citizenship Act, or an indictable offence under any other Act of Parliament i) during the four-year period immediately before the date of the person's application, or ii)during the processing of the application. Because a peace bond does not result in a conviction, a prohibition under 22(2) would not apply.
We trust the above information is helpful
Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Good day,
In regards to your question, please note that our calculations are based on monthly units, and we do not take into account days. When inputting work experience From and To dates, the system only asks for month and year for each entry. That said, the date range is inclusive, meaning the month in the To date will count towards the calculation of full time equivalent units for that particular work experience entry. Example: Using the February 1st date, and assuming the candidate worked for a year (full-time and met relevant definition of work experience), the calculation would be as follows depending on whether To Date is set to January or February:
February 2016- January 2017= 12 months full-time equivalent duration February 2016-February 2017= 13 months full-time equivalent duration
In some cases, if an EE candidate checks the "This is my current job” box to reflect that this work is "Ongoing". As soon as the clock reaches January 1st 2017, the system will award points for 1 year of work experience by calculating work experience for the month of January. However, while officers will account for a reasonable gap of employment in calculating the period of qualifying work experience in Canada, the onus is on the applicant to demonstrate they meet the minimum requirements of the program as stipulated in R87.1. Please note that each application is considered on its own merits with a final decision based on a review of all the information available to the officer at the time of decision.

This is in response to your enquiry regarding the visitors' ability to apply for a study permit from inside Canada.
Generally, students must apply for a study permit before they come to Canada. Some applicants can apply for a study permit from within Canada.
If the applicant meets the eligibility criteria set in IRPR 215, they may apply for a study permit within Canada. In these cases, they are requested to apply to extend their stay in Canada as a student by submitting the application to Change Conditions or Extend Your Stay in Canada as a Student. In that application, they may indicate that their current country of residence in Canada.
Please note that only the following individuals are eligible to apply for a study permit within Canada:
- a minor child in primary or secondary school
- an exchange or visiting student
- a student who has completed a short-term course or study program, which is a condition for being accepted at a designated learning institution
- someone who holds a temporary resident permit (TRP) valid for at least six months, or their family member
- a spouse or common-law partner (and their family members) being sponsored to immigrate, who are: ? in Canada and ? have applied for permanent residence, if eligible

- a family member or private staff member of a foreign representative who is properly accredited (90 days before or after you are no longer authorized to study without a study permit), or
- a foreign national or their family member with a valid study or work permit, who wants to stay in Canada longer to study.
If the applicant does not meet the above eligibility criteria for application for a study permit inside Canada, they must apply from abroad.

threads.subject: Does flagpoling count as an entry to the United States that would require a new FBI Clearance? - REP-2017- 1465
threads.question:
Good evening,
We understand that for Express Entry police certificates must be issued after the last time the individual was physically in the country.
If an individual with a pending ITA flagpoles (does not enter the U.S. but only approaches the U.S. border official to be immediately turned around) to obtain a new Canadian work permit, does this count as an entry to the United States that would require a new FBI Clearance?
Thanks,
threads.answer:
Sent: Tue. 19 Sep 2017 09:45:48
Good morning,
Thank you for sending us your question.
"Flagpoling" describes the situation where clients residing in Canada have the choice of seeking a service from the Immigration, Refugee Citizenship Canada (IRCC) in Canada or by leaving the country, re-entering and seeking the service from the CBSA at a Point of Entry.
The preferred option for clients residing legally in Canada seeking to be admitted is to make an appointment at a IRCC office, giving them the certainty of a fixed date and time and saving the inconvenience of travelling to a land border port of entry. Appointments can be made through IRCC's Call Centre. The waiting time for an appointment is currently less than three weeks.
It has been IRCC's position that taking away the option to be admitted at a land border POE would have a negative impact on client service by eliminating the option to be admitted at the time and place of the client's choice.
If the applicant is not completing any type of formal process to enter into the US before reentering Canadian soil, it is not a requirement to provide an additional Police Certificate.
That said, as with any case, the officer reviewing the file may require further documentation (beyond what the applicant has submitted) in order to be fully satisfied that the applicant is not criminally inadmissible.

threads.question:
When calculating Proof ofFunds, IRCC requests in the Completeness Check policy guidelines that: "The applicant should provide an official letter(s) from one or more financial institutions that lists all current bank and investment accounts as well as outstanding debts, such as credit card debts and loans." (See: [http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/perm/express/intake-complete.asp](http://www.cic.gc.ca/english/resources/tools/perm/express/intake-complete.asp))
To what extent are outstanding debts such as credit card debt, loans, mortgages etc. assessed against the positive balance in bank and investment accounts for those required to provide Proof of Funds.
In other words, are debts set off against assets such that debts reduce the amount of funds available for settlements. I ask this given the fact that debts such as credit cards, loans, mortgages, etc. are typically on payments plans that would only require a smaller payment on principal each month and not a complete payout of the entire loan when the person immigrates to Canada.
I receive questions on this almost every single day.
Regards,
and Citizenship Canedaot Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for contacting the Immigration Representatives mailbox. We trust that you will find the answer to your question below of assistance.
Question: To what extent are outstanding debts such as credit card debt, loans, mortgages etc. assessed against the positive balance in bank and investment accounts for those required to provide Proof of Funds?
Answer: The officer will use all the documents submitted as proof of funds, including any outstanding debts, to understand the applicant's financial situation as a whole, and whether it would be sufficient to support initial establishment in Canada. Applicants can submit a letter of explanation in order to assist the officer in their assessment.
Ultimately, the onus is on the applicant to demonstrate funds which are transferable, unencumbered by debts or other obligations, and available to them with sufficient liquidity to support them and their family members. Proof in the form of official letters or statements from financial institutions confirming available savings or investment account balances, bank drafts, money orders and similar financial instruments are the clearest evidence of such funds. Applicants are advised to provide as much detail as possible.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Sent: Wed. 20 Sep 2017 13:20:51
Hello,
Question: If an individual is in Canada on an lEC work permit and has received an invitation to apply for a new lEC work permit, do they benefit from implied status in the interim? The lEC work permit application will be submitted online.
Response: As a rule lEC clients cannot benefit from implied status. The program is governed by a series of bilateral
agreements/arrangements with its 33 partner countries which, depending on the agreement/arrangement in place, may
require a citizen to return home before they can apply again, if eligible for a second participation (called a discontinuance requirement), may limit the maximum length of time they can stay in Canada (up to 24 months over two lEC participations, for example), or the type of work permit they may apply for (employer-specific (Young Professionals or International Co-op categories) or an open work permit (Working Holiday category)).
Given that for each lEC participation, candidates need to submit a profile into one or more of lEC's three categories, and if picked from a pool, may be invited to submit a work permit application. As such each participation in lEC is separate from the other. All IEC applications are considered to be an overseas work permit application-even though the application process is completely online and the system does not recognized where in the world the lEC client is applying from. Some lEC participants may be able to apply to change their status from "worker" to "visitor' after they have completed their lEC work experience.
When IEC participants can benefit from implied status is limited to very specific situations that are outlined on IRCC's website and is limited to when either an lEC work permit can be changed or extended.
Thank you,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Hello,
Question It has come to our attention that the salary provided on an offer of employment through the employer portal, which recently led to the issuance of a work permit, was incorrect. The salary indicated in the offer of employment is actually lower by approximately $20,000 than that which the employee is actually being paid. Can you please advise what would be the best way to correct the error? Do we need to submit a new offer of employment and obtain a work permit on the basis of that new offer or is there a way that it can be corrected?
Answer
It is important that the foreign national hold a work permit that accurately reflects the job that they are doing in Canada; and, that they are actually doing the job for which the work permit authorizes them to do [see Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR) 183(1)(b) and 185]. It is also important that the Offer of Employment be filled out completely and accurately before it is submitted to IRCC [IRPR 209.11], that the National Occupation Code (NOC) indicated on the Offer of Employment is the correct one for the job and duties the foreign national will be/is doing.
Providing a salary that is higher salary to the foreign worker than the salary indicated on the Offer of Employment submitted to lRCC after the work permit was issued would not require the foreign national to obtain a new work permit. Typically, a foreign worker does not need a new work permit unless there has been a change to the conditions that affect the worker–
i.e. employer, occupation or location. However, several conditions are imposed automatically on the primary employer by the IRPR on issuance of a work permit based on an offer of employment from that employer. These conditions include that an employer must: be actively engaged in the business in respect of which the offer of employment was made; comply with the federal and provincial laws that regulate employment, and the recruiting of employees, in the province in which the foreign national works; provide the foreign national with employment in the same occupation as that set out in the foreign national's offer of employment and with wages and working conditions that are substantially the same as — but not less favourable than — those set out in that offer; make reasonable efforts to provide a workplace that is free of abuse, within the meaning of paragraph 72.1(7)(a) if the IRPR. The employer cannot amend benefit information in the Offer of Employment that was submitted to IRCC after the work permit has been issued to the foreign worker. Proactive notification to IRCC of inconsistencies surrounding working conditions, including salary and benefits, are not required under the International Mobility Program. However, the employer who provided the offer on which the work permit is based is still responsible for ensuring that the wages and benefits are consistent with what was stated in the offer of employment. Employers may be inspected on the conditions listed above and, therefore, they will have to provide proof at the time of inspection that they met these conditions or provide a justification as to why they did not. The employer must
keep all documents related to any changes from the original Offer of Employment submitted to IRCC.
Employers who have concerns that they are not meeting conditions of the Offer of Employment can use the Voluntary Disclosure process (see bottom of page After hiring a temporary worker).
Typically, any substantial change from the Offer of Employment must be justified as per subsection 203(1.1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR). An officer may find that a change in an employee contract that increases the salary is justified under R203(1.1) in that it is similar to a change in the provisions of a collective agreement. In addition, an increase in wages may result in a finding that the employer did not provide "substantially the same" wages if the increase would have affected the ability of the foreign national to qualify for the LMIA-exemption. Wages under the International Mobility Program must meet the minimum wage requirement in the province of employment as per the condition to meet federal or provincial laws. Wages paid that are higher than those in the offer of employment, it may indicate a change in duties that would mean a different occupation than offered. In cases where the employer has promoted or otherwise changed the foreign worker's duties, the foreign worker must receive a new Offer of Employment and work permit prior to implementing the change. If a new work permit for the promotion or change in occupation has not been previously approved and the temporary foreign worker is found to be working in an occupation other than what was stated on the Offer of Employment, this may constitute non-compliance by the employer. Foreign workers are also subject to other federal (such as ESDC who leads the Temporary Foreign Workers Program) and provincial or territorial legislative and regulatory requirements. Employers should also meet those requirements for compliance purposes.]
We hope this information will be useful to you.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.question:

- 30 (1) For the purposes of paragraph 16(2)(b) of the Act, the following foreign nationals are exempt from the requirement to submit to a medical examination:
(a) foreign nationals other than
(ii) foreign nationals who are seeking to work in Canada in an occupation in which the protection of public health is essential,
(iii) foreign nationals who
▪ (A) are seeking to enter Canada or applying for renewal of their work or study permit or authorization to remain in Canada as a temporary resident for a period in excess of six consecutive months, including an actual or proposed period of absence from Canada of less than 14 days, and
▪ (B) have resided or stayed for a period of six consecutive months, at any time during the one- year period immediately preceding the date that they sought entry or made their application, in an area that the Minister determines, after consultation with the Minister of Health, has a higher incidence of serious communicable disease than Canada,
2) Furthermore, can you please clarify in which situations section 30(2) /RPR would apply? Does section 30(2) IRPR distinguish itself from section 30(1)(a)(iii) /RPR, in that section 30(2) applies to foreign nationals that have been approved abroad to enter Canada but have remained in a designated country for more than 6 months before entering, while section 30(1)(a)(iii) applies to foreign nationals that have solely applied? Is my interpretation correct?
30(2) Every foreign national who has undergone a medical examination as required under paragraph 16(2)(b) of the Act must submit to a new medical examination before entering Canada if, after being authorized to enter and remain in Canada, they have resided or stayed for a total period in excess of six months in an area that the Minister determines, after consultation with the Minister of Health, has a higher incidence of serious communicable disease than Canada.
Your clarification on this important matter would be very appreciated.
With kind regards,
threads.answer:
Hello,
Thank you for your questions concerning medical requirements. Please be advised that the department is undertaking efforts to update the Program Delivery Instructions related to this topic.
For ease of reference, we will refer to an area that the Minister determines, after consultation with the Minister of Health,
has a higher incidence of serious communicable disease than Canada as ‘an area’.
In your first paragraph, you ask if a foreign national who is applying to extend their work permit in order to continue to work in an occupation in which the protection of public health is essential would be required to do a new medical exam each time they renew their work permit in order to work in such an occupation despite the fact they have never left Canada.
In response, yes, they would be required to do a new medical exam upon renewing their work permit, as per subparagraph 30(1)(a)(ii) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR).
Question: Does section 30(1)(a)(ii) IRPR apply solely to the first application for the work permit or does it apply to all work permit applications regardless of whether or not it is a first application, an extension or a change of status (i.e study permit to
work permit) notwithstanding the fact that the foreign national has never left Canada?
Response: It has been determined by the Department that the phrase For the purposes of paragraph 16(2)(b) of the Act used in subparagraph R30(1)(a)(ii) applies to any type of application –whether an initial application or renewal, for a work permit or study permit.
As well, a temporary resident would have to meet the requirements of section 199 of the IRPR to make an application from inside Canada.
Question 2: Furthermore, can you please clarify in which situations section 30(2) /RPR would apply? Does section 30(2) /RPR distinguish itself from section 30(1)(a)(iii) /RPR, in that section 30(2) applies to foreign nationals that have been approved abroad to enter Canada but have remained in a designated country for more than 6 months before entering, while section 30(1)(a)(iii) applies to foreign nationals that have solely applied? Is my interpretation correct?
Response: Yes, the two subsections are separate. Example scenarios of how the two parts of the IRPR differ are provided below.
Subsection 30(2) applies to someone who may have been in the following scenario: has completed a medical exam; come to Canada; left Canada; stayed more than six months in ‘an area’; and is now applying again to enter Canada.
Subparagraph R30(1)(a)(ii) refers to someone who may have been in the following scenario:
- has applied to enter Canada, or to renew their work or study permit, for more than six consecutive months;
- can include an absence of less than 14 days in that six month stay; and in the 12 months preceding the date of application, has resided or stayed more than six consecutive months in 'an area'.
We trust this information will be of assistance.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Lock-in age Vs. Actual age-REP-2017-0441
threads.question:
and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada
Hi Officer
Scenario:
The age of step-child of principal applicant under the BC PNP is under 19 years of age when nominated; the child turned 19 before the BC PNP nominee submitted the APR.
According to R25.1(4), the lock-in date for the age of a child of an applicant under the PNP is the date on which the province receives a complete application for provincial nomination from the principal applicant.
In this situation, could the Provincial Nominee elected NOT to include the step-child in his APR as the child already past 19 and is not willing to immigrate?
Regards
and Citizenship Caneda
threads.answer:
Good day,
Thank you for your question.
If the child is 'locked in' at the stage of the Provincial Nominee Program nomination at the age of 18, and if the child is not married / not in a common-law relationship the child meets the definition of a dependent child and must be declared on the IMM 008.
Applicants are required to declare all family members, whether accompanying or not. Failure to declare all their family members on their application could result in enforcement action and the non-declared family members would not be able to be sponsored in the future. In addition, all family members, whether accompanying or not, must be examined, unless the appropriate officer determines that they are not required by the Act or the former Act to examine the family member [R117(10)]. Family members who were not declared and examined are excluded from the family class and may not be sponsored at a later date as per R117(9)(d) unless R117(10) applies.
Non-accompanying family members must undergo medical examinations. They must also establish that they are not
inadmissible for criminal or security reasons.
Non-accompanying family members need not be in possession of a passport or travel document.
Also, note that there has been a change to the definition of dependent child in the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations on October 24, 2017. In the meantime, please see these links for more information.

threads.subject: Citizenship Minor application subsection 5(1) clarification needed pls-REP-2017-1906
threads.question:
Dear Sir/Madam,
Can a minor (under 14 yrs old) apply along with his adult siblings? Parents are PR holders but not yet meet the residency obligations.
In this case which application should be filled in? I think Minor application under subsection 5(2) is not applicable here because the parent is not applying with the minor child, right?
IfI used the minor application under subsection 5(1), I am not quite sure if this is applicable in terms of word "custody". If you advise using this application can we submit consent letters from parents for their son to be granted the Canadian citizenship along marriage certificate and birth certificate?
Kindly guide me with the right application and documentation requested to support a minor application.
All the best,
threads.answer:
Good day,
In the situation described below, the minor would have to submit the Application for Canadian Citizenship: Minors-Subsection 5(1) and meet the requirements outlined in the instruction guide. Note: One of the requirements that a minor applying under 5(1) has to meet is residency which includes the physical presence requirement.
A parent is authorized to apply on their child's behalf presuming there are no custody issues. A birth certificate showing parentage, marriage certificate of the parents and letters of consent are sufficient evidence to support a parent submitting this application on behalf of a minor.
You are correct in that the minor could not apply under subsection 5(2) unless one of the parents is already a Canadian citizen or they apply concurrently with the parent(s).
If the minor wishes to apply with his/her adult siblings, all of the applications should be sent together in one envelope.
Thank you. Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.subject: Can an application for grant of citizenship be made WHILE the applicant is residing outside of Canada-REP-
threads.question:
Dear Officer,
With the coming into force of the changes to the Citizenship Act, there is a surge of potential citizenship applicants and the
following question has come up:
Can a permanent resident who has accumulated 1095 days of physical presence and meets the tax filing requirements of the act submit an application for grant under 5(1) or the Act if they are residing outside of Canada at the time of making the application. I do not see why not, however form CIT0002, Application for Canadian Citizenship for Adults at page 2, No.7 does not allow the possibility to include a residential address out of Canada.
Thank you in advance for your guidance on this issue.
Citoyenneté Canada
threads.answer:
Good morning,
Thank you for your question. Subsection 2(1) of the Citizenship Regulations No. 2 states that an application made under subsection 5(1) of the Act must be made in the prescribed form and filed in the manner determined by the Minister. There is no specification that the application must be made in Canada.
The country of your current address can be noted in the province line of the home address section -if there is not enough space, the country can be hand-written in. The application must be mailed to the Case Processing Centre in Sydney, N.S (CPC-
S) as instructed in the application guide. The applicant must advise where they will be staying in Canada so that the CPC-S can determine to which local office the file should be referred for continued processing. If the applicant has no Canadian address, they should provide their email address along with the foreign address and, if applicable, the contact information of their representative. The local office will either communicate via email or send correspondence to the foreign address or correspond with the representative, as applicable. If the applicant is between 18-54 on the date they sign their application, they will have to meet knowledge and language requirements which must be done in Canada. As per the program delivery instructions on the Oath of Citizenship, persons who are granted Canadian citizenship under subsection 5(1) of the Citizenship Act are required to take the Oath of Citizenship at a citizenship ceremony in Canada.
Sincerely,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

threads.answer:
Hi,
Thank you for bringing this to our attention. We will update the guide for the adult citizenship application as soon as possible.
There have been no recent changes to the date of birth procedures. They are as follows: Date of birth correction
The date of birth on your citizenship certificate will be the same as the one shown on your immigration document unless you:
- have corrected your date of birth on your immigration document or
- have legally changed it after arriving in Canada or
- are requesting a different date of birth for your citizenship certificate and you can provide supporting documents.
If your date of birth has been corrected on your immigration document then you must provide a copy of
- an approved Request to Amend Immigration Record of Landing (IMM 1000) or Confirmation of Permanent Residence (IMM 5292 or IMM 5688), and
- your new corrected Permanent Resident Card (if you have one).
If you have legally changed your date of birth by a provincial/territorial court order then you must provide a copy of
- provincial/territorial court order changing your date of birth and
- completed questionnaire Request to Correct a Date of Birth for Citizenship (CIT 0464)
If you did not change your date of birth by a provincial/territorial court order and your date of birth has not been corrected on your immigration document then you must provide a copy of
- a refused Reguest to Amend the Immigration Record of Landing (IMM 1000) or Confirmation of Permanent Residence (IMM5292 or IMM 5688) and
- completed questionnaire Request to Correct a Date of Birth for Citizenship (CIT 0464) and
- documents to support your new date of birth.
Á Important information: If satisfactory documentation is not provided with the application to support the date of birth requested, the citizenship certificate will reflect the date of birth indicated on your immigration document. If you do not have a provincial/territorial court order changing your date of birth, you must first request an amendment to your immigration document before requesting a different date of birth on your citizenship certificate.

Question:
Is it possible for the Foreign National to start working for the second employer after expiry of the Open Work Permit while on implied status?

month period OR_15 days once every 6 months (but not both).
Applicants can only benefit from these short-term exemptions if the necessary amount of time has elapsed since their last short-term exemption was granted. Consecutive uses are not permitted.
- Example: If a foreign national entered Canada under the 15-day work permit exemption and is required to work in Canada for another 15 days, they will not be eligible to renew their stay as a temporary worker. Six months must pass before foreign nationals are eligible to use the 15 day exemption again.
The following scenarios provide guidance as to when foreign nationals can benefit from short-term work permit exemptions
if they have already used another short-term exemption:
1. If foreign nationals benefited from the 15-day exemption, when may they be granted from the same exemption again? They may be granted a subsequent exemption if they have not been granted a short-
term work permit exemption in the last 6 months.
2. If foreign nationals benefited from the 15-day exemption, when may a foreign national be granted a 30-day exemption or 120-day exemption? They may be granted a 30-day or 120-day exemption once 12 months have elapsed since the date they were
granted the 15-day exemption.
3. If foreign nationals benefited from the 30-day exemption, when may they be granted the same exemption again? They may be granted a 30-day exemption again if they have not been granted a short-
term work permit exemption in the last 12 months.
4. If foreign nationals benefited from the 30-day exemption, when may they be granted a 15-day exemption or 120-day exemption? They may be granted a 15-day exemption once six months have elapsed since the 30- day exemption was granted. They may be granted a 120-day exemption once 12 months have elapsed since the 30-day exemption was granted.

threads.question:
Dear Sirs,
I am a newbie Immigrant Consultant and need your urgent advice on a situation over which I am rather confused and would appreciate your clarification on the following scenario.
A visa-exempt FN (Singapore) has successfully applied for a Study Permit and is now pursuing his education at a DLI in Calgary. It is clearly stated on his Study Permit "***THIS DOES NOT AUTHORIZE RE-ENTRY/CECI
N'AUTORISE PAS LA RE-ENTREE***
How do I interpret this statement? He is from a visa-exempt country so technically he is allowed to enter and leave Canada (with eTA) at will. Yet his Study Permit does not permit re-entry. Does this mean that his Study Permit will become invalid once he
leaves Canada before its expiration and he loses his status as a student?
I would very much appreciate your good advice which is urgently needed.
With kind regards,
Yours sincerely,
ICCRC
and Citizenship Caneda
Zare.Atabak
threads.answer:
Hello
This is in response to you enquiry regarding PGWPP eligibility for applicants who take breaks in their studies.
In response to your first scenario, if the applicant took a semester off (that was not a scheduled break) while completing a program of study, that would constitute a break in the continuity of their studies and would disqualify them from PGWPP. If the student graduated from one program of study, and then started another program of study 4 months later, that break between the two programs would not disqualify them from PGWPP.
In response to your second scenario, the continuity of the studies is assessed based on the letter of completion issued by the designated learning institution which specifies the period when the studies began and were finished. If the DLI considered that the student began their studies in January and they have continuously studied full time since, then the applicant will be considered as continuously studied in Canada. If the written notification from the educational institution indicated that they commenced their program of study in September, but they took that semester off, that would constitute a break in the continuity of their studies and would disqualify them from PGWPP.
Lastly, please note that in the case that the student has arrived to Canada in September but postponed their studies until January, they are advised to change their status to visitor if they decide to remain in Canada until January, or leave Canada and return in January when their studies begin. Please note that if the applicant is in Canada on their study permit, but they are not actively pursuing their program of study, they will be breaking the conditions of their study permit, as per R220 which specify:
The holder of a study permit in Canada is subject to the following conditions:
(a) they shall enroll at a designated learning institution and remain enrolled at a designated learning institution until they complete their studies; and
(b) they shall actively pursue their course or program of study I hope that this information is helpful to you. If you have any further enquiries, you may contact us at Regards,
The Immigration Representatives Mailbox

Hello,
Thank you for your email to the Immigration Representatives Mailbox. Please find below the answer to your questions:
Question 1: Does someone with a Provincial Nomination as a skilled worker (NOC A) need to include proof of language proficiency. The document checklist is unclear.
For applicants applying through the paper based process, there are some Provincial Nominee streams (mainly high skilled NOC O, A or B) which may not have a language requirement. Question 2: Does someone with a Provincial Nomination as a skilled worker (NOC A) need to include proof of funds, for the

Within their application for permanent residence, applicants must complete the Schedule 4 application form and indicate the amount of unencumbered transferable and available funds they have in Canadian dollars. However, an officer must be satisfied that the applicant has the ability to economically establish in Canada as per the requirements found in R87. A foreign national may be deemed inadmissible for financial reasons if they are or will be unable or unwilling to support themselves or any other person who is dependent on them, and have not satisfied an officer that adequate arrangements for care and support, other than those that involve social assistance, have been made. When assessing an applicant's ability to economically establish, an officer will consider all the elements presented within the application, including but not limited to the current job/job offer, language abilities, work experience, education and funds. Thus, all study permit holders must actively pursue their course or program of study while they are in Canada. A stress leave will constitute a long term break from studies and will not be considered as compliant with their study permit conditions. If they would like to remain in Canada during their school stress leave, they will have to apply to change their status (i.e., change to a visitor status, or worker status) or leave Canada and return to complete their program. After changing their status to visitor or worker, students may resume their studies using their previous study permit as long as the study permit is still valid.

threads.answer:
Ms. Acres-Lans,
Thank you for your question.
As per R2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations (IRPR), a dependent child, in respect of a parent, means a child who:
is the biological child of the parent, if the child has not been adopted by a person other than the spouse or common- law partner of the parent, or is the adopted child of the parent
Note that adoptions include adoptions completed abroad and intentions to adopt in Canada, and sponsors must state which situation applies and whether the child is: 1) already adopted, 2) to be adopted abroad or 3) to be adopted in Canada.
However, there is no provision under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act or the IRPR that allow for a child to accompany foster parents to Canada.
